"DID you ever see the prisoner at the bar?" "Oh, yes; that's where I got acquainted with him." A PROVERB says, "Hunger is the best cook." That may be so, but hunger hasn't got anything to cook. _ _

•A BEATITUDE is not very happy when the bee attitude happens to, be on your hand, with the sting ready for business. A THUNDERSTORM made Beranger a poet, a mother's kiss made West a painter, and a penny a- line makes a journalist. IF there is any good in a man it is bound to come out; but it should not come out all at once and leave the man empty. _ _ _ _ _

_ . ArrEn a man has a two-storey brick house picked up and thrown after him by a cyclone, he never again speaks of "trifles light as air." . TEACHER—" Correct the sentence, The liquor which the man bought was drunk.' " Smart Boy —" The man which bought the liquor was drunk.' THEY were having a snarl, and she asked him if there was anything in the past he would like to recall. He heartlessly answered, "Yes, the day you first refused me.' HANDSOME FLIRT (to Bashful)—" What would yon do if a pretty girl came to you suddenly and kissed you ?" Bashful (blushing to the roots of his hair)—" I—l—should be—very much obliged to • her.
THIC advertiser, no matter how small his favours, is like the brave general. He considers his place to be at the head of the column.
"A GENUINE patriot," said an election orator recently, "must at all times be ready to die for his country, even though it should cost him his life 1 "
A NICELY sharpened lead pencil is the only thing in creation that defies the law of gravita- tion. The lighter end always strikes the floor first.

IT is said that great talkers are not as liable to insanity as silent people. Naturally enough those who have to listen are the ones who go crazy. "WHAT are the wild waves saying 2" asked a flip young man of .a sharp girl. "They are saying they are glad they are not fresh," she answered, sweet and low.
THE difference between a long and short yarn is very well illustrated by the difference of one's feel- ings in holding a skein for one's grandmother or for one's sweetheart.

NAVAL EXAMINER: "Now, sir, I will examine you for colour-blindness. What colour is this light?" "How the deuce can I tell unless you take that red globe off it ? " THIMBLES are now lined with india-rubber. They are very nice for mothers when they thump the heads of their offsprings. The concussion does not hurt the mother's fingers.

"WHAT is Smith doing now 7 " "He is travelling with a show." "Pretty hard work, isn't it?" "No, he has nothing to do except to stick his head in the big lion's mouth twice a day. "MA, did you read in the paper about Vaccinat- ing Bees' in Maine 7" asked Mildred. "Why, no, my dear," replied the old lady. "I did not know that bees ever took the small-pox." How do you tell a fool when you see one, Mrs. Jones ? " asked a wearisome old bachelor of a lively young widow. "I usually tell one. to leave," she replied, and the bachelor didn't ask for a diagram. • "WHERE was Bishop Latimer burned to death r ,asked a teacher in a commanding voice. "Joshua knows," said a little girl at the bottom of class "Well," said the teacher, "if Joshua knows, he may tell." "In the fire," replied Joshua, looking very grave and wise. Hinsitonous friend to sentimental youth who writes verses—" That poem of yours, old boy, I saw myself in a dreary waste,' is splendid, Just needs one word to complete it 1" Sentimental youth —"What is it? I shall be glad of any suggestion.' Humorous friend—" Basket.'

HA.RD-UP GENT—" Say, boss, can't yer give a feller a few cents to help him along I" Mr. Delaw- ney—" Why don't you do something faw yaw own living? You had better ask for bwains instead of money." Hard-up Gent—" Well, boss, I asked yer for what I thought yer had the most of." "THE " mower " is taking the place of the dude. It is a man—generally young—who swings his cane like a scythe as he walks the crowded pave. He has one advantage over the dude—a man has a better excuse for kicking him.

SOME one has estimated that the time thrown ~away in this world in courting the girl you want to marry, and who is ready to marry you, would build all the railroads and bridges and tunnels and factories and public buildings. ONE of the stockholders in a brewing company asked the chairman, "Don't you think the advance In hops will tlrtVo some effed on yolli stock?" 'Humbug! The amount of hops we put in our 'beer in* - • ffprit. the siiango stock.".

are out of work and your family are starving; iiud yet I understand that you have four dogs about the house." Uuncle 'Rastus—" Yes, sah ; but I wudden't arsk my family to eat dogs, you' honah 1" A SIMPLE and affecting advcrtisment is the following, translated verbatim from a tomb at Montmartre, near Pails :—" To the memory of M. Jobart, a most excellent husband and father. His Inconsolable widow still continues to carry on the grocery business in the Rue St. Denis, No. 242, near the Caf6 Chinois." A MAN, having been capitally convicted at the Old Bailey, was, as usual, asked what he had to say why judgment of death should not pass against him. " Say ?" replied he, "why, I think the joke has been carried far enough already, and the less that is said about it the better; so, if you please, my Lord, we'll drop the subject." SOME purists object to the use of the word _ _ _ _

render,"-as often applied to the delivery of a song by an artin on the stage; but we are inclined to think such use legitimate, inasmuch as we find in the dictionary a secondary meaning to be "to 'TEACHER—" What are the names of the seven days of the week ?" Boy—" Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday." Teacher —" That's only six days, You hive missed one. When does your mita' go + chr Boy— " When pa buys her a new hat." LITTLE FRITZ, hearing his parents speak of Beethoven, asked—" Mamma, who is Beethoven ?" "A composer," replied his mother. "And what is a composer?" "A man who makes music." The next morning an organ-grinder struck up a • tune in the street, "Mamma," exclaimed Fritz, • eagerly, "there is Beethoven." "I SAW you again with young Smith last even- ing, Miss Smart. It begins to look serious." "Oh, not at all. I really don't care anything for him any more than for anybody else; but then it is such a convenience to have him with me when one wants to stop an omnibus or a cab. lie ,eftn whistle in his fingers so admirably, you know.' "WE don't sell spirits," said a law-evading -

beerseller. "We will give you a glass, and then if you want a biscuit we'll sell it to you for three- pence." The "good creature" was handed down a stiff glass and swallowed it, and the landlord handed his customer a biscuit. "Well, no, I think not," said the customer; "you sell 'em too dear. I can get lots of 'em five or six for a penny elsewhere."

"WHO is that old duffer ?" asked a new gro • man of a milkman, as a well-dressed man Ncrencry- teby "Well, he's one of our most trusted citizens," wat; tLI eloquent reply. "How do you make that out. -Oen owing me ever since I came here." 11„ at're ju.st how we make it out, laughed the milkman gleefully, and the groceryman scratched . his head till..!lo caught en. youniyuL posher, speaking to a lady who is , playing, Can you explain why it is that senti- ments! music alway makes me think of you ?" Young lady—" No, am sure I cannot. But it seems to affect me in the s-...9.me way with respect to yourself, for I never hear a sostamental air but it "always reminds me of you." Masher, with one of his killing smiles—" Indeed 1 And what can there possibly be in sentimental music to cause you to think of me ?" Young lady—" I don't know, unless It is because it is always soft." "CAN you tell me, asked a pundit, "why a conundrum that nobody can guess is like the ghost?" "Shall I tell you now or next month ?" "Now, if you please." "Well, sir, sooner or lator, everybody must give it up."

A It is understood that the Government have de- cided to summOn Parliament at an unusually early period next year. The middle of January is be- lieved to be the date already fixed for th?, pur- pose.

Lord Rosebery has almost regained his usual health. He paid a flying visit. to Waterloo last week during his stay at the Bellevue, and has since gone to Marienbad, where he will remain for some time before returning to England.

A "youthful noble" (as Lord Beaconsfield would have described him), whose racing transactions during his brief career on the turf have not been remarkable for their shrewdness, is said to have lost about .£22,000 at Epsom and at Ascot.

Apropos to the speculations as to the date of the next election, I learn that the Grand Council of the Primrose League has informed the local habitations that the contest will in all probability be fought upon the register which will be made up in July and August next.

The bells of Windsor were rung, and the Corpora- tion banner was displayed upon the Guildhall on Saturday, which was the fifty-fourth anniversary of the Queen's accession. Flags were hoisted upon some of the public buildings and the residences of the Royal -tradesmen in the metropolis. Her Majesty succeeded to the throne on June 20, 1837.

Sir William and Lady Gordon Cumming have been visiting all the tenants and cottagers on the Altyre and Gordonstoun estates during the last week, and have been everywhere received with the 1 utmost Cordiality. They will leave Altyre shortly with Lady Middleton (who is still with them) for Applecross House, Ross-shire, on a visit to Lord Middleton, who has arrived there for the summer.

-- To-day (Saturday) Sir George Biddell Airy, the doyen of British men of science, completes his nine- tieth year, having been born at Alnwick on June 27, 1801. Sir George is, lam happy to hear, in the I enjoyment of excellent health,. and takes the keen- est interest in all matters connected with the astro- nomical and mathematical sciences to which he has devoted his life, and especially in the Observatory at Greenwich, over which he presided for nearly half a century

When the office of President of the Board of Agriculture was established an undertaking was given that no additional charge upon the public should be created, the salary pertainingto the sine- cure office of Chancellor of the Duchy being trans- ferred to the new minister. This arrangement has , not been carried out, a sum of .£2,000 Appearing in the Estimates as the salary of Mr. ClTaplin. Mr. Labouchere intends to move the reduction of the vote by this amount.

The following are the terms of the" instruction" which Mr. Henry Fowler will move on Monday next on the motion to go into Committee on the Education Bill :—" That it be an instruction that the Committee have power to make provision in the case of districts where there exists no school under public control for the introduction of the principle of local representation in the supervision of schools receiving the fee grants." The discussion on this instruction is expected to occupy at least two nights.

There seems to be little doubt as to who will win the election at Carlow. Mr. Parnell is not ready with his 'candidate, and the anti-Parnellites have got their man, a local man, who is personally popu- lar and will have strong support. The great per- sonal influence of the O'Gorman Mahn, who wanted to fight Mr. Parnell originally, will be used against the advocate of "independence." Mr. Par- nell, however, is bound to fight, but as yet he has not come across a constituency in which his success is absolutely assured.

I hear that all the . Evangelical Nonconforming bodies are accepting an invitation to send each two representative members to the International Coun- cil of Congregationalists. Dr. Mackennal has been apprised by the President of the Wesleyan Metho- dist Conference that the Rev. W. 'U. Davison, M.A., Professor in Biblical Literature and Exegesis, and the Rev. J. Agar Beet, D.D., Professor in Theology, at Richmond College, will represent that body. The appointment of such men will be hailed with pleasure by the members of both denominations.

A chance mention in Monday's papers reveals the fact that the third daughter of the Duke of Edin- burgh, Princess Alexandra Louise Olga Victoria, is known in the family circle as "Sandra." No com- plete list of such pet names has been compiled, but it is interesting to know that that of the Princess of yfliqe j 4 " Alix," of Princess Henry of Battenberg " firix,'i of rititeetzg I.7lrttorict of Teck is "May," apd, as all the world knows, or the Duke. of clar- ence is "Eddie," from which last fact it is conje& tured that his father wishes to reign as Edward VII. and he as Edward VIII.

The Norwegian Government are about to try an experiment of an educational character which will be watched with a great deal of interest. They have decided to send to England a large number of engineers who do not hold state appointments to study the peculiarities of English engineering work. For this purpose they have voted 'a large sum of money. 'Among the persons selected by the Govern- ment are those engaged in milling, telephony, the stone industry,and paper manufacture. After these return they will have to present the Government with full reports of their work.

Doctor Commins and Mr. Dickson crossed over to Dublin on Saturday night, in charge of the remains of the late O'Gorman Mahon, whose 'funeral cortege started from the North-wall, Dublin, on Sunday morning, en route for Glasnevin Cemetery, where he was buried near his great rival, Daniel O'Connell, for whom he made way at the famous Clare elec- tion, expecting that O'Connell, who could have gained a seat almost anywhere in Ireland, would make way for him at the general election. He was mistaken, however and hence the coolness between them. The O'Gorman Mahon was really in his ninety-third year.

The t art o Clonmell, who died on Monday, was formerly an officer in the Ist Life Guards, and a chosen friend and companion of the Prince of Wales in earlier and mote volatile days. Before he suc- ceeded to his father's title, he was known as Lord Earlsfort, and the nick name of " Early " stuck to him to the last. He was gay, good-natured, and popular, and in his prime one of the most con- spicuous " men,of the town." He never 'married, and is succeeded in his title by his brother. The estate consists of some 27.000 acres in the South of Ireland—no longer as valuable a patrimony as in the good old days when Sir John Scott, Chief Jus- tice of the King's Bench in Ireland, was raised to the peerage and promoted to the earldom of Clon- melt as an inducement to vote, for the Union.

It is sad to learn that the frosts of last winter I have played havoc with the kingfisher. Mirth Oxfordshire, with its numerous high-banked streams, is a famous resort of this beautiful bird, but Mr. Aplin, a well-known ornithologist resident in that part, tells us that he has not seen a single one since the last severe frost. A similar disappear- was noted after the three cold winters terminating in the snowstorm and frost early in 1881. The dis- appearance of the nightingales is not so easily ac- counted for. In venous parts of England they have been notably growing scarcer from year to year. The wrvneck, once common about Oxford, has also become a rarity, for reasons that puzzle the best authorities. Mr. Aplin, however, does not agree with those who charge these things to the account of the "loafing gunner," and he is inclined to think that the Wild Birds Preservation Acts have done good. The goldfinch, which only a dozen years ago was quite a scarce bird in his locality, is now to be heard twittering all about in the gardens and orchards. In like manner the green woodpecker is reported to be increasing in numbers, and the redstart and whinchat, which before this legislative protection were rarely seen, are now stated to be quite 'common.

_ Sheffield suffered so greatly from the influenza epidemic that we are not surprised that the matter was referred to at the last meeting of the Town Council. We take the following from the Sheffield Independent of June llth

Mr. J. R. LOCKWOOD had given Hotice of a question whether a resolution was proposed at the meeting of the Health Committee to petition the Local Government Board to make enquiries as to the origin, extent, and prevention of influenza ; if so, why it was thrown out, and what action the Health Committee had taken to ascertain the cause and prevent a recurrence of the disease.

Councillor -ARTEII7R JACKSON, M.D., F.R.C.S. : May I ask a question—whether the Chairman of the Health Committee has had any experience as to Warner's Safe' Cure in the treatment of malarial diseases, whether he intends to take any steps to get the shareholders in Warner's Safe 'Cure Co. to divulge the secret which would be of such benefit to the country and the world? The DepuTy MAYOR: The Chairman of the Health Committee will reply. Aid. CLEGG said as far as Mr. Jackson's question was concerned, he had had no experience of Warner's "Safe" Cure. He did not know that he had ever seen the medicine; perhaps Mr. Jackson, as a medical man, knew something about it. Mr. JACKSON: Thero is a bottle. (Produces one). It is to be regretted that this important question was not followed up. The Sheffield Town Council did not know how near they were to the solution of a "secret which would be of such benefit to the country and the world." In the correspondence column of the " Rutland, o_undle, and Stamford Post "'of the sth inst, we notice the following:— To the Editor,—" Perhaps it is not generally known that Warner's Safe' Cure is the best tonic anyone can take in cage of weakness, but such is the experience of one who has tried it. If you think this worth publicity, kindly note in your next issue, and perhaps it will be a boon to some of the suffers from influenza, that is, if they will try it. I give yougg4mame and address, but not for pubiication. T. E. S." ""11' And the Editor says: "I gladly insert it because both myself and my family have taken it for a long time and highly appreciate it, the medicine having done us all good."

"Wild Beasts and their Ways," is the title of one of the most notable books of the year, and is pub- lished by Messrs. Macmillan and Co. It is from the pen of Sir Samuel W. Baker, F.R.S., &c., and gives his reminiscences of Europe, Asia, Africa and America. it is dedicated to His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, who as a great traveller and true sportsman, has ever taken a keen interest in the study of natural history, and by his own ex- ample has given an impulse to those manly pursuits which are characteristic of the British people." Sir Samuel Baker, as the world well knows, is one of the greatest sportsmen and travellers of the age, and it is therefore a matter of course to expect that any work giving his experiences in detail will not only be of interest to the general reader, but also of great value to the average sportsman. "Wild Beasts and their Ways" is all that could be antici- pated of it, and we may say more, for it seems al- most incredible that a single individual could have had so many adventures with dangerous animals of all kinds—and still live to tell the tale. There is no suggestion of personal obtrusion or vain- glory in the manner in which these experiences are related, and yet the plain narrative is sometimes so exciting as to become absolutely thrilling in its interest. Sir Samuel commences with a chapter on "The rifle of the past half century." This, although not of special interest to the ordinary reader, is of the utmost importance to sportsmen, and they will do well to carefully consider what he has to say, and, in the main, take his advice He gives a num- ber of instances in which animals have been enraged, and therefore made all the more dangerous, through the use of a rifle which was unfit for its work, in that it did not kill or maim at the first shot. He describes what improvements have been ef- fected, and also the different rifles which are suited to different kinds of game. He then proceeds to give his experience of the hunting and killing of various animals all over the world, beginning with the elephant, and passing on to the tiger, leopard, lion, bear, hippopotamus, zhinoceros, boar, hyena, antelope, deer, wapita, sambur, and spotted deer. The work is illustrated by Mr. H. Dixon, and there are no fewer than 29 full-page plates, all of them executed in a masterly style. The volume is one cf nearly 500 pages. It is well printed and well bound, and publislled at 12s. 6d. We shall take , occasion as opportunity serves to lay before our readers, by way of extracts, some of the startling stories which the author has to tell.

In the current issue of the Camelot series, published by Mr. Walter Scott, we have " Master Humphrey's Clock," and other early stories and sketches, by Charles Dickens. The volume is edited by Frank T. Marzials, whose introduction is pleasantly written, and supplies a considerable amount of interesting information. As to "Master Humphrey's Clock" and the otherstories which are here published, they have, he says, been" chosen as representing the best of Dickens's least known early works," and those who read this volume gill be ready to confess that Mr. hlarzials has made an admirable selection. The contents include, in addition to 'Master Humphrey's Clock," "Sketches of young couples," " The public life of Mr. Tulrumble, once Mayor of Mudfog," and " The Lamplig,thter's story. "The Westminster Review "for June opens with a paper by Constance Eaglestone, on Prince Napoleon. It is written in a thoughtful and interesting style, and gives a more satisfactory portrait of the late Prince than we have previously seen. "Canada and the Canadian Question" is an admirable review of the work on the subject by Mr.Goldwin Smith. "The story of University Tests" follows, by Mr. Steadman Aldis. Theodore Stanton deals with "Abraham Lincoln," and Ernest Bowen Rowlands gives us" A glance at the history of gambling," which is exceedingly opportune, and upon which we had occasion to comment in our last issue. Other papers are " Pratical Morality," " Memoirs of the Prince de Talleyrand," " Is the Irish problem insoluble ?" followed by the customary articles on science, philoso- phy, politics, history, biography, and the belles lefties. The leading illustrated paper in the " Century" for June, is on "Colonel Win Byrd, of IVestover." There is a fine portrait of the late General Sherman, along with his last speech. and some appropriate verse to his memory, by R.W. Gilder. "Play and work in the Alps" is strikingly illustrated, and the same remark applies to "A miner's Sunday in Colomo." Lady readers will turn with special interest to the paper on "Women at an Eng- lish University" with its illustrations of Clough Hall and Sedgwick Hall, and portraits of Miss L. A. Clough and Miss Gladstone. There is the usual supply of serial and complete stories, Open letters, and bric-a-brac.

The frontispiece for " Scribner's Magazine '5 is a por- trait of Moliere, after a painting by eoypel. There is an article on Moliere, by Mr, Andrew Lang, which we can highly commend for its interest, nicety of criticism, and fairness of statement. F.Sarcey contributes a char- acteristic paper on "The Boulevards of Paris," which is superbly illustrated by G. shoanniot..... Other finely-illus- trated papers are " Saftety oi4 the. Atlantic," " Boys' Clubs,' and "Some photographs of luminous objects." We have part 2 of "The Alabama Courtship," by F. J. Stimson, " Gertnan Schools," by Bliss 'Perry, "The War, as we see it now, " The Point of View," &c. In the " English Illustrated Magazine," Frederick Gale supplies " Becollections of Cricket," with portraits of noted cricketers of a past generation. "The fate of Nana Sahib's Englishman," by Archibald Forbes, forms a capital story. There is an illustrated paper on "The mariners of England before the Armada," by H. Halli- day Sparling. Two other illustrated papers are "The chateau" in France, and "Life in an Australian bush town."

, " Hereward the Wake," by Charles Kingsley, is re- published as a 6d. volume by Messrs. Wei-Milan and Co. The type and paper are good, and as the matter is good it is not too much to say that no better value in litera- ture can be had for the money. The Strand Magazine has made a hit with its portraits of celebrities at different times of their lives. Its the current issue the persons illustrated in this way are J. L. Toole, E. S. Willard, Miss Kate Rorke, the Duke of 'Clar- ence and Avondale, Duchess of Fife, Prince George of Wales, Madame Albani; and Miss Agnes Jansen. Amongst other contents we have "Out .of a pioneer's trunk," by Bret Harte, "Anecdotes of the War Path," "Humours of the Post Office," "Celebrated beauties," with illustrations from pictures by Sir Joshua Reynobis; Gainsborough, and C. Reed. "A night in an opium den," "A home for lost dogs," &c., &c. "The Tenth Society &nate "is a brochure by 'Mr. Alexander Waddell, of Sale, author of " A bird of the air" &c. Mr. Waddell writes in a 'pleasant and earnest style, sifting the experiences he has had in various parts of the country with a view to presenting something to tae reader which is well worth considering. tut his place ought to have been in the pulpit, for, as in the olden time all roads led to Rome, so all our author's experiences lead to texts from Scripture. The work (price Is 6d.) is I printed and published by Mr. John Heywood. "forecastle's Manual "for 1891 is a technical adviser for all connected with companies. It is edited and com- piled by Mr. Walter R. Horncastle, who has had nearly a quarter of a century's experience of advertising, and may therefore be regarded as speaking with authority. In addition to giving an alphabetical list of company issues advertised in 1890, it supplies a large variety of informa- tion on the formation of a company, prospectus adver- tising, &c., with a review of company legislation in 1890. There is every evidence of its having been most carefully prepared. The midsummer number of "The Ladies' Gazette of Fashion" (price 6d.),is adorned with full' page coloured fashion and other plates, and there is a supplement with designs, for initials in needlework. In addition to a large number of engravings there are articles, on " Society and fashion,"" Occupation of odd minutes," "Improve- ment of the home,"" June in the garden,"" Hints on moving," housekeeping notes, &c. . The Queen (price 6d.), for June 20th, has as a supple- ment a charming coloured plate "The mandolineplaver." On the front page there is a portrait of Lady Borthwick. and other illustrations, include," Birthday morning," "The fairy of the moon," "Cup' day at Ascot," " Sketches at the Salon,"" Memorial to Wordsworth," with a series of portraits of ladies_ who have recently dis- tinguished themselves. There is the. usual description of fashions, with personal notes and news. We have alsoto hand" Weldon's Ladips Journal," of dress, fashion,.and needlewprk (3d.) ;.‘6,Weldon's Practi- cal jewelled Embroiderer" (2d.) ; " Mrs • Leach'S Family Dressmaker" (2d.) ; and ." Mrs. Leach's Fancy Work- basket," (2d.)

div.head: OUR FRIENDS IN AMERICA.
div.p: OUR FRIENDS IN AMERICA.

Mr. John S. Green, printer and stationer, 34 Bridge-st., looked in at our Warrington office on, Monday, he having safely arrived from Canada at midnight on Saturday, by the Allan Line steamer, "Sardinian." On the whole, Mr. Green had a•plea- sant voyage home, though at times the trip was somewhat monotonous. The Allan Line vessels take a very northerly course, which, even at this time of year, proved very cold and dull, and as a consequence wet, heavy, foggy, days and nights succeeded each other very quickly, only one really bright clear day being experienced dur- ing the ten days of the voyage. In addition to this, for days together, not even the excitement of a passing ship relieved the tedium of the trip. The ship carried about 300 passengers,half of whom were in the saloon, the remainder being inter- mediates,with just a few steerage passengers. With the exception of about a dozen, all the passengers were visiting Europe for pleasure,and were booked to return during the month of August. Altogether Mr. Green has had a bright, lively, and interesting experience with his American cousins, and returns home from his 8,000 miles excursion looking the picture of health and in every way benefited by his rest and recreation. Whilst in Chicago, Mr. Green spent some days with his former employer,

MIL. H. H. ISAILKER, a late editor of this journal, and our readers will be gratified to learn that he found Mr. Barker most happily circumstanced. During his sojourn across the Atlantic, Mr. Barker has become thoroughly Americanised, and says he has no desire to return —except just for five minutes to see his friends and then leave. Mr. Barker's business keeps him much from home, and he has so greatly changed in appearance during his long absences that even in- timate friends have failed to recognise him. Mr. Barker is naturally of a genial disposition, and fond of fun, and he tells some amusing stories as to the way he played upon the feelings of his friends when he found they could not recognise him, after cut- ting off his beard. For all that,Mr. Barker was his dear old self, and he inquired with considerable in- terest as to the welfare of many Warringtonians to whom he wished to be kindly remembered. Mr. Barker was in excellent health and spirits, and his business prospects were of an enwuraging nature. His present address is The Acme Publishing and Engraving Co., Room 5, Washington Block, corner of sth Avenue and Washington-at., Chicago, Illinois, U.S.A. Another friend whom Mr. Green visited, and of whom the younger members of our towns- people will be pleased to hear, was

MR. R. C. JACUBSEN, who was formerly engaged at Messrs. Guest's Tan- nery in Winwick-st. Since his arrival in America, Mr. Jacobsen has taken to trade journalism, and after five years' experience on a leather trade publi- cation, he has commenced business on his own ac- count. He ie now editor and proprietor of" Hide and Leather," published at 154, Like-street,Chieago, a well written, carefully edited, nicely arranged and beautifully printed journal, which, judging from the healthy appearance of its advertising columns, bids fair to place Mr. Jacobsen in a splendid finan- cial position before very long. Like Mr. Barker, Mr. Jacobsen inquired anxiously as to the old town and its inhabitants, and was very pleased to hear of the prospects of its development in the near future. In common, further, with Mr. Barker, Mr. Jacobsen entertains a very high opinion of Americans and their business ways, and was strong in his opinion of the greater scope there is for business people on "the other side." Mr. Jacobsen, who was in capital health, was buried in his journalistic duties when Mr. Green called upon him. Whilst Mr. Green was converoing with Mr. Jacobsen, one of his assistants laugh- ingly interposed, and presented a copy of an en- graving of the Queen, which. he had found in a paper he had just opened. The third gentleman Mr. Green called upon 'A as a Warringtonian, who is one of the latest additions to the million inhabi- tants of the "Queen City of the West." This gentleman was
MR. JAMES F. BATE,

recently assistant librarian at the Warrington Library, who had arrived in Chicago just twelve months before. He is a member of the reportorial staff of the "Chicago Herald," the leading paper in the great packing city. Although apparently the youngest member of the staff, Mr. Bate has al- ready made his mark in journalism, and his future prospects are of the brightest description. Mr. Bate kindly devoted two half days to showing Mr. Green several sights in the city which he had not previously seen, and Mr. Green is profuse in his thanks to Mr. Bate for the kindness shown to him. As to

MR. JOSEPH ELLISON, Mr. Green reports that he parted with him after a week spent together in Boston, and that he has not since seen him. Mr. Green, has, however, been in constant communication with Mr. Ellison, and from latest tidings he was in good health, and had good prospects of advancement.

div.head: ROYAL AGRICULTURAL SHOW.
div.p: ROYAL AGRICULTURAL SHOW.

At the annual meeting of the Royal Agricultural Society, held on Tuesday at the showyard in Doncaster, Lord Feversham was elected president, in succession to the Earl of Ravensworth, who in retiring described the present show as one of the best the society had held. In the evening the Prince and Princess of Wales and the Princesses Victoria and Maud halted for a few , minutes at Doncaster Station en route to Earl Fitzwil- ' fiam's seat. Their Royal Highnesses had a most enthu- siastic reception from a vast concourse • and the Mayor and Corporation of Doncaster presented the Prince with an address. The Prince and Princess of Wales arrived at the Royal Agricultural Show at Doncaster on Wednesday morning, and inspected the exhibits. Their royal highnesses received a cordial welcome.

div.head: DELMORE FOREST ON FIRE.
div.p: DELMORE FOREST ON FIRE.

A great fire has taken place on Delamere Forest, near Northwich. It broke out in some brushwood not far from the Cheshire Lines Railway, and soon presented the scene of an American prairie fire. Im- mense tongues of flames shot high into the air, and clouds of dense smoke enveloped the surrounding country. The conflagration attracted large numbers of people, who endeavoured to arrest the progress of the fire by cutting avenues through the wood. They finally succeeded; but not before an area of a hundred acres, thickly covered with brushwood mid trees, prindipally Scotch fir and larch, was devas- tated. The property belongs to Lord Delanaere. The residYnce of the Hon. Mrs. Cholmondeloy, at Abbott's Moss, narrowly escaped destruction.

OR, THE CHILD OF THE REGIMENT.
BY SYLVANUS COBB.

CHAPTER XVII. A FATHER'S BLESSING-ANOTHER FUNERAL. The sun was very near its setting when the young captain and Lady Caroline returned frori! their ride. The groom, who catne to take their horses, informed his lady that her Uncle Roland had arrived and was in the house. Her father had gone over to Oxton, but would soon return.

The twain ascended the broad marble steps to the piazza, where Percival announced that he would not re-enter the mansion. Caroline's face was clouded in a moment, and, in her great dis- appointment, she came near weeping. She had thought to pass such a happy evening I But she sought to control herself. Yet, would he hot tarry until morning? "Percival, papa has been very kind, and—and— I am sure he will not—"

"Hush, darling !" He stole an arm around her, and spoke tenderly and earnestly. "I know your father has been kind—very kind—and for that reason I will not impose upon him. You must know that he has made an effort to receive me graciously. Smiling though his face has been, at heart he has felt disquiet. He would have been happier if I had not come." "0, Percy Papa is as open as the day. I know he is proud but he is frank and truthful."

" I know, Carrie—l know all that; but I will not wear out a welcome. Wait until we hear from Old Tom's mission. Dear old fellow! I am sure he will succeed. Wait, dear love, until I can pre- sent to your father a better claim than I can now put forth. lam free to confess to you, darling, that I have come to regard the title and estate of Ambleton, since I have seen the grand old place, as something to be prized. At all events, I cannot deny that I shall be bitterly disappointed if we do not gain back the lost papers." "Certainly," responded the lady, quick to think and comprehend, "because the loss of Ambleton would be the loss of your birthright; and a man would be criminal who could suffer such loss with- out a struggle to maintain his rights." Caroline might have put forth more entreaty to induce her lover to tarry had it not been for the presence of her uncle. She knew that Roland had been contemplating a visit to France, and she had supposed that he had gone. This unexpected visit must be upon business, and that, too., business of moment. And then her father's sudden riding away to Oxton, leaving his brother alone behind— of course it had something to do with. Roland's coming. A fear possessed her that something was

wrong. "We shall meet again very soon I am sure" said Percival, after the groom had gone for his horse; " and when I come again I hope I may tell you of the recovery of my lost papers." Shortly after this they exchanged kisses and blessings, and the gallant young captain vaulted to his saddle and rode away. At a late hour on that evening Roland Archer', of his own accord, and unknown to his brother, sought his fair niece when they were alone in the drawing-room, and told her the story of the mort- gage deeds held against Elmdale by the Earl of Oxton. Having resolved to speak, he presented the ease in its most formidable aspect. "My dear child,' he said, when he saw the look of terror upon her face, "you will pardon me, I know. Could I see your father in such suffering without speaking ?" " 0 ! Uncle Roland ! why did you not let papa himself speak to me ?" "Because he would not speak until it was too late. Poor Dick! he loves you SO well—" "0 ! stop! stop! Let me think! Don't say anything more, please. "0 ! this is dreadful I But—it may not be so bad. They may not take all nor nearly all." "Do not deceive yourself; Caroline. We know that those old mortgages will cover the whole estate, mansion and all. Caroline, my blessed, noble, true-hearted girl, surely you. would have the whole truth, and at once. You know best your own will and purpose; but you, cannot hide from yourself that it is in your power to avert the evil." " Stop ! stop! Say no more ! You mean I can marry with Matthew Egerton ?' "Yes, I mean exactly that—and.lolmdale will be saved."

"Saved to whom ?" cried the indignant girl, starting up from her seat, and standing before her uncle, proudly, erect, with, eyes 'laming, and her lips compressed.. " Matthew Egerton: ie a vile, treacherous man. He does not like papa, because he knows that papa despises him; nor does he like me, though he would marry me. If he takes Elm- dale, be sure my father will not be considered. No matter what he may pledge before marriage let him once claim me for wife, and he will leave papa to suffer all his loss, " What—whatz—does papa say?' "He says—if you will force me to tell you—that he loves you too well to force you to marry with Egerton. the inmates of Eimdale mansion received a notice of the death of Walter Buckley, Earl of Oxton to- gether with a request that they would attend the funeral, which had been appointed for the succeed- ing day. The morning of the appointed day broke fair and beautiful, and at an early hour Lord Elmdale was prepared to set forth. His brother had tarried over, to be present at the obsequies, and he rode in the coach with the earl awl Caroline. It was near the middle of the forenoon when they reached the castle, and as they turned into the broad, circular carriage-way they saw the family coach of Wenham, coming from the opposite direction, turn in directly behind them, with old Tom Crawford occupying a seat upon the outside with the driver.

As they alighted they found Lord Wenham and Capt. Gordon ready to greet them. There was a perceptible constraint in Lord Elmdale's manner as he took the hand of his daughter's lover; but there was warmth in the greeting, and there was heart in the grasp of his hand. His emotion, what- ever it might have been, was one of tenderness rather than of harshness or dislike.
They would not be expected within for an hour at least, so FAmdale took the arm of the general, and led him apart, away into a shady nook of the park.

"Dear Wenham, pardon me for asking the ques- tion; you will readily understand my feelings. Can you tell me—has Captain Gordon gained possession of his family papers yet ?" Wenham looked into his companion's face; then bent his head in thought. . Presently he said: "Dear Elmdale, before I answer you, let me ask you a question. You will pardon me; and, also, you can understand my feelings, considering that Percival is to me as a son. Elave you yet con- sented that he should aspire to your daughter's hand ?"

Lord Elmdale briefly stated the facts, and Harry Maxwell caught the hand of his old friend, and held it in a warm, impulsive grasp. "Dick, old friend I Bless your tree heart for the goodness I felt sure was in it. Take heart, ..nd fear not. Let the discarded aspirant for your daughter's hand do his worst. It will not be much, I assure you. And above all else, 'do you thank God from the very bottom of your heart, for the hour that brought Percival Gel-don to your side."

On their return, when near the main entrance of the castle, they were met by Sir Edmund Cooper, grown quite grey, and very stout, since we last saw him. He paid no attention to Lord Wenham, not even vouchsafing a nod, and to Elmdale he spoke without offering his hand. "111. y lord," he said haughtily, and with consid- erable show of feeling far from pleasant, "a word with you, if you please." _ _ _
"Certain,. sir," the earl replied, with a polite inclination of the head.

Wenham did not forsake his friend, but stopped with him, standing only a short distance apart. "My Lord of Elmdale," the baronet went on, with cuTling lip, "do I hear aright when I hear that you will not keep faith with me ?" "Sir Edmund," returned the earl, with dignity, "I will not pretend ignorance of your meaning, yet I would prefer that you should state your case in different terms. I have broken no faith."

"Didn't you pledge :ne your word that your ilaughter should be wife of my step-son ?" "No, sir. That would have been something beyond my power, as an English parent, to enforce. I never pledge my word to a .thing I may not accomplish. But, sir, this much I will confess; I did sign articles of betrothment between. the step- son of yourself and my daughter." "Well, sir," cried the baronet, now fairly irate, "I have to ask:' Will you keep faith with met Shall the marriage be consummated?" "That is for the lady herself to decids:". And the earl added, with a smile : "I think you would find it a rather difficult task, should your step-son refuse to take the Lady Caroline for a wife, to force him to do it. How, pray tell.me, would you, set about it ?"

"Lord Elmdale, do you mean, to tell me that your danghter refuses to be the wife of Matthew Egerton?' "She does refusci, most decidedly,, and most. emphatically." "So she breaks the faith her father pledged ?" "Sir Edmund," said Elmdale, without the slightest ruffle of a feature, "suppose your step- son had died, would you have come to me and claimed falfillment of that old-time contract ?I'

"Bah ! Why do you put such a question ? ' What bearing has it ?" "A bearing direct," answered the earl. "To all intents sad purposes the boy to whom 1 affianced my child iv dead, and in his place-has grown up a man to whom, I venture to assert, you would-not give daughter of yours. Or, at least, you would not force her to become-his wife."

The baronet was s'tggered. Elmdale 28.67 his struggle, and added: "However, I have no wish to throw all the re- sponsibility upon the shoulders of my child, She has never consented to the union, and when I found that she had gi7en her heart to another, I did not seek to thwart her. Yonder you see them now walking together,, and a staunch old trooper with them. That youth, when a boy of tender age, saved my life at, the risk of ,his own ' • -and my daughter's life he-saved; nice the life of Lord Wenham." "No, no; that in painting , the picture too heroically altogether," said Coopsr, with something very much like a sneer. "1 ha—e-heard the story. I know he piloted a strong body of English.eoldiers to your assistance." "Yes," put in•Wenham, takin a step forward;, 'sand when the brigand chief, seeing that his -cap- ture was care, had send a sad of murderous wretches to put his ?risoners ta.death, iwas that boy who came to the- rescue. , With his own hand he shot down the brigand who Te.ad Caroline in his arms, and he led Ws men who .rescued the rest ot us. But for him we should have been butcherodi before our friends had found us."

" Comeony dear 3ir Edmund," the warm-hearted' general continued, extending Mn hand, and giving. the other mfriendly.grasp, "now show your true self in this matter, andlet Matthew Egerton lead his. own forlorn hope."- " Alas !!!'said tho haronet,,with an eatire change of tone and manner; "that is the very thing dread. Mat is a strong-headed, wilful man' and he will do mischief. You, Lord Eloadale, know just what he will do." " Yes,'.' returned the latter; " azAl I am pre- pared." " Hew.? 'Will you let hire, press his claims upon your estate? Ronember' 'Se is now Earl of Oxton ; everything of p:operty that, belonged to the late earl is 3. im his. You know his disßosition an,. well as I det:' _

_ " Yse,-; interposed Wenham, who saw that. Elm- dale would notpatiently endure .nauch more of. this pricking.; "he fully understands, and will abide the issue.. Ido not suppose the new. earl will exercise autharity, until his predecessor has been laid. away with.' his dead and .gon- fathers."

Ignoring hts mother and his step-father, Matthew Egerton aseeined the place of honour at the castle, . at the church, and at the grsve ; and even the old family lawyer, who once approached him, at the beginning, with a word of caution and advice, was pompously waved aside, and bade to attend to his own business and keep his proper place. The funeral services were ended shortly after noon. Then came a setting of tables in the court- yard, and in the lower hall, and a feeding of the hungry; and when the crowd had dispersed those interested were assembled in the great drawing- room, to hear Mr. Murray read the will; for it was in his possession, and even the expectant heir had not been allowed to see it.
(To be continued.)
SIR RICHARD BURTON'S LIST WORK.

LADY BURTON'S NOBLE SACRIFICE. Lady Burton contributes to the "Morning Pest" an interesting letter respecting her husband's manuscripts. in the course of which she says : " My husband has been collecting for. fourteen years information and materials on a certain subject. His last volume of the '4 Supplemental Nights" had been finished and out on the 13th of November, 1883. He then gave himself up entirely to the writing of-this book,which was called the Scented Garden,' a translation from the Arabic. It treated of a certain passion. Do not any— one suppose for & moment that Richard Burton ever wrote a thing from-the impure point of view. He dis- t sected a passion fiiim every point of view as a doctor may dissect a body, showing its sources, its origin, its: evil, and its rood, and its proper tiaes, as designed by Providence and Nature, as the great Academician Watts, paints them. In private life he was the most pure, the • most refined and modest man that ever lived, and he was so guileless himself that he could never be brought to believe that other men held or used these things from any other standpoint. I, as a woman, think differently. The day before he died he called me into his room and showed me half a page of Arabic manuscript upon which he was working, and he said: To-morrow I shall have-finished this,and I promise you after this that I will never write another book upon this subject. I will take to cur biography.' He said This is to be your jointure, and the proceeds are to be set apart for an annuity to you," and I said, "I hope not ; I hope you will live to spend, it like the other.' He said 'I am afraid it will make a r..,eat row in Engiand,because 'the Arabian Nights' was a baby tale in comparison to this, and I am in communication with several men in England about it.' The next morning, at seven, he had ceased to exist. Some days -.later, when I locked myself up in his rcoms,and sorted and examined his manuscripts, I read this-one. No promise :rad been exacted from me, because the end had been unf,reseen, and I remained for three days in a state of perfect torture as to what I ought to do about it. Durinx that time I reeeived an offer from a man, whose mrne shall be always kept private, of 6000 guineas for it. "1 sat down on the floor before the fire at dark to con- sult my own heart, my own head. My heart said, You can have 6,000 guineas; your husband worked for you, kept you in a happy home, with honour and respect for thirty years How are you going to reward him? That your wretched body may be fed and clothed andwarmed for a few miserable months or years, will you, let that soul, which is part of your soul, be left out in the cold and darkness tire the end of time, till all those sins which may have been committed on accrrunt of reading those writings may have been expiated,‘, or passed away, per- haps for ever ? Why, it would beilist parallel with the original thirty pieces of silver! I fetched the manuscript and laid it on the ground before en—two large volumes' worth. Still my thoughts were—Was it a sacrilege? It was his Magint77l, opmx—his last work, that he was so proud of, that was to have been finished on tha awful morrow—that never came. Will he rise up in his grave and curse me or bless me? The thought will haunt me to death, but Sacßand El Shaykh e: Nafzawih, who were pagans, begged pardon of God and prayed not to be cast into hell fire for having written them., and implored their friends to pray fr them to the Lordthat he would have mercy on them. then I said, Not only for 6,000 guineas, but not for 6,600,000 guineas will I risk it.' Sor- rowfully, reverently, and in fear and trembling, I burnt sheet after sheet until, the whole of the volume was con- 3urned."

div.head: FATAL PIT ACCIDENT.
div.p: FATAL PIT ACCIDENT.

A fall oflroof occurred on Tuesday night in Great Row Pit, Longton Hall, Staffordshire, burying three men. Two were rescued, but a man named Seabridge was not reacbed until Wednesday morning, when he was found to be dead,.
MURDER OF A FRENCHWOMAN
LONDON.

A Frenchwoman, known as Casquette, was On. Sun- day found murdered in a house in Whitfield-st.,.Totten- ham, Court-road. A man named Acheton, her paramour, had absconded, leaving a note admitting the authorship of the crime and threatening to drown himself.
CHARGE OF' WIFE MURDER AT' BLACK-
BURN.

A labourer named Connolly has been arzested• by the Blaekburn policet on a charge of murdering his.wife. The statement is made that shortly before midnight on Satur- day Mrs. Connolly fetched her husband from a, public- house, when he turned upon her, knocked her down, and kicked her savagely. She ran to a neighbour's house saying " Look.what Jack's done." • Within an hour she died from the effects of the shocking injtaries.. The hus- band has already served a term of imprisonment for ; assaulting his wife.

The Prince ad Princess of Wales, accompanied by the, Princesses Victoria and Maud, visited Eastbourne on Saturday,, to open the new children's hospital at Meads, and also-the wing for juvenile patients just added to the Princess Alice Memorial Hospital. The proceedings were mainly of a religious character. The Prince subse- quently expressed his satisfaction on the occasion, and the Princess received purses from. young ladies towards the funds a the institution, The Royal party were afterwards driven to Compton Place, the gent of Lord Hartington, were- they were entertained at luncheon, Later, the Prince opened the children's wing of the Princess Alice Hospital.

div.p: THE IRISH PARTY LEADERSHIP. EXPEC FED RETIREMENT OF MR. JUST!Ii M'CARTHY.

believe, writes a London correspondent, that the retiremont of,Mr. Justin•M'Carthy from the leadership of the Irish party may be expected at no distant date. He is not able to give much attention to the duties of the position, and it has always been recognised that his occupation of the post of leader would be temporary. It can hardly be doubted who his successor wEI be. The position ,will be offered, and no doubt accepted, by Dillon, and the change will therefore not take placountil Mr. Dillon is released from prison. It may betaken for granted, however, that next Session the Irish party will be under the leadership of Mr. Dillon, and that-this change will 'clear off a great many of Mr; Parneirsoup- Porters.

div.p: MR. .PAMELL AND TEE LEADERSHIP

Mr. Parnell addressed a meeting at Balbriggan4eounty Dublin, on Sunday. The attendance was largely com- posed of personamtho travelled by a special train from Dublin. Mr. C,omishey, chairman of the Town Commis- sioners of Balbriggan, presided.—Mr. Parnell, in the course of his speech,said that Mr. Gladstone byte& letter had let loose forces ,in Ireland which he would net live to see the end of. Mr. Gladstone had made three fatal mistakes—first,when he imprisoned him (Mr., Parnell) in 1871 ; next, when he released him, and now, when he interfered in the question of leadership. He considered that the last-mentioned one was so fatal that it woUld prevent that measure •of usefulnecs which Ireland Sin common with Great Britain, would otherwise have ob- tained through his services.

A MILITARY TRAIN .WRECKED.—LOSS OF LIRE.. An alarming and disastrous collision occurred on Sun- day on the Lough Swilly Railway line, about two miles distant from Londonderry. The engine driver named M'Anier, was killed, and his fireman, named Wray, fat- ally injured. A great number of passengers have suff- ered terrible injuries. An excursion train had gone to Fahan, seven miles distant, and leaving its freight of ' holiday makers thexe,en route for Rathtnullen, set out on. its return journey to Derry. When on the way back a military trainl laden with .Donegal Militia proceeding for disbandment at Letterkenny, was seen to go on its own line, a junction of the Swilly Railway.. A collision immediately followed, with terrible force.. The empty train was being brought along with the back of the ,engine foremost. The -escape of its driver and firemen .was thus rendered impossible. M'Anier 'as killed on the spot, his body being terribly mutilated. Wray also sustained fearful injuries. Enormous loss of life would have resulted but for the fact that the first two or three carriages of the military train were packed ;with lug- age, which, to a great extent, broke the blow. One of these carriages was thrown completely over, and the engines, by the violencieof the impact, were knocked entirely apart. Thenurnber of injured is not yet known, but many have already been eonveyedto hospital.. Hun- dreds of people speedily assembled in the fields near the scene of the collision, and the greatest excitement pre- vailed as the mounted soldiersi bandaged and bleeding, were borne away. A.laige number of the men sustained injuries, and'twelvendn-commissioned officers and pri- vates were conveyed,to Derry fnfirmary, while others .who wereless seriously injured were attended to on tire spot by Iddil diicffirA. It is'belieVed that the light traits ,was returning to Derry to assist in taking out the second special, but on the other hand, it is stated that the driver had written instructions from the' inana,ger of the line to remain at the jurictiort until the special arrived there, and to assist it at that tpoint. John D,oherty, guard of the light train, and the only survivor of that train, was afteiwards a,rrested by the police, and will be brought before the magistrates. •

TIIE EXAMINER SATURDAY, .JUNE 27, 1891 THE ASSISTED EDUCATION BILL. j WARRINGTON BLUE COAT SCHOOL. ONE HUNDRED YEARS AGO. A most interesting document has been put int o our hands, by Mr. J. McClew, hairdresser, Horsemarket-st.. being a report of the state of the Blue Coat Charity School in Warrington, front January Ist, 1784, to January Ist, 1785. We print extracts from it, which, as relating to the state of affairs that prevailed in Warrington more than s. century, ago, cannot fail to be found of interne,. The Blue Coat School was founded in 1711. so it had been in existence a little more than 70 years when this report was issued. It will be observed that the ie.port speaks of the institution being in its infancy, and of the buildings being then comptete, andthe establishment formed—from which it may be inferred that, although the charity had been founded so long t before, the buildings—which we assume are the buildings now standing—bad only then recently been erected. The Charity seems to have been con- ducted, at the time of the report, en the half-time principle, the boys beingemployed half the day in the rarding, spinning, winding, and weaving of cotton, and the other half day in attending to the the three R's. As ior the girls, their employment was spinning, knitting, sewing and the ' work of the house. So 'far asi,he report shows, nothing in the shape of learning was taught to them in those days. tlt seems to have been considered unnecessary even to communicate the three R's to • the female side-of the house, which consisted of ten The be,ye in the school numbered thirty. Looking back through the changes df more than a century,we still find many familiar names both among the trustees undin the list of annual subscribers. For instance, we ' have the then representativesbf the house of :Blackburne of Orford; of Hornby of Winwick ; alackburne of Hale; Ranks of Win- stanley ; Patten of Bank; Leigh of Golborne ; and Lyme and Iyon of Appleton. The-names of others of the trustees have entirely died out of Warrington, but Mr. Tapping was probably the brother of Mr. Councillor linger Topping, a family until-recently . well-known in Warrington. Amongst the sub- scribers—for in those days charity was supple- mented by -subscriptions—we .fnd again many familiar names, such as the father of the late Mc. John Ashton, of the firm of Ashton and Woods, solicitor, Warrington; Mr. Brint, now Lepresented by the Turners; Mr. Walter Kerfoot, at one time head of the firm now represented by Messrs. Green- all and Backton ; Mr. George Litton, represented by the late Major %Litton ; Mr. Wm. Orrett, one of the founders of Wilderspool brewery; Mr. J. Parr, now represented by the chairman of Parr's Banking Company.;, -Mr. Peter Seaman,,now represented by. the Nicholson family; Messrs. Travers, now repre- sented by Major Pickmere, and Mr. Dakin, now re- presented, by the Rev. E. D. Gerven. The cotton-manufacturing -work was, in 1785; or course done by hand. There is a rather puzzling item of ..£3Btlls. -'sd. for corn, but, so far as the balance sheet- shows, they did not grind for them- selves at thelßlue Coat School, for there is an item. of .£4l Bs.ild. paid for meal at that time. Part of the material for spinning was flax. It was grown near Warrington, and, in living memork, flax was cultivated by farmers as part of their crop, and wAt afterwards spun. It was bleached in what were called" bowcrofts." A very large one belonging-to the late Mr. Edward Gaskell—father of Mrs. Robert Davies—occupied the southern corner of Mersey- 'st., and Church-st., where the flax was washed and dipped. At that time the stealing of a hank of yarn from a 4‘ bowcroft " wasponished with death. Alto- gether the report is a most interesting one,and a per- fect representation of the-early state of our Blue Coat institution. • It may be added, that the original Blue Coat School was situated hear Trinity Chorch,and within the last thirty years the children on Sundays paraded, morning and afternoon, through the town to that &lurch. One of our informants further adds that he remembers the old weaving shed, with the broken looms lying about. It stood on the site of the present pretty little-chapel behind the existing school. ,He also remembers part of one of the old weaver's beams, which.,used to be fastened and locked to any runaway --scholar's leg, the unfortu- nate -scholar having to drag it about the school, or, wherever else he had to go, as a punishment and a safeguard against his truant propensities. It was attached to .his leg by &short chain, and went by the name of 3, Old Betty." The master, it is added, used to extract the boys' teeth when required. and cut off -any warts that appeared on their hands and faces. The report we have referred to contains a view of the Blue Coat School, and is beaded : A report of the state of the Clue Coat Charity School in Warrington, from danuarya,,l7B4, to January..l, 1785." It then goes on to saf : •, The Trustees of the Blue Coat School are happy that they have it now in their power to submit the state of the charity to the public inspection. This could not be done before.(because it couldnot be done with precision) in the infancy of the Institution. But as the buildings are now completed, and the establishment formed, the annual 'expenditure may be pretty accurately ascer- tained,, and the public judge of its situation,. and see what farther improvements it will admit or require. The ,views,which the Trustees held forth to themselves in the structure and furniture were convenience and stability. It was considered that no narrow or tempor- ary plan, which just answered particular exigencies, was worthy of a charity, designed to serve future -ages; and this too, (as it is to be hoped) with a still—accumu- lating fund,and a still—increasing beneficence. And indeed, the complacency, with which every eye beholds it, is a pleasing testimony to the Trustees, that they have not attended to these views in vain. In the admission and support of objects, the views, thsy ;proposed to themselves were strict impartiality, and decent frygality. The ;election of candidates has been left to a determination which is incapable of any false bias or undue influence, a fair ballot; and the maintenance cef the household, • conducted with the utmost frugality which was compatible with decency and comfort.; that the benefits of the charity might be extended to as many objects as possible. The Trustees have but one thing more to observe, which the public cannot be as good judges of, as they themselves-are-; .and that is the distressful scenes they have been witnesses of, in the admission of candidates I and which, it.is to be hoped, the liberalitrof the public will enable them every day more and more to.aLlevi- ata. There is now in the school thirty boys and ten girls, which are completely clothed, lodged, and dieted by this charity. The boys are one half the day employed in carding, spinning, winding, and weaving of cotton, and the cANer half of day attend their learning of read- ing„ writing, and arithmetic. The girls are employed in spinning, knitting, sewing, and work in the house. The buildings being sufficiently large, and in every respect convenient for accommodating upwards of 120 ,children, the Trustees are desirous, as soon as the fund will admit, to make an addition of a few more ; whieh they are in hopes soon to be enabled to do, from the increase of the boys' labour, and the generous liberality of the public. Those who choose to promote and encourage this pious charity and intend to be benefactors by their latt will, have the following form recommended to them. Item. I give and bequeath unto the Treasurer and Trustees of the Blue-Coat School in Warrington, the sum of -for the use of, the said school, which said sum I will and desire may be applied for the further support of the said charity.

N.B. it was unanimously ordered and agreed, that no child shall be admitted but what belongs to the town- ship of Warrington (until the charity is extended) except such as are recommended by a benefactor of £2O or upwards, or an annual subscription of £2 25."

I VISVANTARA THE BODISAT.
A TALE or THIBET.

In the Bkah-hgynr, a Thibetan biograpical pia of Buddhist saints, consisting of three hun-i dred and thirty-three ponderous folio volumes, is contained the following poetic and pathetically touching account of Visvantara, the princely Bodisat or Buddhist saint. Stripped of its my.no- logical supernaturalism, the story doubtless records an actual historical fact. Such a person as Visvan- tara really lived, and was famous throughout all Central Asia for the beauty and purity of his character, and his self-denying position. -He flourished In the age of Christ, and it is a beauti- ful thought, that while in Palestine the Divine Man was teacbing. the multitude in his Sermon on the Mount that it was more blessed to give than to receive, and exhorting them to "give to him that asketh thee, and from him that would borrow of thee turn not thou away," far away, amid the mountains of Thibet, an earnest heathen heart was striving to foldl to the utmost letter this command of an unknown Saviour. The following account of this famous Buddhist saint, or Bodisat, is very much condensed from his life as given in the Thi- betan Bkah-hgyur.

King Visvaiitra reigned in Visvanagara, and his son and the heir to his throne was Visvantara. The colour of the prince's complexion was golden, his forehead high-arched, his nose acquiline, his eye- brows were interlacing, and all his joints and limbo were complete.

To the -prince, in his childhood, were given eight nurses—two for carrying, two for suckling, two for cleansing, and two for playing and these fed him on milk, curdled milk, butter, melted butter, butter foam, and divers other excellent kinds of nutriment, so that he grew rapidly like a lotus in a pool. The young Visvantara, in whom dwelt pure faith and virtuous feeling, was considerate on the welfare of others, compassionate and addicted to magnanimity, kindly towards men, of a yielding and generous nature, bestowing presents freely and quite dis- passionately, and assiduous in giving away. When men heard of this excessive generosity on his part, numberless crowds came to beg of him, and all these he sent away with their expectations completely fulfilled.

When the prince reached man's estate, be took to) wife the beautiful Madri, and in the oourse of time two children—a son and a daughter—were born to the pair. Long ere this, however, the goodness of Visvantara had made him celebrated throughout the whole world, and already men called him Bodisat. Then did Sakra, the king of gods, from his throne in heaven take knowledge that the earth was full of Visvantara's praise, and Sakra deter- mined to try the heart of the Bodisat.

So it happened that one day, as the prince was riding in his sandal-wood chariot which gleamed with steel, coral, silver, gold, rubies, sapphires, and turquoises, and the covering of which was the skins of lions, tigers, and bears, some Brahmans met him on the way and said:
"0, youth, may you be victorious! Through all the world are you renowned as the Bodisat that gives all things away; give us, therefore, thy chariot."
And Visvantara swiftly alighted from his chariot, and with joyful heart he gave it to the Brahmans, saying: _ _ _

"3o may I, giving away the world, become possessed of wisdom." Afterwards Visvantara was riding upon his ele- phant, Rajyvardhana, which was of inccmparable size, and the whiteness of which equalled jasmine blossoms, white lotuses, snow, silver, and the clouds.. And certain Brahmans met him, and said: "0, Prince, may you be victorious! In the world with beings divine and not divine you are renowned as an all-giver. Therefore it is meet that you should give us this elephant."

- And Visvantara swiftly alighted from his elephant and joyfully gave it to the Brahmans, saying: "8o may I, giving away the world, become possessed of perfect insight." Now, when King Visvantara heard what his son had done he was very angry, and ordered the Bodisat to leave the country. And the faithful Madri went forth with her exiled husband, and Visvantara dwelt in the forest of penance and spent his days in reflection and his nights in prayer. The inhabitants of Visvanagara mourned the loss a their prince with loud lamentations, and the heart of the king was touched, and he sent. a messenger to his banished son, saying: "Oh, son, give up making presents, and return to thy father and thy people," And Visvantara replied: "0 Lord of the world, the earth and it:, moun- tains may perhaps be destined to overthrow, but I cannot turn aside my mind from giving!" And the Bodisat, with his wife and children, dwelt in the forest of penance. Afterwards Madri went forth one day to gather roots and herbs for their food, and in her absence a Brahman came and stood before the Bodisat say- ing:
740 Bodisat, may you be victorious! The gods praise you as the giver of all things. I have no slave, and, therefore, give me your children." And the heart of Visvantara was very heavy, and he said:

"Nay, 0 Brahman, take me and spare my children ? " But the Brahman mocked him. "Is it thus that the Bodisat kw:Ds his vow to give away the world that he may have heaven ? " Then Visvautara, groaning, and with tears in his eyes, gave his children to the Brahman. Now Madri, when she returned and heard what her husband done, fell upon the earth uttering sad cries and sounds of wailing; but she chided not her lord, seeing that he was striving to gain the heisht that surmounts the endless anguish. Then Sakra, the hig of gods, determined to sub- ject Visvantara to one mere test; and himself taking the form of a Brahman, he came to the Bodisat and said:

"0 Heaven-aspiring one, may you be victorious I Bakra, the god of gods, has wondered at your mag- nanimity. Give me, therefore, as a slave, this lovely sister, Madri, your wife." Then the prince wept and lamented; but he gave Madri to the Brahman. Now when the god perceived the marvellous steadfastness of the Bodisat•he put off his Brahman form, and, assum- ing his proper shape, the hermitage of Visvantara was lighted up with a great brilliancy, and many thousands of the bright-eyed gods filled the air with sounds of shouting and rejoicing, and their song was:

"-Oh, the great deed of surrender! Blessed it Visvantara the Bodisat 1" The legend, of which the above is but the briefest summary, goes on to relate how the Brahman, with the prince's children, goes into their grandfather's City to sell them as slaves, how they were recog- nized and rescued, and how the father sends an un- conditional invitation to his scn to return to his people. With greater fame than ever, the humble Bodisat comes back to Visvanag,ara, and the lords, the princes, the governors, and the kings of all the surrounding nations continually heaped rich gifts upon Visvlntap, and the more the Bodisat received the more he gave alTilY, and the poor of his land were blest.
