div.head: DENT AT TIAYDOCK.
div.p: DENT AT TIAYDOCK.
POUR MEN KILLED.

A shocking accident occurred at the Kin a Pit, llaydock, near St. Helens, on Thursday night, by which four men were instanteously killed and two others received injuries. The pit is one belonging to the extensive firm of Messrs. Richard Evans an Co., and for some time past the sinkers employed by the firm have been engaged in carrying out some alterations and extensions down the shaft. The sinkers have been in the habit of descending and ascending the shaft of the pit in a hoppet or a sort of a iron bucket or tub, fastened to the winding chain by four books meeting overhead. On Thursday, five men • named 'Marshall, Sharp, Cawlfield, M'Cue, and Farrell, were engaged in the sinking operations, and started work at two o'clock in the afternoon. At six o'clock they ascended the shaft for the purpose of having supper, and at the conclusion of the meal the whole of the men got into the hoppet for the purpose of descending the shaft. All apparently went well until the men reached a spotabout ninety feet from the bottom. It is supposed that about that spot the bottom of the hoppet caught against the timber at the sides of the shaft and was overturned. Certain it is that four of the men—Marshall, Sharp, Cawlfield, and M'Cue—were precipitated to the bottom of the shaft. The other occupant, Farrell, clung to the chains with desperation, and on the arrival of the " hoppet " at the bottom of the shaft he was found lying insensible i inside. A man named Jonathan Floyd, who resides n Park-road St. Helens, was standing at the shaft bottom awaiting the arrival of his fellow-workmen, and two of the men in falling struck him heavily and knocked him down. An alarm was immediately given, and on several men reaching the spot, a terrible spectacle was presented. The bodies of the four unfortunate men, who had dropped the 90 feet, were mangled almost beyond re- cognition. Heads were smashed and limbs fractured, and one spectator described the sight as a sickening one. Death was found to have been instantaneous in all the four cases. The bodies were taken up the shaft, and were removed to the lecture hall connected with the col- lieries to await identification. The man Floyd, who was the least injured, was removed to his home at St. Helens, in one of the tramcars of the St. Helens and District Tramways Company, and Farrell was taken to the Haydock Cottage Hospital in an insensible condi- tion. The identification of the four men who lost their lives was accompanied by some affecting scenes. Their names and addresses were ascertained to be Albert Mar- shall, of Earlestown ; Thomas Sharp, of Warrington- road, Ashton-in-Makerfield, who was only recently married; Michael Cawlfield, 32, Wood-st., Earlestown ; and Patrick M'Cue, 13, Warrington-road, Ashton. The injured man William Farrell, lived at Florida- cottages, Haydock, and had recovered conscious- ness late en Thursday night. The terrible occur- rence cast a gloom over the neighbourhood. It was found after an examination that one of the chains of the hoppet had become detached from the winding chain, and this would cause it to lean on one side. The engine winder William Hardman, is an experienced man, and it was stated that no blame was attached to him for the sad calamity. The police authori- ties were informed of the accident soon after its occur- rence, and Police-constable Potter was the first officer t. arrive on the scene. The bodies of the four men were removed ta the Lecture Hall, from the pit brow, in the horse ambulance carriage kept at the colliery offices. The sides of the pit shaft are timbered all the distance from top to bottom, and this, we understand, is the practice adopted in nearly all collieries.

div.head: STACK FIRE AT NORTON.
div.p: STACK FIRE AT NORTON.

About two o'clock on Sunday, three stacks of meadow hay were discovered to be on fire on land near the Ship Canal cutting in the occupation of Mr. Peter Wor- thington, of The Cottage, Norton. Only one stack had been on fire originally,but the flames had spread,through the action of the,wind. At four o'clock the Runcorn Fire Brigade were sent for, but did not arrive on the scene until nearly six o'clock. Mr. Jackson, cab proprietor, who contracts to supply the brigade with horses had not an animal in his stalls, and nearly three quarters of an hour were spent in a fruitless endeavour to obtain horses to draw the engine. At last application was made to Mr. W. Hankinson, who is a member of the Board of Com- missioners, and he at once complied with the request,and two of his horses quickly transferred the engine to the place where it was required. For six hours the Brigade poured water on the burning mass, directing their efforts chiefly to saving two other stacks from destruction and they were completely successful. The amount of hay co nsumedis about 70 tons, worth about £2OO. The loss is fully covered by insurance in the Yorkshire Assur- ance Society.

div.head: LIBERAL UNIONIST DEMONSTRATION.
div.p: LIBERAL UNIONIST DEMONSTRATION.

On Wednesday night a Liberal Unionist demonstration was held in St. James's Hall, London. Sir Henry James, who occupied the chair, said that the object for which the Liberal Unionist party had been established had al- ready been attained. They had a right now to ask their opponents if they wished they had succeeded in carrying Home Rule in 1886, and whatever answer was given the vindication of the Liberal Unionists was complete. Ire- land had now acknowledged the Queen's Government, crime bad passed away, and the plan of campaign was defeated. The Liberal Unionists, in assisting to ac- complish this, had done their duty alike to Ireland and to the Empire. A resolution of confidence in the Government's Irish policy having been passed, Lord Hartington said that Unionists desired nothing better than that the next general election should be fought again on the issue of Home Rule, but their opponents would no doubt do all they could to confuse the issue with the vaguest and wildest of generalities. But the Unionists must do all. in their power to prevent for a second time that great fraud and imposture being practised on the people. He claimed that so far as social reforms were .concerned the present Unionist Government had dealt or attempted to deal with all questions in the Glad- st.2nian programme.
MINERS' DEMONSTRATION AT SOUTHPORT. CONGESTED TRAFFIC.

Southport was on Saturday the scene of the third an- nual demonstration of the Lancashire and Cheshire Miners' Federation, and with fine weather, the popular Lancashire watering-place was thronged with visitors. The long procession was marshalled on the shore, oppo- site the Victoria Hotel, and, in the presence of large crowds, moved off a little after noon. There were about 50 bands, with numerous banners, and the miners pre-, sented a very respectable appearance, while the extent of the procession made it a very imposing demonstration. At No. 1 platform the Mayor of Southport (Councillor Pilling) opened the proceedings by offering the miners a hearty welcome to Southport, and re- ferring to their orderly conduct on the oc- casion of their previeus visit to the town. The following resolutions were carrred at both plat- forms:—" That, in the opinion of this mass meeting of Lancashire and Cheshire miners, a permanent eight hours day for underground workmen must be procured by Act a Parliament, and, seeing that this question is of such vital importance to the health,safety,and wellbeing of miners generally, we agreerto vote for no candiditte who will not consent to vote for the miners' eight hours I Bill. Wealso wish to 'impress upon the present or any other Government who may bring in an Employers' Liability Bill that no Bill will be acceptable to the miners, which contains a clause allowing workpeople to contract out of its provisions. Seeing that a strong organisation is necessary to obtain the just rights of working-men, we pledge ourselves not only to stand by our unions, but to use every legitimate means to get every man employed about collieries to become members of this federation, and also of the Federationof Great Britain. "Seeing that our representatives have held two successful conferences with the Continental miners, and seeing that all • miners are agreed on the Continent and throughout Great Britain (Durham and Northumberland excepted) to obtain an eight hours day by legislation, we consider the time has arrived when an International Federation of Miners should be established. We much regret the appointment of the Royal Commission on Labour, believing that it will have a tendency for the time being to keep back the Miners' Eight Hours Bill and other labour legislation, and knowing that Royal Commissions in the past have been lengthy in their inquiries 'and produced so little good to the working' dlaSs-es. Seeing that the great labour interest is soarcely repre- seated in Parliament, and beTievin,g that it is necessary to bring to, bear upon any GoVernment a preponderaiing- influence to move them in, the direction of legislating oh questions directly affecting labour, we. consider that a large increase of labour members in,the House of Com- mons is needed we therefore pledge out :unbounded Suriport in ' the return to seats in Parliament of Mr. Samuel Woods, -for Ince, . and Mr. Tho Mas Aspinall, for Wigari." An eetraordirlarY delay occurred in the despatch of trains carrying the excursionists ,bit 4 to their homes. At ten o'clock at night 10,000 people were waiting for trains which did reit-come alongside the platfoetn. the #lines - having been blocked, partly by an accident, but' inainly theektes- sive traffic. The small hours of the morning arrived, and still no trains ,Were available: Many of the ezZ•cursionists perambulated the Streets; some found lodgings; others, reposed on the turf banks of the line and in private gar- dens,'bUt several thaisands remained at the sta,tion, where they, daneed to the strains of a brass band. The, place was well lighted and the sceee was most faritastic. There were many women with ohildren among the be- lated travellers: Fortunately, the weather was warm and dry. it was broad daylight before the trains, were enabled to clear away the traffic. "

SOUTHPORT Seems to Suit the eel- Fern Miners tiom, ' hers' as a place-for demonstrating,: onstra and they have for the second tim :- shown good sense in selecting it. There is nsc reason why they should not combine pleasure with business; and,. having both objects in view, hum could they do, better than go to the sea-side? Life in a coalniina: is not particularly cheerful in its, 3urroundinga.,;. but Southpo. with its boulevards, gardens,and (general look of brightness and beauty, an admizable and refreshing contrast. The miners recognise this; hence the enormous attend 4 ance at the demonstration. It is estimated that at least 50,009 persons took part in the procession,. and that the total number of visitors—for the re;ners take-their wives with them—was consider- ably oyez -100,000. This is a good thing for, Southport„ whatever the superfine idlers may say who wish to, "keep Southport respectable," and would not: have a collier come "between the wind and their 4 nobility." Assuming an average ex,• - penditurs. of two shillingsper head, only, it moans that theinvaders would expend £lO,OOO in the town. tr CHARLES DUKE was the principal speaker at the open-air meeting; and he had an experience in getting to Southport Tithich was probably unique. In commencing his address he said:—" I do not;c know that I am in. very good form to make aspeech to you, because your demonstration has so completely demoralised your railways that my arrival has been made late and somawhat painful. I reached Wigan on time, as the Americans say,. from London, not s, minute late.; but from Wigan to here I have been standing up), with others, peeked like herrings in a guard's van for about three hours of time, and I fear that lam somewhat he worse for the process." How- ever, as the result showed, Sir CHARLE4S had not been upset in mind by the rough uSage to which he had been subjected. Eris speech was thought- ful and moderate in statement, and should be :carefully considered by those who do uot see their way as yet to asking Parliament to establish an eight hours day for miners. It is significant that the opposition amongst colliers to a Parliamentary eight hours' day comes from the workers in Durham wad Northumberland, many of whom are now working six and seven hours per day. But what of the boys in that part of the country? Sir C3ARLES said they worked long hours, and he was loudly applauded when he asked :—"Why do not the miners there by trade union effort, which they state was successful in getting their own hours reduced, get the hours of •the lads reduced also ?"

The speaker was equally pertinent in pointing out that the people who now said workmen must look to their trades unions to reduce hours and not to Parliament were the very men who in the past had been most opposed to trades unions. lie urged that the case of miners deserved special consideration because their occupation was a

dangerous one and unfavourable to health, £TII because it was to the advantage of employers and employed that the change, whenever it was made, should be on a permanent basis. Touching the question of labour representation in Parliament? Sir CHARLES plainly told his hearers that the ;natter was in their own hands; and! that if , inciustrial communities were unrepresented it was "because a great number of trades unionists prefer sport or some other interest above political representation.' These are words of sense' and soberness which ought to be- well pondered by the Workers in eveiy town in the Kingdom. If they we 'helpless to-day, it is because they do not con-- bine tk:r• make use of their opportunities. Consi6r for a rnoment the situation in this part of ths' country.. We have Warrington; St. Helens,. Widnes.Blvision,and Newton Division represented ' by rneu whose training, habits, and inclinations are on the side of the Asses and against the masses. The workers are all powerful' in these con- stituencies,-if they care to put forth their strength ; and, to speakiof the miners clone, if they would only take as much interest in politics asthey do in racing, they would certainly effect a change both at St. lielens and Newton. As to Warrington, it is enough to excite the laughte, of the gods to imagine any workman who thinks at all on labour questions voting for Sir Gilbert GREEN-Ma.: If there is one article. more than another which insures an enormous-profit to the manufacturer, with a ridiculously- small expenditurocupcm-labour, it is intoxicating liquor. We say nothing here of the moral side of the- question, thoug:i f that is one which working-men ought certainly to' 'consider.' Evohrtion is slow in these matters, bat' we are hopeful that it will be sun ; and there can' be no question that the process, will be aideVby such magnificent demonstrations, as that at Siuthport on Saturday last.

THE Conservatives of the New- Conservatives at ton Division' had a pleasant- time Lyme ?ark- of it at Lyme• Park, on Saturday. There is ne such thing as bribery and corruption now-a-days),and Mr. T. W. LEUH; M.P.; must feel that it is a blessed privilege to be able to invite his actual and possible supporters, to a gala day at his father's park, at Disley. There was a fair at- tendance—for where is the free and independent elector who has not a hankering for a June pic- nic? There would doubtless have been more people present if the miners of the district had sot been demonstrating at Southport, on the same day. They could not, like Bhyie Roche's bird, be in two.pla-ces at once, or they: would have taken to the races, if not to the speeches, which were supplied atLyme Park. The member for the division, in addiessing his followers, afEected to. believe that the bottom had been kneeked but of the Home Rule ship; but, judging from the re- sults of the by-elections, he must have. confuse& Home Rule with the Government. If the-liherals are supposed to helmhappy when they 'ars rapidly gaining ground, • what must be the- miserable plight of the Tories, when they are as rapidly los- ing it? Perhaps, Mr.. Lr.on intended his, speech to be taken "kinder-sarcastic "—for he sometimes ,strokes the cat the wrong way. Indeed,:there is noother method of making sense of his etattement that the Government "were put into offibe to ,settle the Irish question, and he thought they had done so most effectually." This,following upon the assertion that theArish were engaged in breaking each other's heads. is rather a neat way of twit- ting the Government ia general and tin, Irish 'Secretary in particular upon the result of their message of peace to the Sister Isle. Witir,regard to "the boon of Fire Education " which M,rli.Boir says had "just beeaconferred," it seems to us that it is a trifle prematureto pr.t in a claim for credit. In the first place, the boon has not yet been!con- ferred, and, if Alr...autzrzy, and some otheriCbr- servatives can have their way, it will not be con- ferred at all. In the second place, the change 'which is proposed does. not really free educa- tion ; for it carries the absurdity in the face of it of charging school &les for children from three to 'five years of age, while abolishing the fees,..where they are abolished,- of children from five te,four- teem The Bill as.it stands. pleases nobody; .it is. "neither fish, fleshgowl—nor even good red.her- ring."

, Sir W. Manama/cr follovred, and was, not made happy by the reminder that he wa..% ".one who was once a -Liberal but was now a Conserva- tive: It is an intelligible course when a man goes, forward—like M.A.Gtaios,roNa—from Toryism to. Liberalism ; but when he halts by the way, or goes back, it is usually for, place or pension. Some- body called out, "Bread and cheese" whilst Si WILLIAM was speaking; and Sir WlLLiam, in- stantly replied that "that was a solid; found- ation for anything: He ought to. know, for he is greatly misiudged if "bread and cheese" have not had _something,_ to do with his turning. Tbry. His speech was-devoted chiefly to praising,the foreign and colonial policy of the Government,which, he said, had "'not been challenged by a single member of the Radical party." Buwhy.? For the excellent 7aason that •it was to a large- extent a Liberal pc-hey. The Tories have simply walked in this resp,ect in the path markcaxiut by Mr. CAADSTONE. There was. a time when they had a foreign polioy of( their own. It was, a. Jingo policy; but the- country would not have it; and they are driven to adopt- ing the vh,,,ws of the Liberals in foreignand colon- ial mattere—just as they are with regard• to what they call Ftee Education. It is true 'there seema to have been a bit of old-fashioned Toryism in the conduct,of affairs at Manipur, but it has turned out in every way very badly, and there is nobody to defend it—not even Sir Wii-JAN' Irlanniorr. But to return to the "-outing" toDialey, it passed off very-well ; the weather was fine; the sports were interesting ; and what moreeauld any good Tory, require ?

Walling 14:&., poet who hoped to meet his Day. boat love in the better land said heaven would not be heaven, without her; and Warrington would certainly not be Warrington without Walking Day. It is. an old and much- prized institution, and long may it flourish ; for is it not associated, when the weather is fine—all, ;that weather4,—with almost everything that adds to the pleasures of life ; with cessation, from toil, with bands„and banners, and happy excitement in the sight el gaily-attired children, all alive With the sport which begins with the procession, and continues amid games, and sweets, and nuts, and milk and buns through the whole of the long summer's day? As The .beauty of delight makes lovers glad

Gazing on one another; aßd, as gladness, like laughter, is contagious, the ehildren in the gaiety of their hearts make the' elders gay. They open the eastern windows That look towards the sun, Where thoughts are singing swallo And the brooks of morning run. It costs something in the way of time and
prepav,

ation to be ready for Walking Day—to say nothing of the actual expenditure in new suits and new frocks; and it is a pity when the weather is wet. But the law Of averages holds good. Last year it was bright in the early morning, but the day turned out very wet. Yesterday morning was not bright; and for an hour or two there was a very uneasy feeling. What if there should be a repeti- tion of the thunderstorms of the two previous days 1 The prospect was appalling, but prospects change, and the change in this case was a happy • one, for the sun began to smile, and then every- body smiled, and the result was a smiling day, if not a smiling morn. Warrington certainly never looks better than it does on a fine Walking Day. The sun gets a fair chance, for there is a tempor- ary removal of the volumes of smoke which usually everhang the town. The wealth of colour which is supplied by the procession and the decorations is thus seen, as it ought to be seen ; and for once in the year the narrow irregular streets becomb really picturesque. Why cannot the town be at all times free from black smoke? Something could and hould be done to lessen it; but for the present let there be "surcease of sorrow" as to this and other troubles. The brief holiday which is given to the workpeople of Warrington has begun, and we hope, with fine weather and purses well lined, they will thoroughly enjoy it.

On page 3 there will be found an account of the Warrington Blue Coat School as it was known 4` One hundred years' ago -" and on page 2 some news as to Warrington friends in America, which has been furnished by Mr. J. S. Green since his return.

Tussaud's waxwork exhibition has been des- troyed. It was a "melting moment" for the dis- tinguished company, when the fire broke out; the beat proved more than they could stand ; and they finally" ran away."

It is stated that the shares in the coffin furniture syndicate have depreciated to the tune of £250,000. There is a "dead" loss, it seems, in the coffin business as in other trades, at times. Indeed, it is suggestive of giving up the ghost when £5O shares dwindled down to £1 per share.

Mr. Herbert Spencer is becoming aweary of ex- plaining that he is not a materialist ; but he ex- plains once more, in a letter to the Ethical Associ- ation of Brooklyn, and thus strikes out in conclu- sion :—" In my earlier days I constantly made the foolish supposition that conclusive proofs would change beliefs. But experience has long since dis- sipated my faith in men's rationality."

The foolishness of the wise 11IPICinley is every day being made more apparent. The tariff on lead ore is causing the Mexicans to set up smelting works of their own rather than pay the duty im- posed on them, with the result that a new home industry will be commenced. Thus the M‘Kinley Act is killing the geese which have laid the golden eggs—a not unusual thing with Protection.

A Correspondent who signs himself "A Good Friend " wishes to know how it is that the Corpor- ation permit people to hang clothes lines across the street at night. He says it has resulted in a man's head being" nearly cut off." We are quite sure that the Corporate officials know nothing of this breach of the bye-laws ; and if our "Good Friend 'S will be good enough to name the street the cm- plaint will have speedy attention.

St. Mary Woolnoth is one of the London city churches which is well-nigh empty every Sunday. Sometimes the Rector is tempted to address the Sexton, as Dean Swift is reported to have done, and begin—" Dearly beloved Roger." The other Sun- day there was a larger attendance than usual— there were actually eight persons in the church. There was a reason for it—it was wet. Some people use their religion as a cloak; others make it serve as an umbrella.

The new Bishop of Lichfield is, after all, the Rev. Canon Legge, Vicar of St. Mary's, Lewes- ham. He is a brother of the Earl of Dartmouth; he is an able man, and is described as "abounding in good works of every kind." Touching the cere - monies attending the confirmation of a bishop, Lord Grirnthorpe, in a letter to the " Times " says —"The solemnity is not one which becomes more: impressive the oftener you perform it." He speaks of it, indeed, as "tremendous and mendacious humbug."

The clergy as well as the laity are being disabled by illness. Canon Greenall, of Grappenhall,is try- ing to recruit at Rhyl ; and Canon Dodd, who re- lieved him in the pulpit a short time since, is him- self amongst those who have now reached he convalescent stage. Going higher still up the ecclesiastical ladder' we have news of the illness of both the Bishop of Manchester and the Bishop of Liverpool.

With the arrival of warm weather, there has been a decline, a slight decline, of the epidemic of influenza. The death-rate of Warrington is still 50 per cent. above the average ; and sufferers can- not be too careful in nursing themselves. The term influenza as used in connection with the epidemic has been in one respect unfortunate ; it has caused people to treat attacks of this peculiar illness too lightly, with the result in many cases, on returning to work or business too soon, of a relapse which has proved fatal. "Hasten slowly" should be the motto for the convalescent.

The St. Helens branch of the Irish National League have repudiated Mr. Parnell and all his works and ways; and they are now directing their attention to getting rid of Mr. Seton-Karr, at the next election, as member for the borough. They will do it if they work hard, and work unitedly. As Roman Catholics, they have an incentive to work in remembering that Mr. Seton-Karr treated them with contumely in voting against the Roman Catholic Disabilities Bill which was brought in by Mr. Gladstone.

The post mortem examination of the body of Alfred Brown, the cyclist, who died suddenly, at Latchford, on Saturday afternoon, revealed what might have been expected under the circumstances —enlargement and fatty degeneration of the heart. It is hardly necessary to say that cycling is not for people who suffer from enlargement of the heart. The difficulty is to know when the heart is diseased; but where there is the slightest suspicion a medical man should be consulted, and his advice should be acted upon.

Sir John Gorst, Under Secretary for India, has been getting it hot from Lord Cross, the Chief Secretary for India. It was thought he would resign, after the way in which his superior rounded' on him in the House of Lords for what he had said, in the Commons, during the Manipur debate. But he clings to the Treasury Bench, and makes believe that his withers are unwrung: He has tried to explain himself away, but in doing so he has given himself away. It would have been more to his credit if he had resigned.

The Prince of Wales visited Eastbourne on Saturday, and on Sunday his taste for gaming was denounced from the pulpit. If he reads or hears of a tithe of what is said about him, he will realise that he is regarded as a power for good or ill. This ought to set him thinking. He has arrived as a grandfather at the years which are supposed to "bring the philosophic mind." Ile will know as he never knew before what Shakespeare meant by saying : Princes are the glass, the school, the book, Where subjects' eyes, do learn, do read, do look.

Lord Churchill, writing from South Africa, is as consistent as he is candid in explaining why he is away from Parliament at the present time : "Politics for a time attracted him little. The principal measure before the House of Commons, which was being pressed forward by the Govern- ment and by the party to which he belonged, he disliked intensely, and while he was not prepared to take part in any opposition to the measure, from motives which friends would appreciate, he was resolved to give no vote and say no word in its favour." This is pretty hard on the Irish Land Bill. Lord Randolph is looking ahead; he can see where the measure will break down.

On Tuesday, the magistrates of Warrington had before them a notorious character named Ernest Eastman, who had been twenty-eight times con- victed of various offences. According to the evi- dence of the police, the prisoner, whilst drunk and disorderly, had assaulted two women. One of them had sustained a wound in the head in which P.C. Dean said he could insert two fingers; and it was added that the house was like a slaughter- house. The case was clear against the double- dyed ruffian; and the bench sentenced him to— what? To one month's imprisonment!! It is true the woman whose head was laid open was the ruffian's wife; and perhaps that made all the differ- ence in the eyes of the magistrates.

div.head: FIRST AID TO THE INJURED AT RUNCORN.
div.p: FIRST AID TO THE INJURED AT RUNCORN.

About eleven o'clock, en Saturday night, Joseph Mor- gan, of the Stone Hills, slipped and fell while walking up Delph Bridge. The back of his head came in contact with thepavement,and a severe wound, which bled free- ly, was inflicted. P.S. Woolley, fortunately was in the neighbourhood, and after examining the wound h 3 made a bandage of the man's muffler, bound up the wound, checked the flow of blood, and sent the man home. Sergeant Woolley is a member of the Ambulance Society. RuNconN BICYCLE °Lug. A number of the " wheelmen " of Runcorn have just organised a club under the title of the Runcorn Bicycle Club,and the membership has already.assumed satisfactory proportions. The affairs of the club are managed by a committee consisting of Messrs. J. Turnbull, W. Mack, G. Marsh, J. Nickson, G. Nicholson, and R. Morton,and the officials are: Captain, C. C. Le Couteur, Sub-Captain, E. S. Lea, bugler, F. Le Couteur, treasurer, F. Rushton, and secretary, C. Handley. The club colours are dark blue and the badge is a shield inscribed " Runcorn 8.C." The annual subscription is 2s. 6d. per annum.
ONE PHASE OF THE SOCIAL PROBLEM AT WIDNES

At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, John Dagnall was charged with having on the previous night slept in the Widnes Alkali Company's Chemical works, without visible means of subsiEtence and not given a good account of himself.—P.C. Messenger proved the case,and the prisoner said he was out of work and could not get a job anywhere,and he could not sleep in a field in weather like it was that night.—Superintendent Noblett said the prisoner threw himself out of employment of his own freewill. He had been three times convicted of neglect- ing his wife and family and five times of drunkenness. On Sunday his wife and children were found destitute in the street and were brought into the station for shelter. He would not work.—Mr. Deacon (to prisoner) : You have been here so often and must have known you had no right where you were.—The Prisoner: A man can't go and make a hole in the water and end himself.— Mr. Deacon : You can go to the Work- house. If you won't take the trouble to work, you must go to prison for seven days. •

_ BRUNSWICK SUNDAY SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY, RUNCORN. The celebration of the anniversary of the establish- ment of Brunswick Wesleyan Sunday School is an event of interest in the town outside the extensive circle of Wesleyanism, and the present occasion was no ex- ception in this respect. The spacious chapel of St. Paul was well filled at the morning service, and in the evening the edifice was not equal to the demands made upon the accommodation, and many were unable to gain admit- tance. The preacher was the Rev. F. L. Wiseman, 8.A., of Birmingham, a believer in the forward movement, and an active worker in the cause; his labours in Birm- ingham having been crowned with splendid success. He delivered two well thought-out and practical discourses, and his eloquent periods acted with telling effect upon his numerous hearers. The collections, in aid of the school funds, reached nearly £4O. A third service was held in the chapel on Monday evening, when the Rev. Chas. Garrett. ex-President of the Conference, occupied the pulpit. There was again a large congregation, and the collection realised a satisfactory amoilet. ASSAULT ON A LOCK-TENTER AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Joseph Row- lands, alias Porter, was charged with assaulting a lock- tenter named John Inman.—complainant said on Mon- day night, the 15th just, he was in charge of No. 8 Lock on the Bridgewater Canal. The defendant was there with a narrow boat, and without any provocation he took hold of witness by the left arm and left leg and tossed him over. His arm and shoulder were injured, and he had since been under the care of Dr. McDougall, and unable to work.—ln cross-examination witness ad- mitted that he had unloosed the rope of defendant's boat because he had no right to 6c,0 through the lock when the tide flats were there.—The defendant said nobody must loose his boat's rope or he would loose them. If com- plainant had been a young fellow—he told them straight —he would have dropped him into the lock, but he never lifted a hand to him; he only snatched him down with taking the rone off him.-1 he defendant was fined £1 including costs, or 14 days. He declared he would go to gaol, as he had not doneanything,but he afterwards paid the money. RIVAL SHOEMAKERS AT WIDNES.

At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday,Walter Baron, a shoemaker, summoned Thomas Hall, master shoe- maker, Mersey-road, for having, on 'I hursday, the 18th June, threatened to assault him, whereby he was afraid he would do him some bodily harm. Mr. J. W. Knowles prosecuted, and Mr. Swift, barrister, defended. It ap- peared that on the afternoon in question, complainant and a friend stopped opposite defendant's shop. The defendant pushed the friend aside, and when the complainant told him to leave him alone, defendant pushed complainant against the shutters of an adjoining shop, and made use of several sanguinary threats. Com- plainant said he was afraid defendant would do him some violence. In cross-examination complainant ad- mitted that two hours later he went to defendant's, and told him he would make him pay for what he had done. The defence was that complainant was in the habit of standing in front of the shop window, and obstructing the light of the workshop, and annoying the workmen. The defendant had merely pushed him away, and the complainant was in no fear. Mr. Swift pointed to his conduct after the occurrence. The case was dis- missed without hearing cases for the defence. div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JUNE 27, 1891.
PARAVFIN LAMP EXPLOSION AT WIDNES.

, A serious paraffin lamp accident occurred at Widnes on Sunday, in the house of James Concannon, of 1, Cromwell-st. About a quarter to ten a young woman named Catherine Concannon, employed as a domestic servant, attempted to turn up the light of the paraffin lamp which was suspended from the ceiling of the kit- chen when an explosion took place. The burning oil covered the neck and arms of the girl, who suffered the greatest agolty. Dr. gutchinsen? who was at once called in, considered her condition so dangerous, that he ordered her immediate removal to the Accident Hospital. THREATFNING WITEr A ENTFE AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn Petty Sessions;•on' Monday, Thomas Brett was charged with being driltilt and disorderly. P.C. Shaw said the prisoner was very drunk on Saturday night, on Waterloo Bridge, and was using bad language. He told him to be quiet and go away. The prisoner re- plied that "No one—bobby could. make him," and he drew fcrth a pocket knife. At once the constable seized his wrist, and wrested the weapon from his hand. —The prisoner informed the Bench that he had no in- tention of using the knife. Mr. Reynolds told him he had better keep such things in his pocket when he had had drink. The police might have brought a much more serious charge against him than they had.—A fine of ss. and costs was imposed. •

PICNIC TO DELAMERE. The Railway Hotel picnic club took their first annual outing on Thursday to Delamere Forest, under most un- favourable circumstances, rain pouring down almost all day. The party travelled through Newton, Kingsley, and Hatchmere to Delamere Forest, and thence to Mr. Walker, Eddisbury Lodge,where a substantial repast was done justice to, the company afterwards having their portraits taken in a group by Mr. Pye. Mr.Griffiths, the manager of the Railway Hotel, is to be highly compli- mented for the manner everything was arranged, the party thoroughly enjoying themselves, although the day was so wet. The party on returning to Runcorn, were entertained by Mr. Griffiths to a splendid spread, to which ample justice was done. THE LIVERPOOL AND ST. HELENS RAILWAK. The Liverpool, St. Helens, and South Lancashire Railway Bill came before Lord Morley in the House of Lords yesterday week unopposed, and was al- lowed to pass.
B2I7TAL ASSAULT ON A PAILAMOITSC AT WIDNES.

William Walmsley. a labourer from If ortli-st,was brought before the Widnes magistrates,on Wednes- dayr charged with unlawfully wounding Mary McDevmott, with whom he cohabited. Oh Tuesday night at ball-past eleven Mrs. Dermott who was in bed, heard a disturbance in the streets and got up with the intention of seeing what was the matter. When shr got downstairs she met the prisoner, who said "You are the--one I've been looking:for," and he felled her to the gramed with his flit and while she was lying there,. he savagely kicked her. Ile:tben procured a boot and using this as a weapon cruelly battered her head, causing serious wounds. She was .under the care of Mr.. Hudson.—The prisoner was mmmitted to the quarter Sessions for trial.

This Bill, which has already passed the Comniona-,. came on Thursday before the Rouse of Lords Select Committee, presided over by the Earl of Elgin._ The Bill among other things, gives power to the promoters to subscribe to the undertaking of the Wrexham, Mold, and Connah'S Quay Company any sum not exceeding £lOO,OOO, to the Wrexham and Ellesmere Company any sum, not ex-ceeding .£50,000, and to the Liverpool, St. Helens, and South Lanca- shire Railway Company £20,000. BMIGHATION.—Intending emigrants to New York, Boston Philadelphia, San Francisco, Canapla, China, Japan, Aus- tralia, or New Zealand, should take tickets (lowest rates) at the " Examiner" Office, by Cunard, alciun, American. Aus- tralian, Oriental, and other lines.—John Walker, agent, "Examiner ' Office. Bewsey-st.. Warrington.—Advt. TRIAL OF A NEW ISLE OF MAN STEAMER.

on Wednesday the new steel twin-screw steamer Tynwald, built for the Isle of Man Steam Packet Company by the Fairfield Shipbuilding and Engi- neering Company, Govan, made her trial run on the Clyde. The vessel has been specially designed for the Channel passenger traffic between the Isle of Man and England, Ireland, and Scotland, first-class passenger accommodation having been provided. The steamer will carry between eight and nine hun- dred passengers. The dimensions are-265 ft. long, 34 ft. 4 in. beam, 14 ft. Gin. (moulaed) depth. The engines are of the triple-expansion inverted type. The electric light is fitted up throughout. The ves- sel has eight water-tight bulkheads, and is in every respect one of the finest passenger vessels afloat. On the measured mile a mean speed of 1938. knots was run, and a maximum speed of 19.5 knots. This is fl knots above the guaranteed contract speed. The vessel was taken down the Clyde as far as Pladda Light, and returned, cruising on the way, into Rothe- say Bay and Lech Long. The capabilities of the Tynwald were tested critically, and at the dinner Mr. Malrea, chairman of the directors of the Isle of Man Company, expressed himself as highly satisfied with the result, the maximum speed being main- tained easily and without forcing. A LIVERPOOL TRADESMAN AND HIS RAILWAY FARE.

Thomas W. Baker, provision dealer, Temple-st., was summoned before the Widnes magistrates to answer acharge of having travelled on the London and North-Western Railway without having pre- viously paid his fare, and with intent to avoid pay- ment.—Mr. A. E. Preston prosecuted. It appeared that on the 3rd June, the defendant was seen at Lime-st., Station to take a ticket to Edge-hill, and from information wl,ich came to the know— ledge of the officials, the guard of the train watched him at Edge-hill. The defendant, alighted, and re-entered the compartment when the train was on the move. At Crewe he walked about the platform, had a drink at the refreshment room, and crossed to the North Stafford platform, and after the tickets had been examined jumped into the train for Stoke. A collector followed him and demanded his ticket, and defendant pretended to search for it,but failed to find it,then offered to pay his fare, but the collector refused to receive it. Detective Freeborough then caused defendant to leave the compartment, and asked him why he had booked to Edge Hill and not to Stoke, and he replied that he had been drinking, was muddled, and did not know what he was doing.—The Bench imposed a fine of 20.4. and costs 14s. . .

The register of voters which will be prepared in July and revised in September of this year will be of the utmost importance, ana it is neceseary that it should be as complete and accurate as possible. On this register, says Mr. W. Handley in a circular he has issued, the next County Council election on March Bth will be conteste'd,and is generally antici- pated that a general election will also be fought on the same register.

During the present week a meeting of active Liberals has been held at the Runcorn Liberal Club with a view to carrying out the work effectively, and there was: no lack of offers of assistance. The town has been divided into districts as usual, and Mr. W. Ockleston has been appointed chairman of Runcorn North and Mr. P.Speakman, C.C., chairman of Runcorn South. Last, night Mr. Ockleston met his workers at the club, and to the accompaniment of a cup of coffee and a whiff of the fragrant, weed discussed the How and When of the situation. Mr. Speakman will have a similar gathering next week. •

For the same purpose Widnes Division Liberal Association have divided Widnes into wards, and ward meetings will be held witbin the next few days to make all arrangements. Remember, elec- tions are fought and won in the Revision Courts.

A great improvement, and one which has been long needed, is on the point ot being completed at Runcorn Railway Station. Formerly the height of the steps of the carriages from the platform was so great that it was a tiource of inconvenience and annoyance if not positive danger. especially to ladies, who had frequently had to make a jump for "terra firma." By lowering the metals a foot and rai§ing the platform a foot the platform has been brought nearly to the lever of the carriage steps and entrance and exit can now be made with corLfort and ,:safety.

A petition. inspired by the tradesmen of Widnes, is shortly to be presented to the Lord High Chan- cellor with the object of procuring better County Court facilities in that town. At present the Widnes office is only open for a few hours on two days in the week, and the various books are kept at the head office in St. Helens, causing much incon- venience and delay to suitors whenever they desire ,any information. The petitioners wish a separate office to be established at Widnes and open daily from 10 to 4 and that a separate set of books shall be kept. In support of this request it is pointed out that the Widnes County court district contains a population of 45,000 and that the average number of plaints entered for each sitting of the Judge is 200, or one-third of the whole number entered in the St. Helens Court of which Widnes Is a branch. Under these circumstances the demand made is a reasonallle one and will no doubt be granted.

The four-cornered duel invented by the irrepres- sible Mr. Midshipman Easy, will sink into insig- nificance before the many-cornered duel that appears likely to take place when Widnes is a borough and the first election of councillors takes place. The candidates of five electoral organisations and a few independents would be a hotch-potch sort of contest that "no feller" could understand, and the ratepayers would be puzzled beyond endur- ance in deciding on whom they should bestow their suffrages. Although some persons have an objec- tion to politics being introduced Into local affairs, there is no doubt that the political element will be introduced sooner or later; and the best thing that could happen for the town would be that the Liberal and Conservative clubs should enter the fray at the start and put an end to the cmfusion that other- wise will arise.

The last electoral association with the tit le of the Tradesmen's and Householders' Association, was formed on Wednesday evening. About 26 trades- men put in an appearance, but the proceedings were far from enthusiastic—in fact the interest was of a very half-hearted character. Very few more than half voted on the proposal to form the association, and there was an apparent reluctance to accept official positions. Eventually Mr. W. Hodgkinson was elected president; )!Ir. A. E. Calvert, vice-president ; Mr. F. H. Pankhurst, trea- surer, and Mr. F. Lawrinson, secretary. The Corn-

mittee consists of Messrs. D. J. Brooks, C. Brig- stock, LP. Lewis, C. ilynn, W. G. Bucknall, W. H. Thomas, and H. CYDogyrrell. It will be of interest to Runcorniaus to know that the first steamer that sailed on the Ship Canal and the only one now navigating it waters was.formerly the property of Messrs. Timmins, engineers, who made and fixed the engine and boilers themselves, the hall being constructed by Mr. Roberts, boat builder,ofehester. The steamer, which is named Jenny, after the dat2ghter of Mr. Yam Timmins,. was sold to the late Mr. Walker a year or two ago.

Cavan Wood. the vicar of Bancorn, is reruch exercised in his nye: zd about lite clause in the scheme of the Cottage Hospital,. which prevents I ministers of religion from; serving on the Manage- ment Committee of the Institution. In a letter to 1 a contemporary he endeavours to show that minis- ters can meet together and discuss mundane mat- ters without the introduction; of religious dife- rences ;and he contends that the clause is a viola- ;lion of the first principles of fair play, and contrary to the spirit of the scheme which has been adopted. ;Surely the Vicar's memory must be very "short'. if , he has forgotten what ocanrred at the first meeting,; called to start the hospital movement. The flock over which he has the spiritual guidanee,andmuch, ,influence in ordinary affairs, turned up in most un- usual number,, and the charge that they came with design has never been denied—in fact, it has been admitted that there was a special " whip" up, with the avowed purpose of protecting that useful insti- tution, "The District Nurse Fund." The character of the audience was reflected in the committee ap- pointed, and three members—influential gentlemen —declined to act, because of the religious element introduced, and the unrepresentative character of the committee.

The Vicar says Mr. Lake by his motion introduced the religious question when it ought never to have been mentioned. The fact is.that the religious ques- tion had been very much introduced previously,and threatened to wreck the whole project of founding the hospital; and Mr. Lake's motion was intended to,and to all appeal ance has sacceeded ,in eradicating it altogether, for there now is a feeling throughout the, town to work for the success of the cause i 7 tea- pective of sect or party. The Vicar claims to be treated as an ordinary man in this matter, but he cannot forget the "certain grace" bestowed "in ordination" which, according to his argument, places him on a higher plane than other men. Clergymen, and ministers (is there any difference?) are regarded as the leaders and champions of their particular sects, and conamand a certain following irrespective of reason and argument, and were they placed on the committee in the present state of religious difference in the town, sectarian divisions. am afraid would take place too fiequently for the good of the hospital. Whatever committee is appointed differences of opinion must arise, and debates may sometimes be of a heated character, but they will not be tinged with religous animosity, the most virulent of all. It is for the good of the hospital that the Vicar should acquiesce, as the other ministers appear to have done, in the decision of the meeting. Can he efface himself for that end?

Fifty members of Runcorn Tonic Sol-fa Choir, of which Mr. John Holford, G.T.S.C., is the able con- ductor, intend to take part in the celebration of the Jubilee of the sol-fa system which will be held at. the Crystal Palace next month. Mr. L. C. Venables, who will conduct the concert by provincial singers, held a rehearsal of the Runcorn contingent. on Thursday evening. He expressed his pleasure at the progress made, and complimented the choir and Mr. Holford on the state of efficiency attained.

div.head: WIGAN OUTRAGE.
div.p: THE WIGAN OUTRAGE.

At Wigan on Thursday,Edward Kelly was brought up on remand charged with the attempted murder of Matthew Webster and Ellen Kerfoot, on the 14th inst. Prisoner was again remanded for seven days awaiting the prosecutor's recovery. Upon inquiry at the infirmary it was ascertained that Webster was progressing very favourably.
THE CHARGE OF THROWING A LIGHTED LAMP AT
A MAN.

At the Occasional Court, on Thursday morning, before Major Pickmere, Theresa Stanley, was again brought up charged with throwing a lighted lamp at Matthew Taylor, with whom she lived at Cuerd- ley, but it was stated that the prosecutor would probably be unable for a week at least to appear, and she was further remanded till July 3rd.
RAILWAY ACCIPBNT AT bT.. HELENS JUNCTION.

- On Monday morning a Rhocking accident occurred on the railway at St. Helens Junction, by which a young married man named Douglas McGowan, a point oiler of Liverpool, was knocked down and run over by a Liverpool engine and brake van and his right leg cut off, in addition to which he sustained other injuries. Dr. Cassey, who was immediately called,ordered hisremoval to the Liverpool Royal Infirmary.

div.head: NORTHERN ANGLERS' ASSOCIATION.
div.p: NORTHERN ANGLERS' ASSOCIATION.

The Local Council of the Warrington centre of this association have much pleasure in announc- ing that "Anglers' Fares " to many places of interest have been secured, on the C. L. C., M. S. and L., and Midland Raii.ways, and that further concessions are anticipated. Travelling cards will shortly be in the hands of the members. It may be of interest to Anglers generally to learn that active steps are being taken to secure cheap travelling on other railways. The Rivers Pollution Question is also receiving the attention of the Northern Association.
DASTARDLY ATTACK ON A SLEEPING MAN AT
WIDNES.

Before Mr. T. Sutton Timmis at Widnes Police Court, on Saturday, a labourer named Bryan Pavers of 9, Maigh-st.. was charged with wounding Mary Costello, aged 14 years of age. The girl lived with her parents in the same house as the prisoner, and there was bad feeling between the two men. On Sunday morning the 14th inst., at four o'clock the prisoner broke open the door of the bedroom where the Costellos were sleeping, and, uttering a threat struck at the father with a brush. Has aim was bad and the blow struck the girl on the forehead rendering her unconscious. An alarm was raised and the prisoner then smashed his weapon against, the door. He was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial. SUMMER FASHIONS now Showing at J. & w. DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—Adrt. THE PROPOSED SANITARY DEPOT FOR ST. HELENS. The Local Government Board have intimated to the Corporation that Mr. Samuel Joseph Smith, C.E., one of their inspectors, will hold an inquiry at the Town Hall, on the Ist July, respecting an application by the corporation for sanction to borrow£l,loo for the purchase of land and build- ings in Boundary-road for the purposes of a sanitary depot. At an inquiry regardingother matter= held before Major-General Carey on the 29th April last, ' the subject was then introduced and discussed. Strong objection against the proposals of the cor- poration was taken by local solicitors on behalf of property owners in the locality, and it was urged , that as public notices of the intention to inquire into the subject of the new depot had not been ' given, there was a good ground for not acceding to the application. Since then the Local Government Board have had the matter under consideration, and have decided to hold a new inquiry, after public notice, as stated. BASSIxETTEs.—J. S. Garland, Ironmonger, 51, Bridffle-st., Warrington.—Advt. IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE. On Monday night a meeting was held in the Public Hall, St. Helens, under the auspices of the St. Helens (W. S. Blunt) branch of the Irish Nation- al League. Mr. M. Hackett presided, and there was a fair attendance. The Chairman said they were almost, at the eAd of the struggle, and in order that the end might be all the more glorious it was necessary that the whole of the Irish people should he organised. Mr. Kelly proposed " That we, the Irishmen of St. I.lelens, pledge ourselves to support by all the means in our power the leadership of Mr. McCarthy and his Parliamentary supporters." Mr. Broidy supported the resolution, which was carried. Mr. Burns, of Oldham, delivered an ad• dress, in the course of which he said that Mr. Par- nell for his private desires had wilfully abandoned his country. The only hope of Ireland lay in the united action of her children, and he was glad to find that in St. Helens they were united on that question. (Applause.) Mr. Boyle, the League organ- iser for Lancashire, also addressed the meeting. The following resolution was also passed "That we call upon our countrymen, the electors of Carlow, to return a representative to Parliament to Parliament who will support the policy of the Irish party under Mr. Justin McCarthy, and thus assist in securing Home Rule for our native land." The pro- ceedings terminated with a vote of thanks to the Chairman. SUMMER FASHIONS now Showing at J. & W. Durrox's , Sankey-st.,Warrington,—Advt.

div.head: NESTON POISONING CASE.
div.p: THE NESTON POISONING CASE.

At Neston Petty Sessions, yesterday morning, Mary Emily Scruby was charged on remand with feloniously attempting to poison her husband. Edward Roderic Scruby, grocer and provision dealer, who resided at Glad- stone-road, Great Nestor). by administering to him white precipitate of mercury and ammonia, at Great Neston, on the 12th of the present month. The court was densely crowded, and great interest was manifested in the case by the people of the locality. The case was remanded or a week, and the prisoner allowed out on bail.

WILL OF THE LA.TE MR. CHADWICK.

Probate of the will dated 7th March, 1891, of Mr. George Edward Chadwick, late of Ferndale, Bold, who died on the 25th April last, at Blackpool, leav- ing personal estate valued at £27,236 us. ed., has been granted to the executors, his brother-in-law, Mr. Charles Edward Hindley, his father-in-law, Mr. James Warburton, and Mr. John Burgess, to each of whom for the executorship the testator bequeaths ..£3OO, to Mr. Hindley a further £2,000, and to Mr. Warburton .C5OO. He bequeaths to his stepmother, Mrs. Elizabeth Chadwick, .C5,500,his plate, pictures, furniture, and household effects, horses and car- riages, and the use and enjoyment for a term of his house Ferndale ; to his sister-in-law, Mrs. Hannah Chadwick, £1,000: to Mrs. Eliza Ann Turnbull, .€2,000 ; to the four children of her husband's, Mr. Thomas Turnbull, by a former marriage,Xloo each; and to the testator's aunt,Mrs. Betty Hilton, £l,OOO. lie devises and bequeaths his residuary estate in trust in equal shares for his nephews and nieces, John Chadwick, Mary Hindley, John Chadwick Hindley, Wm. Chadwick Hindley, Herbert Turnbull, Emma Turnbull, and Mabel Turnbull.

A STIMGEON CAUGHT IN THE RIVER.

Csnsiderable excitement was caused in the neigh- bourhood of Fiddlers Ferry, on Wednesday evening last by the capture of a large fish in the river Mersey. It was first observed near one one of the cheverils by two men employed at the waterworks. With great difficulty they got it out of the water, when it was found to be a sturgeon measuring upwards of 7 feet in length. After being viewed by a number of people, it was ultimately sold to Dr. Gerrard, of Widnes, for 255.

div.head: WRSLRYIN SUNDAY SCHOOL.
div.p: WRSLRYIN SUNDAY SCHOOL.

The Walking Day in connection with the Wes- leyan Sunday School was held yesterday afternoon. The procession started from the school at one o'clock, and proceeded by way of New-st., along the Warrington-road, then down. Baker's-lane and Station-road, and afterwards along the Chapel-road and Brookside to Hall Nook; thence the scholars proceeded to the Recreation ground for an hour's play before tea. At various places along the route, the scholars were generously provided with cakes, sweetmeats, &c., by a number of friends, while at the Hall Nook, Mr. Garnett kindly permitted them to go through his gardens. At Penketh Lodge, Mrs. Walker kindly provided each scholar with a glass of lemonade and a packet of sweets. Carts were lent, for the conveyance of the scholars, by the Penketh Tanning Company, and Messrs. Stretch, Bennett, Garnett. Pickton, Jno. Jackson, and Cross. The scholars were provided with tea at 4 o'clock and the teachers and friends at 5 o'clock. After tea everyone returned to the Recreation i Ground where a variety of games were indulged n until 9 o'clock. At 9 o'clock a return to school was made, where, after a timber of balloons had been set up, the scholars were given gingerbread and cakes, and then dispersed.

Dr. Madden, the Protestant Dean of Cork, died on I Thursday. It is announced that Mr. R. Davies, Menai Bridge, Anglesey, has given L 35,000 towards the Welsh Calvin- istic Methodist Jubilee Fund. Iri the action brought against Colonel North by Mr. Cutler, architect, for £2,718, balance of an account for professional fees, the jury on Tuesday gave a verdict for the plaintiff for the full amount. The Lord Chief Justice gave judgment accordingly, and refused to stay men- d on.

div.head: INTEITVIEW WITH AN INJURED COLLIER..
div.p: INTEITVIEW WITH AN INJURED COLLIER..

The man William Farrell, who was in charge of the gang, lies in the cottage hospital. Farrell stated that Dr. Hayward's assistant (Mr. Harling) had examined hitn. Elie injurievan.principally internal, caused by the body of the deceasertinan Marshall falling heavily upon, him. Farrell stated that during the afternoon he and six sink- ers and Thos. Sharp, vrbo was a bricksetter, had been at work four hour when he sent the four men (who were killed)and rioydto the top to get something to eat. About four hours in the shaft was as much as they could stand on account of the heated atmosphere in which.they were working. rwo.other men, named Robert Davies and James Duffy, stayedidown to examine the sides of the shaft. These two men were sent up by the hoppet,„ and on their arrival at the top the other five men got into it for the purpose of coming down. Farrell was on the :.platform, ffrom whiclrthe menworked while bricking up the sides of the pit, the platform then being about feet ;front the bottom or a little over 500 yards from the sur- face. He heard a shout, and then felt a heavy weight upon him, wad at the same time he became conscious that several men had fallen down, There was not a sound born any one of them, but he heard a moaning higher upthe :shaft. He thougnt then the hoppet wa.ssuspended,and that somebody was hanging from it. He called out to know who it was, and Floyd replisd that it was him and that he wanted hap, Farrell thereupon gave the signatto• the top for the cage to be lowered, and when this was done Floyd was seen inside, but in a terrified condition. larrell could not give any detailed account of the removal of the bodies up the shaft as he became very ill. His appearance in the hospitalindicated that he was suf- fering acute pain; and it is stated that his condition is very critical.
Floyd, who was seen at Parit-road, had passed a fairly. good night, but was still suffering from the fright, and amok he had received. THE NEW SHAFT.

The officials at the colliery cffices of Messrs. Richard nvans and Co. were most courteous to the Press repre- sentatives. Mr. RObinson explained that the work of sinking deeper was commenced over a year since. The shaft was then about 280 yards deep, audit was decideil tow° about 240 yards lower, in order to reach two.valu- able seams of coal known as Om Rushy Park and Little Delph. The shaft-is 18ft. in diameter, and for the pur- pose of the work a scaffold made of boards, to nearly cover the whole- of the shaft . was constructed. This had folding doors in the centre' so that if the scaffold or platform was. any distance up the shaft, the hoppet could be sent through to the bottom. I There are bearers at certain distances upon which, when i the scaffold is drawn up, it can rest. These bearers con- sist of cross beams in the sides of the shaft, the utmost projection being 2ft. The hoppet, which is of iron and of considerable weight, is 31t. Bin. at the top, tapering down to 21t. Min, at the bottom. and stands 4ft. 61n. high. Although it has no guiding rods, same as an ord- inary cage, it swings clear of the bearers lift. all round. The theory of the hoppet having struck one of the bear- ers and tilted has been put forward, but considering the dimensions that seems alnsost an impossibility. Mr. Brighouse, the county coroner, has been communicated with and an inquiry will be held.

div.head: HEAVY THUNDERSTORMS. LOSS OF LIFE AND, GREAT DAMAGE.
div.p: HEAVY THUNDERSTORMS. LOSS OF LIFE AND, GREAT DAMAGE.
IiSTARRIZCGTON.

Late on Thursday nigh,t,, a • terrific thunderstorm swept over Warrington.. ft had been preceded by tremendous showers of rain., which came down with cataract-like force, which was quite pheno- menal. The peals of thunder were startling in their suddenness and resonance, and these, with the lurid electric flashes which lit up the atmosphere, in quick succession completely destroyed the equani- mity of not a few of the female sex,and made some males feel uncomfortable. Consternation and dismay would,we fear,be excited in the minds of many wak- ing juveniles, by the storm, apart from the physical fear they might feel, for to the excited fancy of childhood, each clap of thunder, joined to the the wild patter of the rain would seem to sound like the crack of doom for their Walking Day pros- pects. During Thursday there was a heavy down- fall of rain, and the sullen mutterings of thunder were heard at intervals in the afternoon. ST. lIELENS : SUBSIDENCE OF A ROAD.'

The storm of thunder and lightning accompanied by torrents of rain which passed over St. Helens about nine o'clock on Wednesday night occasioned very serious damage in Liverpool-road, one of the busiest thoroughfares, and there foilowed a serious interruption of traffic. The Corporation have been for months engaged in the construction of a vast intercopt- ing sewer through the borough, and in connection with the scheme sewerage operations were being carriedout in Liverpool-road. The roadway had been excavated to a depth varvi64 frox ten feet to thirty feet, and the only room allo;ved for the gbeet traffic was the width of the St. Helens and District Tramway Ccmpany's lines, Liverpool-road being' on the route to Prescot. After the storm on Wednesday night it was found that the road at the corner of Arthur-st.,and near the Grapes Hotel, had subsided, and an immense quantity of dirt and rubbish had been thrown to the bottom of the sewer working. Planks and bars used for propping the sides of the excavated road had been carried away by the subs;dence, and a temporary wooden trough for run- ning away the water from the old sewer had been smashed to pieces. Happily the unfortunate accident was discovered early. The paving stones and tram lines had kept their positions, but there was a vast hollow space underneath, and if one of thetrams had passed al@ng the ' road before the subsidence was discovered, the conse- quences, in all probability, would have been of a still more disastrous character. Orders were immediately given for the stoppage ot all traffic along the road, and the damaged portion was fenced off. The water from the old sewer found its way along the new axcavations, and ultimately down the newly constructed sewer. From an early hour on Thursday morning workmen were engaged repairing the broken trough for the old sewer, and in banking up and timbering the road where the subsid- ence had occurred. No damage had been done to the new sewer.

div.head: HOUSE STRUCK,
div.p: A HOUSE STRUCK,

Shortly after nine o'cl;c.k—on-Wednesday night, during the heavy thunderstorm which passed over St. Helens and district, the Foresters' Arms, Rookery, near St. Helens, was struck by the lightning. The electric fluid descended the chimney, scattering soot and rubbish over everything in several of the rooms, and causing a serious fracture to one of the stone walls of the house. There were several customers in the house at the time, and it is stated that the building trembled for several seconds. Fortunately Mr'. John Rigby (the landlord) and his family escaped unhurt, though the incident occasioned a great deal of alarm and excitement. COLT KILLED AT PRESCOT. On Thursday morning, a fine colt belonging to Dr. Hall. of Prescot, was found dead in the field where it was out to grass. It 13 supposed that it was struck by lightning during the storm. • RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

These towns were visitell by a severe thunderstorm accompanied by heavy rain on Wednesday evening. The storm continued during Thursday, and at midday the sky was so overcast with dark clouds that gas had to be resorted to for light. Owing to the sewers being incap- able of carrying away the immense quantity of water slight floods have occurred in various quarters but no serious damage to property is reported. The works of the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Co. were flooded, and the workmen carried on the operations with much incon- venience. A small quantity of material was damaged.
NEWTON DIVISION CONS ERVATIVFB AT LYME PARK.

The annual excursion, promoted by the Newton Division Conservative Association, took place on Saturday, under favourable circumstances, to Lyme Park, Disley, the home of Mr. T. W. Legh, M.P. for the division. Soon after half-past ten, two trains, well-filled with excursionists, evidently intent upon enjoying themselves, left Earlestown for Dis- ley, which was reached without mishap after half

_ past twelve. It was mast unfortumite that the miners' demonstration at Southport should take place on the same day, but this was not the fault of the colliers in the Newton Division, wise dele- gates voted for June 27th, but were outvoted by ' another section of the Federationfand June 20 was decided upon. Had the fates raled otherwiserthere Ls not the slightest doubt, with the beeutiful weather which. prevailed, that the Railway ‘'em- pany would have been called upon to proviCe far raore accommodation than under the circumstances was needed. As it was. about 900 peeple turned up, and were rewarded with a very pleasant °sating. Alighting at Disley, the exTursionists at onto set aboat the task ef climbing the two miles eA hilly country, which intervenes between Disley village and Lyme flail, the work-, being made more. laborious by reason of the overpowering rays of the midday sun. Many shirked the task of footing the • distance, and essayed the j-mrney in wagonettes. Arrived at the Park, some sougkst the shelter-of the trees, whifeothers betook themselves for a ramble through the grand old hall, whose antiquities. were a, source of wonderment and admiration. A spacious marquee was erected on the grounds- for refreshments, which it is needless to say was well patronised. St. Thomas's brass band,Ashtonpwas in attendance, and during the after- noon, played selections of music for dancing. At two o'clock a programme of athletic 'Torts was commenced and carried through without mishap. The fjidges for the pedestrian events were Dr. Mather and Dr. Patterson, referee, Mr. J. W. div.head: SCHOOL TOWER STRUCK BY LIGHTNING:
div.p: SCHOOL TOWER STRUCK BY LIGHTNING:

• I The lightning struck the tower of St. Saviour's School, Live'rpool, about eleven o'clock, shattering it very badly. The fire brigade and salvage corps were called out. There were over 700 children in the schools when the tower fell, among whom a great panic ensued. Many fainted, but fortunately none were seriously hurt. The tower being situated at the front of the buildings, and falling outward, did not crash through the school, other- wise the results would have been frightful. The tower had no lightning conductor. MISCELLANEOUS. An inquest was held near Aberystwith, on Thursday, on two young men mined Evans, who were killed on Wednesday evening by lightning, which struck a farm- house in which they lived. A severe thunderstorm passed over the neighbourhood of Uttoxeter on Thursday, and Doveridge Church was struck by lightning and set on fire. The storm was general around Melton Mowbray. In the town a house and stable were struck by lightning and set on fire. The flames were subdued by the fire brigade.
Kettering was visited by the storm. and at Warkton Rectory the debris of a high chimney fell into the room where Lady Stewart was sleeping, but without injuring her.

The storm was very severe throughout North Leiester- shire. At Whitwick.the end of a house was demolished, but the inmates escaped. In some parts of London the thunderstorm was severe, and the streets were flooded.

div.head: LATEST
div.p: LATEST

Reports to hand veste—rdaay—f—r-or.n the various parts of Wales show that the thunderstorm of Wednesday and Thursday was the most severe of the past twenty years. The upland farmers report they have losses of sheep and cattle which were struck by lightning on the hills. The rivers are greatly swollen, and many dwelling-houses in the lowlands are flooded. A little boy, the son of a miner named Jones, was carriel down by the floods and drowned in the river Taff at Abercanaid.

div.head: PUBLIC MEETING.
div.p: THE PUBLIC MEETING.

At the conclusion of the sports, all the visitors were summoned to an open air meeting, an impromptu plat- form. having been made out of the lurry. MT. T. W. Legh, M.P., presided over the meeting, and with him on the lurry were Mrs. Legh, Sir W. T. Marriott,Q%C.,M.P. for Brighton, Messrs. W. H. Arnott. C.C. (Lowton), W. Valiant (Ashton), C. B. F. Borron (Newton),,W. Holland- Owen (Rainhill), A. H. L. Evans (Haydock), F. Staple- ton Bretherton (Rainhill). Around the platform we noticed Messrs. R. Stuart, G. F. Clarke, J. E. Pa.rdey,W. Catterall, A. Bennett (Warrington). T. Haseldine, and many others, workers in the Conservative cause. Mr. T. W. Legh, rising to address the assembly, said, in the absence of his father, who was unwell, it was his duty to bid them a hearty welcome there that day. He apologised also for the absence of Mr. Bromley-Daven- port. M.P., and Mr. Seton-Karr, M.P. Fleregretted very much that their demonstration had clashed with the colliers' demonstration at Southport, but it was not the fault of the organisers of that meeting,because they had fixed upon that date, when the colliers had chosen another date, and it was their loss that they were not present. He could not help being reminded of a similar meeting held there two years ago, at which time the Home Rule agitation, which he was inclined to term the most successful political imposture 'of modern days, was in full swing. The Parnell Com- mission was going on, and the leaders ef the Opposition were tumbling over each other, in their attempts as to who should cover Mr. Parnell with the most fulsome adulation. (Laughter.) The Plan of Campaign was in full operation, and the union of hearts and hands had attained possibly its highest development. Since then he thought he might safely sly they had knocked the bottom out of the Home Rule ship ; at any rate, if they had not done so, the Unionists had made such a hole in that craft, that he doubted whether she would reach har- bour in safety. (Applause.) Ireland was now more prosperous than she had been for some time, the Plan of Campaign was utterly bankrupt and defeated; as for the union of hearts and hands, that had long ago given way to breaking of heads, and .the only sign that thee was such a question as Home Rule before the public at the presezt time, was the account of the way in which Irishmen celebrated their Sunday; the way they kept holy the Sabbath Day; that was,by knocking each other about. (Laughter.) These were considerable achieve- ments,and if the Unionists had to depend upon theirlrish policy alone, they would not have much to complain of. They were put into office to settle the Irish question,and he thought they had done so most effectually ; at any rate, Home Rule was dead for a long time to come. (A, Vaice : "For ever.") They were all accustomed to hear him *speak, and in all probability would have to listen to him a great deal oftener than they cared to do. (" No no.") He had therefore taken an opportunity of bringing down a gentleman who was better qualified to speak on these subjects than himself, and he thought he could safely leave Sir W. Marriott in their hands, and if he could not persuade them to put their trust in a Unionist Government, none else could. (Hear, .hear.) Their best policy was to support Unionist candidate!. People often asked him, and other people, as to why it was that the Lancashire constituencies, which were com- posed principally of working-men, returned Conserva- tives in such large numbers, and he never felt the slightest difficulty in answering that question,because ha always replied that Lancashire people were generally re- cognised as the most intelligent portion of the British elec- torate. (Applause.) Mr. W. Valiant, Ashton, then moved the following resolution : " That this meeting heartily congratulates her Majesty's Government on the tranquility and con- tentment existing in Ireland, and desires to express its absolute confidence in their adminstration of home and foreign affairs." Mr. C. B. F. Borron, Newton, seconded, and said the Government ought to command their support, and he was proud to see on the platform one who would speak on the acts they had performed. (Hear, hear.) The resolution was then put and unanimously carried. Sir W. Marriott, M.P., on rising to respond was re- ceived with cheers. He expressed his regret that there were no opponents of the resolution present, because he liked to address a mixed meeting in the hope that what he might say would have some effect on those who differed from him, and turn them from the error of their ways. (Laughter.) In introducing him Mr. Legh had referred to him as one who was once a Liberal and was now a Conservative. He begged to say that he was what he had always been, acting upon what were called Liberal principles, and he did not think that there had been during this century a more Liberal Government than that of Lord Salisbury. (Cheers.) There was a good deal of gammon in political names. They meant one thing at one time and another at another time. (A voice: "Bread and cheese.") Well, that was a good solid foundation for anything. (Laughter.) The names of Liberal and Conservative were not very old. They had cnly been in vogue 60 yet.rs, before which the two parties were known by the names of Whigs and Tories. In 1831 those who favoured the Reform Bill of that period took the name of Liberal, and Sir Robert Peel in- vented that of Conservative for those who were opposed to it. If the Liberals of that day were alive, if Lord Melbourne, Lord Grey, Lord John Russell, and Lord Palmerston were alive now, would they be on the side that was called Liberal, with Mr. Gladstone at its head? (" Nc.") Not one of them. Just as they had only a few years ago John Bright supporting them in the great Unionist contest they had been carrying for- ward, so they would have had all the old leaders of the Liberal party supporting Lord Salisbury, no matter whether they called him Liberal or Conserva- tive. (Cheers.) At this moment the Unionist Govern- ment was not supported alone by Conservatives, but it included the great leaders, all the intellectual men, and the flower of the Liberal party, and all he could say for himself was that he was bop a few years before them, because he joined Lord Salisbury two years before they did. (Hear, hear.) Why should not Radicals support the present Government? If they were true to their own principles they certainly would. The Liberal motto which the Radicals had tried to filch away and say it was their own, the motto under which their Liberal forefathers fought, was peace, retrenchment, and reform, and he i said if they wanted peace, f they wanted retrench- ment and reform they were bound to support Lord Salisbury's Government and to object to any Go- vernment of Mr. Gladstone's. (Cheers.) Other speakers addressed the meeting, and Mrs. T. W. Legh afterwards distributed the prizes gained by the competitors in the athletic contests.

• Within the past fekv inonthS, there has been formed the Lancashire and Cheshire AsSbciation for the Exten- sion of University Teaching,havingLord Derby as Presi- dent,and the 'following vice-presidents :--:-The Right Hon. Mr. A. J. Balfour, M. 1"., Chief Secretary for Ireland.; Sir H. E. Rokoe, M.P.' Mr. J. T. Brunner; M.P., Mr. W. Rathbone. M.P., and M'r.G: H. Rendall. The 'se,cretaries are :—Mr. J. C. Gray, and Mr. J. H. Fowler, of Man- chester, The Aisociation has, just made an application to the CheshireCoinity Cduncit fora. grant of £5OO, out of the fund at the disposal of the Council, for the pur- poses of technicil instruction. The application, points out that under the auspices of the. University of Cam- bridge 63 courses of lectpres had been,givenduring the , last On years in the two counties ; and 73 courses dur- ing the last five years under the auspices of Oxford. The Victoria University has taken an active part. In the work since 1886, and about 40 courses had Oen given' under its direetion;a large majority of them on scientific • subjects. The centres at which lectures have been given in Cheshire include Chester, Crewe, Nantwich, Alderley 'Edge, Altrincham, Cheadle, Frodsham, Knutsford, Run, corn,and Wallasey. Experience had shown that a courses of lectures to a purelyrworking-class centre could.not be self-supporting, and there were many localities which 'could not easily raise the amount required. It was to promote the establishment of courses in the poorer dis- tricts, and especially in working-class centres, that the ' grant was asked for. Such a grant would be used only to assist courses on subjects coming strictly within the 'scope of the Technical Instruction Act.
