div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.

NAVVIES AND THE POLICE. At Oakmere Petty Sessions on Monday, James Fish- wick, labourer, Froasham, was charged in custody,with being drunk and disorderly and assaulting the police on the 6th June, and John Wass and James Wass, Ship Canal navvies, were charged with assaulting the police and attempting to rescue the prisoner.—P.C. Price stated that he was called from his station at Helsby, and found • Fishwick standing outside the railway Inn, drunk, and using foul language. Witness went to him and said if he did not go home he would have to lock him up. Fishwick gave him a severe kick on the leg, and after some struggling he was able, with the assistance of a man named Millington, to put the handcuffs upon him. They were on their way to the police station, when James Wass got behind him and struck him heavily. Knowing that Fishwick was handcuffed, he went after Wass to apprehend him, and when about to seize him,his brother, John Wass, tried to trip him and struck him. They eventually succeeded In getting them to the police station.—P.S. Deane said the Superintendent had asked him to tell the Bench that it was hardly safe for one officer to go on his beat beCause of this class of men,and hoped that the magistrates would deal severely with them.—The Chairman said as Fishwick had been in gaol for a fortnight, he would be let off on payment of 20s. —The other two men who interfered with the police, would have to go to prison for a month, without the option of a fine. It was a very difficult thing for the officers to do their duty, and people must be taught that they were not to interfere with them. Walter Millington and John Morris, who had assisted the constable, were thanked by the magistrates and given ss. each. THE EASTHAM SECTION FINISHED.

An important stage has been reached in the making of the Manchester Ship Canal. The Eastham section is at length completed, and within a fortnight the boats which traffic at Ellesmere Port, and on the Shropshire Union Canal will take the new course to the sea. These final operations at the Liverpool end of the waterway began as stated in our last, on Thursday night week. The thin line of land between the deep trench and the Mersey, at a point near Ellesmere Port was then cut. When high tide came the water rushed through the narrow embra- sure with a great noise, poured itself on the firm bed of clay below, and ran with speed till, three and a half miles away, the lock gates at Eastham formed an impregnable barrier to further progress. Each succeed- ing full tide has sent in a flow of water. which Mr. 'Leader Williams, the engineer of the canal, has most ingeniously regulated. Monday morning's tide brought i the water n the cutting to an indicated depth of 20 feet, and by the evening tide on Puesday the full 26 feet was reached. There is an opening at present in the embankment opposite Ellesmere Port, a very short distance above the completed section, to per- mit the passage of boats from the Shropshire Union Canal to the Mersey. This will be i mmediately filled up, and, as already stated, there will be in future but the canal way to the sea. The flooding of the section has made an astonishing difference in the outward look of things. Running alongside the Mersey, the completed Ship Canal, it may be confessed, looks just a bit insigni- ficant. It s.s really of a very tolerable width, but the liver waters beside it stretch far out like an inland sea. This comparative insignificance in looks will not trouble Mr. Leader Williams. He has been spending these last few critical days at Eastham, and he is delighted be- yond, measure that the beginning of the end has so suc- cessfully been reached. His activity has been untiring. On Monday he gave his afternoon to candidates from whom he is to select a harbour master for the port of Eastham.

, HOW THE WATER WAS LET IN. The story of the last few days has not been told quite enrrectly in the newspapers, and it may be well to give it Machin the words of the engineer to a party of visi- tors whom he ',received on Monday. The first blunder :made was the statement that the water was let in through the lock gates at Eastham. The opening was made three and a half miles higher up, within a few hundred yAltds of Ellesmere Port. A hole 12 feet wine was cut on the Thursday morning, and this has been gradually enlarged Unit is now 60,feet. ,There was a large gathering to .witness these initial operations. Most of the directors of the company, were present ; the navvies, pick and shovel lon shoulder, congregated together, and the adjoining 'railway lines were crowded with engines. The approach of the tide' to its full height was watched with some anxiety. When' finally the gap was reached and the tor- rent ran first over a shelf of clay, then leaped a sheer. 20' feet belnn. and hastened towards Eastham, there was a cheer of mingled reliefand triumpli,above which soußded the shrill whistles of the locomotives, ,The arrangement for regulating the flow of water, was complete., There, were timbers, piling, and shuttering to keep in the waters at the dam. If the Mersey came in too rapidly the drop- ping of a few shaters was an effectual 'check. Mr. Wil- liams states' hat the main 'pbrtibns of the dam • will be taken out bistearn navvies and dredgers. , , Bi6IGE :rAtFI c, &c: • • : This work will occupy about a fortnight, and after that, the trade of Ellesmere Port will be taken down-the canal,the gap in the ernbanktnent opposite the Port being closed. Within a very few-weeks afterwards the section of the canal between Ellesmere Fort and the 'river ' Weaver, a length of about six miles, will be filled with 'water in a-similar manner. This.will result in the salt trade of Northwich and Winsford being passed through the lock which is. now completed near Weston,: and so on along the canal. The trade of these ports consists mainly of barge traffic and coasters. For traffic of this sort it will ,not be necessary to dredge at once down. to the extreme depth, as the, draught of these veisels is much

less than that of the large ships ,which will ultimately pass through the canal. It should be said that the Weaver and Ellesmere Port traffic will pass through the middle or 50ft. lock. The ocean ships will be served by the inland, or 801 t. lock; and there is a 30ft. lock for very small craft indeed. Dredging operations in the completed portion, to secure a uniform 26ft. depth, will begin at once. The machinery for this purpose, and for the greater work of scouring a channel from Eastham to deep water, is at present idle in the river. A mighty vessel of iron, called " The Atanchester," is lying within sight of the greenheart gates which guard the canal. Another large vessel, the property of the company, is at Ellesmere Fort; and a third is hired from the Ribble Navigation Company. Two other 'Powerful dredgers have been furnished by the ports of Ayr and Dumbarton, and these will very shortly enter the canal by the Eastham gateway and rend up the soil from the bed till the necessary depth is in all places reached. Before the visitor of Monday left the neighbourhood of Ellesmere Port, attention was called to a very fine sub- stantial dock wall which has been built by the great railway company. which so powerfully opposed the pro- moters of the Ship Canal. From these preparations it is evident that with the opening of the canal the railway company expect to 6evelop a large coal traffic. During the week there have been many sightseers at Eastham, and admiration of the work accomplished has been general. Already a few small boats have been launched on the canal, and Manchester people who wish to complete their idea of the enterprise cannot do better than run over to Liverpool and take the ferry to the canal gates. -

div.head: WEDNESDAY.-FULL SUPPLY OF WATER.
div.p: WEDNESDAY.-FULL SUPPLY OF WATER.

The depth sought to be attained in the completed Eastham section of the Manchester Ship Canal was reached yesterday. No more water for the present, therefore, will be admitted, and the temporary weir at Ellesmere Port, through which the water was diverted from the river into the bed of the canal, has been closed. The body of water which now lies in the canal is 23ft. deep, rind being sufficient for all practical purposes,will, in all likelihood, remain undisturbed until the work at both ends of the section--Eastham and Ellesmere Port —is sufficiently advanced to allow of the en- trance of shipping. No defects of a serious nature in the first section have been discovered, Mounting a locomotive, a start was made from East- ham on the river side, and the huge mound which lies en the river bank just before reaching Ellesmere Port, and which is now such a conspicuous feature ih the landscape, was soon reached. A brief inspection of the works aVEllesmere Port revealed the fact that the efforts of the engineers are now being directed to keeping in the water which has been impounded. The shutters of the Weir have been closed and a strong dam in addition has ban constructed. Returning on the land side of the canal, an opportunity was afforded of in- specting the banks on the opposite side. The few flaws which have discovered themselves are being repaired, and little difficulty is anticipated by the engineers in putting them to rights. The depth of water which now lies in the canal is ample for the traffic which at'first will be carried, such as the barges and coasters which sail from Ellesmere Port and the River Weaver, and this traffic, it is anticipated, will be commenced in three or four weeks. At the mouth of the canal at Eastham land is being prepared for the erection of five houses, in which acconalmodation will be provided for a harbour master and pierhead men. The works at the comlaleted section are naturally the centre of attraction for large number of visitors, among whom are to be found men of high position in the engineering world. Among the visitors on Wednesday was Mr. Menacoll, chief engineer .of the proposed Nicaraguan Canal on the Isthmus of Panama. The completion of thfh section has naturally resulted in the discharge of a large number of navvies,"about 1,500 having been paid off during the last fortnight, and the large quantities of planr used in this portion have been transferred to the sections further on. TESTED BY THE STORM. A MISHAP TO GOVERNMENT COMMISSIONERS. Work was generally suspended throughout the eastern section of the Manchester Ship Canal on Thursday ow- ing to the torrents of rain, which poured down almost uninterruptedly. Only a few men were engaged here and there in operations wbich could be carried on under some kind of shelter. No more severe trial has had tube faced since the cutting assumed anything like a finished appearance. On the whole, the ordeal was got through with comparative immunity. The outlook generally was of the most dreary descripcion,and very few pedes- trians ventured forth from the shelter of the hotel and the tea booths in its vicinity. The private saloon carriage used for high officials and distinguished visitors was chartered for a journey at ten o'clock, it being the intention of the Ribble Commis- sioners—Admiral Sir G. Nares. and Mr. Wolf Barry (who have been appointed by the Government)—to proceed along the works to Salford. The storm, however' was beating too fiercely upon. them, and after reaching Elles- mere Port, the expedition was abandoned. Short as it was, it did not pass off without mishap, for the engine which had the.saloon in tow crashed into a waggon as it was nearing Ellesmere Port. One buffer of the ongine was doubled up, and a rough shock was experienced. Fortunately, no personal injuries were sustained ; but the Commissioners evidently thought they had had enough of adventure, and went off to London.

div.head: V YRN WY WATER, SCHEME.
div.p: THE V YRN WY WATER, SCHEME.
WATER IN THE TUNNEL.

The leakage in the tunnel is causing a great' deal o difficulty, but it is altogether different matter to the tem- porary pipe line. On the river, where the " boiling " appearance of the water indicates the spot where com- pressed air is escaping, and where, in consequence of the escape, water found its way into the tunnel under the river bed, two barges are now moored. They have been brought from Rock Ferry, laden with clay, and on Thursday, men were engaged in pitching into the river this substance by the aid of spades. To an outsider it seemed rather a wasteful proceeding to throw good clay into the water with such prodigality, but, of course, there was an object in it. To non-technical minds a matter of this sort is rather diffi- cult to understand, but it would seem that the mishap in the tunnel was caused in this wise. It is requisite for the safe carrying on of the boring operations that there should be a substantial amount of clay or river mud in- terveniog between the water and the tunnel, and the shifting nature of the material on 'the bed of the river here appears to have so lessened that intervening amount that the compressed air forced a way through, making a breach, by means of which the water entered. The object of the engineers in throwing into the water a few bargefuls of clay is to make the bed of the river more secure, anous guard against the possibility of escapes of air. IMas computed that by Thursday evening some 250 tons of clay had been used for that purpose. At the present time there is in the tunnel a depth of water of from four to five feet, but the officials who have to cope with the difficulties at Fiddler's Ferry say that it is only a question of a few hours' work to clear that away when everything is ready for that process. When the water has been got rid of, there will remain to be dealt with a certain amount of sandy sediment, and altogether it is thought that the result of the accident will be a delay of about a week. Ifs that proves to be the case it will not, after all, bg such a serious business, especially when viewed in the light of previous delays. The actual amount of tunnelling work that has been driven is 125 feet, 122 feet of which has been lined with permanent sast-iron rings, and to this little, if any, damage has been occasioned. On the Cheshire side of the river a shaft has been sunk to a depth of 30 feet, and lined with castiron cylinders. When this shaft has been completed it will be ready to meet the tunnel, and thus complete the con- nection. Since the water got into the tunnel, some of the men have for the time being been throwdout of work, and having time on their hands, they have zone in for sport. They did so, too, to such purpose that on Thursday an enormous sturgeon, several feet in length. was brought ashore. It was captured with great glee, and was lodged in an outbuilding connected with the inn at Fiddler's Ferry. Meanwhile the men laughingly discussed the point as to what should be done with it, had friendly disputes as to its ownership, and otherwise made merry. With regard to the temporary pipe-line, it may be added that all was in order at Fidler's Ferry on Thursday evening. It was stated that the water was going through all right, but that a few alterations re- mained to be made. They are not expected, however, to at all affect the water supply. THE PRESCOT RESERVOIR.

On Wednesday forenoon, the supply of water from the tempoiary pipe for the Prescot reservoirs was very satisfactory so far as the flushing arrangements were concerned. The reservoir bed was covered with six or eight inches of water, and the gang of men, numbering about 40, engaged by the Health Committee of the Liverpool Corporation, worked hard and perseveringly in the scraping, sweeping,and dredging of the uncleaned portion of the bed. The toilsome job was finally coin- oil Wednesday evening, and to all appearance a flushing of the whole of the bed will leave the reservoir ifna fit state to receive its store of water for doniestic consumption from Wales. On Thursday there was a steady flow of water from Vyrnwy into the Prescot Reservoir. The flushing of the bed went on s3.tisfactOrily, and the flow of water, coupled with the heavy downpour of rain, almost completely cleaned the whole of the bed.

PREFERMENT OF A WARRINGTOIV CLERGYMAN. We are informed that the Rev. H. Gibson Smith, M.A., second master of the Warxington Grammar School, late scholar of St. John's College, Cambridge and associate of Owen's College,Manchester has been appointed to the Rectory of Halewood by the patron, the Rev. Canon Warr. Mr. Smith has been Sunday assistant in the Parish Church of Childwall for the past six years, and his services both as a preacher and a reader have been• much appreciated by the parishioners. The gross value of the living to which be is appointed is £370 per annum, with a house. The rev. gentleman came to Warrington about ten years ago, to commence his duties at the Grammar School, among the pupils of which he is very popular, and he has also alarge circle of friends outside that institution by whom his departure from Warrington will be deeply regretted. For two years after his arrival in the town, the rev, gentle- man officiated as Sunday curate at St. Paul's Church, to which he was ordained. For two sessions' 1888-9 and 1889-90, he was president of the Warrington Literary and Philosophical Society, and during his connection with it read able papers on the following subjects :—" The Phenomena of Sleep,"" Plato," and "Stoicism."

AN IRATE MOTHER ATTACKS A TEACHER. At the Warrington Police Court on Thursday, Kate Lusby or Dalton, 5, Roger-st., was charged with assaulting, on the 23rd inst., Miss Jessie Pod- more, a teacher at the Brick-st. school. Mr. Jenkins, solicitor, appeared for the prosecution on behalf of the managers of the school; and said he wasinstructed to press for exemplary punishment to suppress this kind of lawlessness, which was too common in the locality. On the 22nd inst., a little boy named Charles Dalton, stole, child-like, from a pencil box in the school a musical toy used in the school, and ran out to get home with it. He was overtaken by a teacher named Miss Kidd, and he was punished by being made to stand on a desk a few minutes. About a quarter past nine next morn- ing, the defendant, the child's mother, came into the school,and asked the complainant how she dared to punish lictr child, and without giving her time to explain that she was not the teacher she sup- posed, struck her violently several times on the face and head. it would never do to allow parents to come, and without any inquiry or the slightest knowledge of the circumstances, assault teachers in this way. The defendant also used very violent language to Miss Hetherington, another pupil teacher.—Miss Podmore and Miss Hetherington hay- ing given conformatory evidence, the defendant,who pleaded guilty, expressed her regret that she had struck the wrong teacher.—Mr. Jenkins said he did not ask for any advocate's fee or allowance for wit- nesses; and through his intercession, the defendant was let off with a penalty of 105.., including costs.

div.head: SUDDEN DEATH OF A CYCLIST.
div.p: SUDDEN DEATH OF A CYCLIST.

On Saturday afternoon Mr. Alfred Browh, aged 29 years, who was employed at Messrs. Timley's tannery, Mersey-st., and resided at No. 12, St. ary's-st., Latchford, started for a ride on his bicycle as far as Grappenhall. He called at the Railway Inn, Latchford, and asked at the bar for a glass of beer, but before being supplied he was observed to fall to the ground; and to all appear- ance he died almost immediately. Dr. Ronald was promptly'P brought to the spot, but on his arrival he pronounced the deceased to be no more. An inquest was held on Monday afternoon at the Golden Lion, Latchford, by Mr. H.C. Yates, coroner.—Mrs. Brown, widow of the deceased, said her husband hurried home from work on Saturday, ate his din- ner—which consisted of potato pie—hastily, and then rode away on his bicycle, with the intention of going to a bowling main at the Dog and Dart, Grappenhall.—Johnpreen deposed to being in the parlour at the Railway Inn, on Saturday afternoon, when Brown arrived on his bicycle. Leaving the machine outside he came he came into the parlour, and, calling for a glass of beer, felt in his pocket for the. money. In withdrawing his hand, he dropped several coins on the floor. He stooped to pick them up and, failing, stooped a second time, and then fell off his seat on to the floor. Witness thought he was in a fit, so laid him on his back and undid his shirt. He siglied twice and died. When he came in he was perspiring, but did not look over-fatigued. The lanilord fetched Dr. Ronald.--John Thomas Ward said he was in the public-house when Brown arrived. Brown ordered some beer, but before it could be brought, he fell under the table. He did not seem at all Acited when he came in. Dr. Ronald stated that about a quarter past two he was called to the Railway Inn. He thete saw the deceased lying on his back in the parlour. Life had been extinct about a minute. That morning he had made a post-mortem examination, and found considerable enlargement of the heart with fatty degeneration, thereby impairing the action of the valves? which was the cause of death; The hurried comsumption of his dinner, followed by the exer- tion of bicycle-riding, produced a train of circum- stances which would account for death. It was unusual to find such enlargement and degeneration in a man at this time of life.-,-The Coroner: Is that natural degeneration? Originally; it is constitu- tional.—His widow has told us that some of. his relatives have died from consumption. That accounts for it, then. You have the hereditary ten- dency to it.—lf he had taken his dinner quietly and had gone quietly, he might have been alive to- day.—The Coroner, in summing up, said he thought the jury would agree that, in the interest of the publican, and for the satisfaction of the wife of the deceased, it was wise to have had a post - mortem examination. The jury returned a verdict in accordance with the medical testimony. The deceased has left a widow and child. There have been a number of deaths in the deceased's family wizlin the past few years.

div.head: CAPSIZING OF A STEAMER.
div.p: CAPSIZING OF A STEAMER.
FIFTY LIVES LOST.

SAN FRANCISCO, WEDNRSDAY.—The mail arriving from Japan yesterday, brings news of the capsizing of the steamer Yap, engaged in the coasting trade. The casualty occurred on the 4th inst., and fifty, of the crew and pas sengers were drowned.

div.head: WIEDEMANN-WALPOLE CASE.
div.p: WIEDEMANN-WALPOLE CASE.

Notice of appeal has been served on Messrs. Hughes and Hughes by the defendant's solicitor. Defendant asks that the judgment obtained by the plaintiff be set aside and entered for the defendant as far as regards the breach of promise, on the ground that no material corro- borative evidence was advanced in support of the plain- tiff's case. The appeal will probably be heard in a month's time.

div.head: MAGISTRATES AND LICENSES.
div.p: MAGISTRATES AND LICENSES.
IMPORTANT ANNOUNCEMENT.

At the meeting of the Justices of the Petty Sessional Division of Cerne Abbas, near Dorchester, on Wednesday Mr. J. Batten, -on behalf of the bench, said :—We think it right to mention publicly that, at the next annual licensing meeting, it is very possible the bench,in the exercise of the discretion conferred on them by the general licensing act, will take into consideration whether, after fully providing for the reasonable wants and convenience of the public, it will not be for the bene- fit of the inhabitants of the division, especially having regard to the encouragement of thrift an temperance, that some reduction should be made in the number of licensed houses in the division." The announcement was made quite independent of any case before the Bench. There are a large number of " tied " houses in the neighbourhood.
CHURCH CONSECRATION AT ST. HELENS

On Thursday afternoon the Bishop of Sodor of Man consecrated the new chancel of St. Thomas's Church, Westfield-st.,St. Helelis. In addition to the erection of a chancel, the edifice has been re-seated and other im- provethents have been carried out. The total expendi- ture has been about £3,300, and of this amount about £2,800 have been raised. At the ceremony the at- tendance was very large. The Bishop conducted the service, and the clergy who took part were the Rev. J. C. Pigot, vicar; Rev. B. Percival, curate-in-charge St. Paul's Mission; and the Rev. M. Binney, vicar of Sutton. There were also present the Revs. H. S.' Bolton (Raven- bead), .G. .Lakeman (St. Mark's), C. Brown (St. Thomas's), T. J. Preece (Kirkby), Powell (Knotty Ash), G. B. Thurston (Sutton), J. M. Ceurtenav (parish church), W. G. Sale, (Bavenhead), and B. -S. Clarke <Eccleston). The,Bishop preached from the wprcis " Who went about doing good ', (Acts x., 38), and" urged that it .was the duty of all . professing Christians to follow the example of their ,Master, whose whole life On earth was spent in , deeds of mercy and kindness. He was thankful to report that he. W 43 gradually regaining strengths and no doubt, in Cred's,providence, and with. the well-earned rest that was before him, it would not be long before he was restored to them and to the work he loved so well. ,

NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
CRICKET.

The Sale cricketers, says the "Athletic News," will remember their initial fixture with the Warrington club, for though the first-named were favoured with the luck of going in first, on a splendid wicket and in splendid Weather, they were got rid of for 118 after batting over two hours. Warrington made short work of this total, and Won the match out of hand in 75 minutes. War- rington have to thank the grand display of batting by S. M. Crosfield for the victory last Saturday, and the hard-hitting amateur, fresh from his achievements with the county against Oxford and Yorkshire, played in a merry fashion,and rattled up a score of 65 before he was got rid of. He gave a chance when he was 37, but otherwise his play was delightful, It is not always easy to find a new bowler who has got the right grit in him, but Warringtm seem to have dropped across one who will develop into something out of the ordinary if he keeps up his rate of progress. Harrison, the youth in question,has jumped into popularity with his colleagues, I and the style in which he shaped last Saturday showed I that he was made of the right stuff.

Sale had not been beaten this season until last Satur- day, when they tried a new lot of opponents in the players of Warrington. They found themselves badly handicapped at the finish, the Wildersp ml Causeway (or something like that) club running the Saleites'to a standstill in the last few laps. This comes of playing new fixtures. If an unbeaten certificate is required Sale will have to keep to the old lot and venture int:o regions where scoring is done at the rate of nearly two runs a minute.

A week ago, says a writer in the "Athletic News," I pointed out the success of some of Lancashire's veteran batsmen. Another was showing how the thing should be done on Saturday. This was R. P. Woodhouse. "Bob" has been playing for Preston for many, many years, and it must have stirred the hearts of the fre- quenters of West Cliff to see the old warhorse knocking the Broughton bowling about to the tune of exactly 100 before Porter, the Derbyshire pounty man, got at his wicket. His success was all the more striking seeing that only he and Addie could make much of thee'Brouot- . ton attack.

•At Old Trafford on Saturday the Oxford University cricketers were defeated by Lancashire in one innings. As last year, the contest between Sussex and Cambridge University produced some tremendous scoring. Indeed on this occasion the runs made in the match-1,402 form a record total in important cricket in England. Cambridge won by 48 runs.

The Liverpool and District match with Yorkshire says the "Liverpool Mercury," which closed on Satur- day in a brilliant win for Liverpool of 34 runs, must be voted an unqualified success—a development that should have an important influence in establishing this district in the forefront as a cricket centre.

At an inquest held at Bolton, on Thursday, upon Richard flowarth,who was reported to have died through being hit by a cricket ball during a recent match, Dr. Scowcroft stated that death resulted not from the blew, but from intestinal injury produced by excessive run- ning whilst batting for his club, to which any cricketer might be liable under similar circumstances. Verdict in accordance with the medical evidence was returned.
At cricket on Thursday Surrey beat Yorkshire by an innings and 27 runs; Sussex defeated Oxford University - by nine wickets ; and Kent, alter an exciting finish. beat Warwickshire by 3 runs.

div.p: CYCLING.

The "Manchester Guardian "of Monday says :—" A week hence Manchester will provide the athletic-loving public with a series of competitions in which the Ameri- can visitors will be opposed by the best men on this side the Atlantic. Somehow we arealways disposed to affect a disbelief in the times accomplished on the other side, and to flatter ourselves that "we will show them when they come over here" how little they are to be relied upon."
CATHOLICS AND FREE EDUCATION.

A large meeting of Roman Catholics, convened by the Westminster Diocesan Society, was keld in St. James 'S Hall, London, on Wednesday night, to protest against •the Government Education proposals. Cardinal Mann' ing was to preside, but owing to failing health was un- able to do so. He wrote saying that Catholics were novi ma dangerous and critical moment, and he hoped God would guide them to swing the Christian schools of England.—Mgr. Gilbert presided in his absence, and said Catholics looked upon the Bill as one which weakened the responsibility of the parent to the child. ResolutionS were passed approving of public money being granted for the education of those unable to pay school fees, but not for others.

INQUEST AND VERDICT. The inquiry into the murder of the little girl. Barbara Waterhouse, at Horsforth, nen Leeds, was on Monday resumed by Mi. J. C. Malcolm, coroner. The accused Walter Turner and Ann Turner. were again represented by a solicitor. Inspector Sowerby, chief • clerk in the Leeds Police Force, stated that on Friday, June 12, mrs• Turner came to the Police Office in the Town Hall at about six o'clock in the evening. Witness had an inter- view with her in the" key room." She made a long and incoherent statement, as to having on the Monday previous found in the coal cellar at her house in Hors' forth a bundle wrapped in a shawl. Witness sent for the shawl in which the body was found. Other witnessee gave evidence, and after a short deliberation, the jurY returned a verdict of "Wilful murder "against Walter Lewis Turner, and found that Ann Turner was an az' cessory after the fact. IMPORTANT DISCOVERY. On Tuesday morning, as Mr. Donald, vice-president of the Bradford Trades Council, was walking in the country near Bradford he found what is believed to be the missing bed quilt, which may tend to clear up the mystery connected with this murder. Mr. Donald Ices accompanied by a St. Bernard dog, and when near the Seven Arches, Bingley, on the banks of the river,Aire, the animal brought him a rag which aroused his susPi' cions. He looked and found scattered among the grass fragments comprising almost the whole of a bed quilt" It is a faded blue counterpane of cheap material, pro- fusely stained with blood, and hacked in many place!, evidently by a knife. Dr. Donald returned home quiciv ly, and at once communicated with the police. The fragments of the article were only found at half-past ten, and to all appearance this is the article for which the police are searching. PRISONERS BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES. At Leeds, on Tuesday, Walter Lewis Turner, and Aril his mother, were again charged with being implicate: in the murder. Prisoners already stand committed e'S the coroner's warrant, the former for wilful murder, alla the latter as an accessory after the fact. Before the was opened, Mr. Wilkinson, the presiding marristratel; referred to a statement in a Leeds newspaper, -that the last occasion the prisoners were "summarily 11.,ie manded." They were nothing of the kind. Every ea`" - was taken that both sides were consulted. On the plication of Mr. Williams, treasury solicitor, in wbleer Mr. Willey, prisoners' solicitor, concurrred, the moth a _ and son were remanded for a week. It is stated that further remand would probably be required.

TRIENNIAL RE-UNION AT WARRING- ION TRAINING COLLEGE. On Saturday, the triennial re-union of the past students of Warrington Girl's Training College took place. A service was held in the morning, there being a large congregation,comprising several hun- dred young lady students, past and present, in the Parish Church. The Rev. Morley Stevenson, prin- cipal of the college, read the prayers, and the Rev. F. W. Willis, rector of Warrington, the first lesson, the second being read by the Yen. Archdea- con flarber;:of Chester. The sermon was preached by the Dean of Manchester, the Rev. E. C. McClure, from Romans, xvi, 12, "Salute Tryphena and Try- phosa who labour in the Lord." After the service, • luncheon, whioh it may be mentioned was of an excellent character, and at Which the company were waited upon with most admirable prompti- tude, was provided in the Hamilton-st. Schools, the caterer being Mr. Speakman, of the Saracen's Head, Wilderspool. Four hundred and nineteen persons sat down to dinner, nearly 400 of whom were ladies; and it may fairly be presumed, from the aspect of the proceedings, that a more cheerful and enthu- siastic company were never brought together in Warrington. The Dean of Chester occupied the chair, • and there were also among those present the Rev. Morley Stevenson, principal of the colbge, and Mrs. Stevenson, the Rev. F. W. Willis, the rector, and Mrs. Willis, the Yen. Archdeacon of Chester, the Dean of Manchester, the Rev. Canon Penrhyn and Mrs. Penrhyn, the Rev. D. S. Hodgson and Mrs. Hodgson, the Revs. C. E. Jackson, H. D. Madge and G. F. Williams, the Rev. 0. P. Whalley and Mrs:Whalley, the Rev. F. Slater and Mrs. Slater, the Rev. J. D. Best, the Rev. A. G. Holmes, the Mayor (Alderman R. W. Francomb) and the Mayoress, Mr. Mrs., and Miss Buckton, Mr. and Mrs. Willcocks, Mrs and Miss Timmins, Mr. Amos, Miss Ferriman, Miss Timewell, Miss Dalloe, Miss Perry,Miss Dun, Mr. Wright, Mr. and Mrs. Woods, Mr. Pearse, Dr. Watkins, Mr. Dew- burst, Miss Beatty, and Miss Goddard. The room was most picturesquely decorated with festoons and groups of flags, flowers, etc., and opposite the entrance was conspicuously exhibited the motto "Semper agens, semper quietus," (always doing, always quiet). The dinner having been concluded, the chairman rose to propose the toast of The Queen, and the rest of the Royal Family.'; He said if that day had not been the 20th of June, he was quite sure the toast would have received the most hearty welcome, but as that day was the 20th of June, the anniversary of that upon which she began her happy reign, lie was quite sure they would drink her health, and that cf the royal family, with unusual enthusiasm. It was no exaggeration to say that it was impossible for this country and our colonies to over- estimate the debt which they owed to their sovereign, for she not only reigned over us with the power and the Sway of a gentle sceptre, but also by those virtues which commanded our admiration.—The Yen. Archdeacon of Chester next, amidst enthusiastic applause, propos( d tl e health of the Dean of Manchester as the preacher of the day, and said he was pleased to find that since he had become dean of Manchester he had not justified the fear that he would dissociate himself from the Training College.—The Dean of Manchester, whose rising created loud and continuous applause, said he had been sub- jected to a little absurd chaff by some who said the reason he continued so attached to the college was that it was a college of the softer and loftier and superior sex—(loud applause and laughter)—and int of those sterner and baser creatures—(renewed laughter and ap- plause)—called men. (Renewed laughter.) However that might be, he had no intention to dissociate him- self from the College. He held it to be one of the honours of his life that he had been honorary secretary to the College, and notwithstanding the responsibilities of the duties of a dean he had no intention of placing his resignation in the hands of the Comrnittee.—The Chair- man then proposed the health of the principal of the College. He asked those present to join with him in the Must hearty recognition of the work which that gentle- man was now doing, and in the fervent hope that it would continue to be equal to what it was now. It must be gratifying to*the managers of the College and those educated in it to know that in one subject it stood first of all the training colleges in England, in another second, in another 3rd,and in another 6th. The toast was received With clamorous and enthusiastic applause, which was renewed on the Rev. Morley Stevenson rising to respond. lie commenced by remarking on his reception, and Observed that there was one thing that Warrington stu- dents were undouttedly noted for, that was enthusiasm. <Renewed applause.) In the course of his speech,which was received with applause or laughter, at frequent Points, the rev, gentleman remarked, amidst laughter and great applause, that there were some present who Were in the college more than 40 years ago. With the existing management he did not fear fgr the future of the coll, ge. The health of the college was never better : they had' not even had influenza—(laughter)--though some colleges in the country had had to be broken up, While from others many students had had to be sent away through the disease. -The Warrington students had not disgraced themselves in that way. (Laughter.) He was not going to tell them any more news ab out the college, because now it had its own magazine, and all the news of the college was most ably reported there. Mr. Stevenson referred to-the death of his predecessor, Mr. Stubbs, a few months since, remarking that so long as the college existed, his name would be held in res- pect and affection. He also made reference to the late Canon Hopwood, a former member from the first of the committee of the college, than whom, he remarked, the institution had never had a truer friend. He then ex- pressed his pleasure at seeing present Mr. Williams, his former heiper in the college, and his brother-in-law, Mr. Whalley. (Loud applause.) He announced that that time three years hence would be the jubilee of the college, and said he expected then to see there every past stu- dent—(laughter)—and he was going to make special ar- rangements by which all might be enabled to come. The Rev. F. W. Willis proposed the health of the visitors, coupled with ' the name of the Rev. J. D. Best, principal of the Chester Training College. In the course of his observa- tions, Mr. Willis said Warrington had a dark side which they could see for themselves, hut assured the visitors that it had a very bright side, and referred to the great kindness he had experienced in the town. He mentioned incidentally as one of its bright aspects that he had been told that there was a prospect of there being salmon ill the weir at Warrington in 20 years' time. and caused some laughter by observing that a friend had written to him that he heard there was some very good trout fishing near Warrington.—The Rev. J. D. Best responded, being enthusiastically received.—The Mayor proposed the health of the chairman. He took occasion to say, some- what humourouslf, that the absence of influenza was no doubt due to the good management of the Corporation (laagliter) for although they had a great amount of smoke they had a very great amount of good health also. He thought their • river was terribly polluted, but still believed that in 20 years there would be salmon in It. He also believed that sciende would completely destroy the bad effects of smoke. (Applause.)— The Chairman having responded, the company dispersed, and returned to the Training College, where in the dining hall a meeting was held under the presidency of the Rector, for the put pose of Making a presentation of a handsome.electro-Plated set of tea table utensils and a set of silver spoons, to the Rev. 0. P. Whalley, formerly tutor at the college, by the students of the institution in the years 1888-91. The Chairman, in a very happy and humorous speech, made the presentation, and referred to the coming Marriage of Mr. Whalley.—Mr. Whalley, who looked in Very delicate health, and referred to his having beert-for some time an invalid, thanked the students in terms of Much feeling relieved by an overflow of humour which kept his audience in an almost constant state of mirth- fulness. He resumed his seat amidst considerable ap- plause.—The Rev. C.E. Jackson in an equally humorous speech, which was equally appreciated by the large audience, chiefly of young ladies, present, thanked the Rectcr for the part he had fulfilledt and the meeting concluded.—There were private meetings of the students during theafternoon. . Tea was provided in the grounds, and in the evening there was a service in the chapel, and also a concert in the dining-hall, and dancing arid other diversions were indulged in
THE QUEEN AT THE WEDDING OF
MISS PONSONBY.

The wedding of Miss Ponsonby, daughter of the Queen's private secretary, to ttlonel Montgomery, of the Scots Guards, took place on Monday afternoon at the Chapel, Wellington Barracks, London, when the Queen, who went specially from Windsor, honoured the occasion by her presence. The service was read by the Rev. Frederick Ponsonby, the bride's uncle, the Dean of Hereford, and the Rev. Mr. Armvtage, and the ceremony was witnessed by the Prince and Princess of Wales and a brilliant as- semblage.
DESTRUCTION OF TUSSAUD'S WAX- WORK EXHIBITION.

A. fire broke out, at an early hour on Saturday morn- ing, at Messrs. Louis Tussaud's Waxwork Exhibition in Regent-st., which destroyed the figures, &c., in the extensive galleries and ground filor, but happily the col- lection of instruments of torture, lent by the Earl of Shrewsbury and Talbot, escaped, they being on exhibi- tion in the basement. The fire raged with unabated fury, illuminating the whole of the surrounding neigh- bourhood until the building was completely gutted, the nof and galleries falling in with a tremendous crash. Little damage was done to the surrounding property, enly one house at the rear suffering.

WIFE BEATING AND FURNITURE SMASHING.

Benjamin Taylor, boatman, of 7 .Brook-st., was summoned before the Runcorn magistrates on Mon- day to answer a charge of assaulting his wife Eliza. —Mr. Lake appeared for the complainant and Mr. Burton defended. From the statement of Mr. Lake it appeared that on Thursday last at noon Mrs. Taylor went to the Derby Arms to tell her husband that his dinner was ready. He followed her home cursing all the way, and on entering the house he threw the dinner in all directions all about the place and then proceeded to smash the dinner things. Ile chased his wife out of the room, and just as she was going through the doorway he struck her and knocked her against the wringing machine. She returned into the room,and he stood over her with an axe and th reatened to kill her. The daughter intervened and persuaded him to put down the axe. The defendant then smashed nearly the whole of the furniture,which belonged to the complainant,who was a widow when he married her. The complainant confirmed this statement,and said the defendant had re- peatedly assaulted her.—The defence set forth bg Mr. Burton was that on the morning in question the defend- ant and his wife were drinking together at Henry Cow- ard's and went home together. On getting to the house she took all the keys, went through the front door, and told him that when next he came home all the furniture would be gone and he could do what he liked. The defendant said he would rather break it,and he did smash an eight day clock and a pair of drawers. The defendant denied most positively that he had ever struck his wife, but he had suffered very much from her violence. On Saturday night she went to Coward's and without speak- ing a word struck him in the face with her fist, a fact which showed what kind of a woman she was.—A boat- man named T. Smith was called to show that the com- plainant had said she only wished she could get her hus- band to strike her and then she would take proceedings, but the Bench ruled that his evidence was not admiss- able.—The defendant was bound over to keep the peace for six months in his own recognizances of £5 and pay the costs 225.

On Saturday, the twenty-seventh annual festival of the London and North-Western Railway Com- pany's servants from Edge-hill and Liverpool was held on the Castle Hill Field, by the side of New- ton Lake, kindly lent for the occasion by Colonel M'Corquodale, J.P. The company's employes, to the number of over 2,000, who journeyed,' in three specials from Liverpool to Newton, besidtis having extra carriages on the ordinary trains, were accom- panied by the Traffic Department Band from Edge- hill, which played throughout the afternoon and evening for the dancing, which was freely indulged in. A heavy programme of races, Sm., was started promptly at 2.45. and kept going with good order and regularity. After the programme )f sports had been gone through the prizes were distributed by Mrs:Hee, wife of .Mr. Frank Ree, district goods manager, London and North- Western, Liverpool, and an adjournment was then made to the large pavilion, where all the officials and a large number of others had tea. Sir,—Kindly permit me •now to bring my remarks on this subject to a close. 7. There is certainly nothing recorded of the acts and -words of Jesus that coUld even be wrested to countenance , the idea that he ever intended that his church should be a great political institution, and his ministers highly alaried and livened °dicers of State. On the contrary, the principles which he taught and exemplified in his walk and conversation before men were about as oppo- • site to such things as they could well be. The institu- • tion which he planted with his life and watered with his • tears and blood was a heavenly, spiritual church, whose fundamental and controlling law was supreme love to , God and man. Sucha church could never require or receive aid from kings, politicians, and other men of the eworld ; and could only accomplish its purpose by the ~effectual working of the Divine Spirit in the hearts and , consciences of men, turning them from darkness into light,and from the power of Satan unto God. Moreover, • such an institutiou was, from its very nature, sure to -excite hatred and persecution,wherever it found its way and was seen to yield the peaceable fruits of righteous- meas. If they persecuted me, they will persecute you also,-said Jesus to his followers ; and after an experience of forty years Pael was constrained to record his convic- tion that he that will live godly in this present world =lust suffer persecution. Of course, a spiritual, unworldly church of this kind -would, find little or no favour with people who seem to have their portion in this life, and could never provide places and endowments for right reverend and most :reverend,Lcrd Bishops. But ecclesiastics have a keen eye for the present as well ao for the future, and an ,ardent desire to make the best of both worlds, if at all .possible. And being men of learning, and mighty in the scriptures and other ancient lore they have set up an in- stitutienwhich they call " the,eiaurch," which suits their purpose admirably. They are, of course, too loyal to Jesus to repudiate his headship altogether, but with a -fine sense of expediency they haveput him into the back- ground. Ever since the days of that potentate of in- -famous memory, Henry the Eighth, who threw off allegiance to Rome and set himsa up as Tope, the Kings and queens of this country have posed as heads of the church and defenders of the the 'faith! The reverend fathers are amongst the warmest and most energetic supporters of -these pretensions, and gladly make solemn ,oaths offering the sovereign's supremacy in all matters ,civil and eceiesiastlcal in this realm—although the master whom they profess to follow has commanded them to swear not at all! Having thus set up their head, no matter what character may be, the good bishops pray for him daily., and several times on Sundays, as a" most religious and gracious majesty " ! (The value of these devotions may be -roughly estimated by the revelations of the recent gambliag scandal at 'Tranby Croft.) And again, when the royal armies go forth to plunder and destroy people ,who have Eever injured them, and whose faces they have never seen' the reverend peace- . . makers conveniently forget their Lord's injunction to love their enemies, and do good to them that hate them, and insult the Divine Majesty by invoking His blessing upon men whose occupation is to rob and murder His own creatures! But worse still. When the carnage is - over, when tens of thousands of brave men have been cruelly slaufhtered, other thousands wounded and maimed for life, and multitudes of widows and orphans added to the pauper roll, these reverend apostles of the Prince of Peace set their bells a ringing, and chant "Te Dennis" for a glorious victory! But awful and blasphemous as all this is, it has its uses for', Church and State." The pride and ambition jf Ccps,ar Rye, much gratified by the proceedings, and his

faithful henchmen, the grand titles, high se• • tishoPs, have their reward. in assembly as sprs' . egos, and seats in the Legislative ever, are one ..cual Peers of the Realm! These, how- church • a portion of the blessings of the bishops' • aze— The institution which Jesus founded has, in all ,se, been a poor and despised "little flock" composed of the poor of this world, rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom which is yet to come. But the church of the reverend fathers is a different thing altogether. It em- braces kings, princes, warriors great and small, titled landowners, and others who live in idleness and luxury on the toil and suffering of the labouring classes. Nor are the poor altogether excluded. Actuated by a pious zeal for the principle that God is no respecter of persons, ' the fathers admit some of the humble classes to their sanctuaries where they occupy back seats, wondering at, but not understanding, the high-sounding phrases and fine music of "the service." Once mere: " Strait is the gate, and narrow is the way which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it," said Jesus to His followers. But the reverend fathers have improved upon this by a wider gate and broader way of their own invention. By the process known as infant baptism they can manufacture Christians by thousands, and when these man-made disciples die, re- gardless of what their lives may have been, "the Church" generously buries them in sure and certain hope of a glorious resurrection to eternal life ! In a free and easy establishment like this persecution for Jesus' sake is, of course, out of the question: because, outside the doors of the tabernacle, the men of "the Church" and the men of the world are so much alike, that it requires very tlete observation indeed to detect any difference bet Ween them. And my reader must not blush for shame or allow angry feelings to arise when I tell them that this magnificient establishment, this gilded caricature of the Church of Jesus of Nazareth only costs the British people about eight millions of money per annum I What a paltry charge for such splendid results! And *hat a pleasing contrast to the purseless, scripless condition of primitive Chris- tianity! 8. Readers of the New Testament are familiar with the simple and laboriouslife of Jesus as a niinister of his owngospel. Poor and friendless in a worldly sense, dressed in the garb of a Jewish peasant, without patron- age or pay from the Roman Procurator who then ruled in Jerusalem, and hated and persecuted by the religious teachers of his own people, he went forth on his great mission as the Saviour of the world. Truly, this seemed a strange and unpromising beginning, for such a wonder- ful enterprise ; but God's ways are not men's waNs,nor his thoughts like their thoughts. 'The scene of his laiours was Galilee, then the most important region in Palestine, containing, according to Josephus, more than t'wo hundred towns and cities, many of them teeming with inhabitants. Travelling on foot, and under every con- dition of :weather, he visited all these pnpulous centres, preaching in the synagogues, in the streets, by the sea s'aore, and on the mountain sides; and healing all man- tier of sickness and disease among the people who 'crowded around. Can we weeder then that he was i often footsore, weary, and hungry, and glad to embrace the hospitality of the humblest of Flislollowers. And in all this toil, and in all these privations, there was no ap- peal for tithes and endowments, and no collection boxes were passed round on His behalf. He who was meek and lowly in heart was quite content to receive his daily bread trent the people who., although poor themselves, gladly ministered to his wants. The modern invention of clerical holidays was unknown to Jesus. He was in earnest about his work, and ha'cl no time to waste in pleasant trips to distant regions for rest and change of air while thousands were perishing around him for lack ,of that salvation which he alone could give. His rest I and refresinne:a were foran-d at nights on the silent hills of ;.G-alilee, while his own-stars were looking down upon him as tee communed with his Heavenly Father. And this laborious, this wondeffel teacher, had no palace, no fixed dwelling place 'el any kind. To use His own pathetic language, "The foxes had holes, and the birds of the -air had nests; but the *Son of Man had not where to lay his head." I feel almost ashamed'to present the reverend fathers in contrast with sucharAife and ministry as this. Men of the world, politiciens as well as priests, dwelling in palaces, and enjoying -salaries ranging from £15,000 to £O,BOO per aenum, they are very far removed indeed from the social position which their Lord and Master was pleased to occupy. And what shall I say of the 7dbours of these reverend fathers, who have liveried servants to welt upon them, secretaries to manage their affairs, and chaplains to perform their devotions? That they do not live absolutely idle lives I freely admit. They cOnsecrate churches, ordain priests,confirm the man-made disciples, and now and then read a sermon for raising funds in aid of "The Church." But of in season and out of season labour after the pattern of Jesus they have no record at all. In the highways and byeway3 and great 'centres of population, their voices are never heard bat- tling with sin and sorrow. In fact, the " common people" know them not, and only get a glimpse of them occasionally as they roll past in their carriages. And yet these lordly'shephercls need rest and change of air for the benefit of Weis health! Hence we find them ,enjoying themselves at garden parties and other amusements of the aristocracy, and leaving their flocks for months at a time to the mercy of wolves in sheep's clothing, while they recruit their wasted energies in fashionable resorts at home and abroad! To sum up in a sentence, my solemn, deep, conviction is, that modern Christianity is disfigured and discredited by these arch-priests of the State. In conclusion, I thank you, Mr. Editor, for the space you have kindly given me, and hope at no distant date to send you something more for "The Examiner."—Yours 'aithf ully, lONA.

div.head: WEDDING AT L YAM.
div.p: WEDDING AT L YAM.

On Wednesday afternoon the wedding of Miss Mary Astall, daughter of Mr. Jehu Astall, Booth's- lane, to Mr. P. Clare, took place at St. Mary's Church, L)in.m. The Rev. G. W. Guest officiated. The bride who was given away by her brother, Mr. W. Astall, was dressed in fawn-coloured material, and carried a beautiful bouquet of tea-roses and ferns. The bridesmaids were Miss Edith Burrows and Miss Edith Clare (sister of the bridegroom), who were dressed in grey beige, and carried bouquets of glorie de dijen roses and ferns. There was a large collection of valuable and useful presents, amongst which was a beautiful clock, in glass case, the gift of the choir and Sunday school teachers of the Par- ish Church, the bridegroom having been for several years a chorister, and Miss Astall being a Sunday school teacher. The happy pair went during the afternoon, amid the good wishes of many friends,to Llandudno, to spend the honeymoon. Mr. Lawley, of the Plough Hotel, supplied the carriages.

MARRIAGE OF MR. PA.R.N.ELL AND MRS. O'SHEA. it is stated that Mr. Parnell and Mrs. O'Shea were married at Steyning, near Brighton, on Thursday morn- ing, the ceremony being a very quiet affair., only the necessary officials and witnesses being prcsent. It is understood they afterwards left for London, thence to proceed to Paris to spend the honeymoon. The local registrar, it is said, received no notice of tile intended marriage until Tuesday last, Mr. Parnell being described as a bachelor and a member of Parliament, and Mrs. O'Shea as a spinster, the recently-divorced wife of Captain O'Shea. It is understood that the two wit- nesses arrived at Steyning and returned to Trighton by train, while Mr. Parnell and Mrs. O'Shea drove by road. The wedding took place between nine and ten o'clock. A second ceremony is to take place in a London church. THE WEDDING SUPPER PARTY. Late on Thursday night Mrs. Parnell (late O'Shea) made the following communication from 9, Walsingham- terrace:—" Mr. Parnell was married to Mrs. O'Shea this morning at nine o'clock, at Steyning, in the presence of the registrar of the district. The marriage will be solemnised later on at a London church, there • ha,ving been some difficulties in obtaining a ,license for the purpose. After the marriage Mr. and Mrs. Parnell drove direct to ft, Walsingham-terrace, Brighton. They remained there during the day, active prepara- tion being • made for a supper party, which was held in the evening, but to which only a few personal friends were invited. Doubts were entertained as tb whether the parties could be married at Steyning,having strict regard to the law. These are set at rest by the following explanation :—Mr. Spearing is registrar of Aldrington parish. Aldrington is in the Steyning Union, and 9, Walsingharn-terrace, is situated in the parish of Aldrington, and although in the King's-road, is outside the Parliamentary, municipal, and parochial boundaries of Brighton. Mr. and Mrs. Parnell are still at Walsing- ham-terrace. INTERVIEW WITH MRS. PARNELL. A press representative called at 9, Walsingham terrace, yesterday morcing. but Mr. Parnell declined to see anyone. Mrs. Parnell, however, stated that there were no facts to be added to the reports already circu- lated and published. Their plans are not yet decided upon, but for the present they will reside in Brighton, and they intend to snake they house at Walsingham- terrace their principal abode. They expect to stay there until Parliament is prorogued. Mr. Parnell will continue to attend the House of Commons during the remainder of the session.

Dr. Macrorie, bishop of Natal, has announced his resignation of the see. The foundation-stone of the Church House, which is to occupy a site near Westminster .Abbey, was laid on Wednesday afternoon by the Duke of Connaught. The inflow of Irish harvestmen has set in, and already between two and three thousand have passed through Holyhead. The Railway Rates Cm:omittee on Wednesday decided against a clause embodying the agreement for special rates come to between the London and North-Western Railway and th 3 South Lancashire traders. At Batonya, in Hungary, some labourers incited by Socialists, made an attack on the Town ; and the gendarmes, being called to quell the disturbance, fired on the rioters, killing three of them, and wounding eight others.

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SAT URDA , J UNE 27, 1891,,
WALKING DAY IN WARRING-

TON. Walking Day this year, which was observed yesterday, was celebrated with considerable teat, being happily favoured, unlike its predecessor of last year, with delightful weather. The elementsry conditions which had prevailed on Wednesday night and during Thursday had not been calculated to inspire any very great corifidence in the breasts of the thousands ck! juveniles anticipating their annual treat. The iidvent, therefore, of yester- day morning with some promise of a fine day, and the agtisequent ablin.dant fulfilment of the promise, was to them an occasion for considerable rejoicing, while the bright sunshine which streamed down upon them as they promen- aded through the streets made the display all the more imposing. The children connected with the various churches, as also the Nonconformist schools, assembled at their respective schools at an early hour of the morning, and from there° those schools taking part in the general praces- sion, proceeded to its starting point, that part of the park in front of the Town Hall. The Non- comformist and. Catholic children had independent proNSSiott° through the principal streets, prio- , to their departure for the different ply Of recreation selected for them, or betook • ./-- 7. selves direct to railway stations, whence ti-,,_:.,,,,,.e conveyed to their destinations. The ore cession from the park was as followP , z—Brine Coat School and band. Ladies' School of T _., .auustry. Work- house School, Parish Church Se' . ..dool and band. St. 4c Anne's School. St. Barnabas ,hool mid band. St. Po.uls's School and band, St.. Paula's mission School. Holy Trinity. St. Mary's, and Factory Yard Mission Schools,in connection with Holy Trinity. St. Peters's . School and band. Atnmanuel. (Reformed', Church. \ The Ragged Sch aol and its drum and fife band, and ._ _ .
r last the7 S—alvationist School and band. The mar- shals of the. procession. were Messrs. A. Woods'

Dewhurst, tnd-J. P. Leigh. The route of the procession, which started about ten o'clock, was from the park through the west- gate, through Sankey-st., Arpley-st., Wilson-Patten at., past Arpley Station, Bridge-it., Buttermarket- st., Church-st., to the Parish Church, where service was held, commencing soon after eleven o'clock. The sight which was presented as the procession- ists were marshalled on tplie green sward in front of the Town Hall, and then conducted through the streets, with flags, banners, and bannerets; high in air, there being manifold pleasing contrasts of colourin.the dress of the members, the banners, and the uniforms of the various bands, was of a most picturesque character. The animated strains of the various bands brougl,t together in the park, and the bright sunshine and stirring music, combined to produce a most inspiriting effect both on the public and those who took part in the proceedings. Among the spectators in the park we observed the Mayor, and a number of other magnates of the town. What might be described as a perfect forest ot banners were borne by the pro- cessionists, some of these being exceedingly beautiful, and many of them captivating the attention by their splendid pictorial representations, pleasing devices, and piously appropriate mottoes. The Salvationists in their striking uniforms added much to the picturesqueness of the procession. The Nonconformist and • Roman Catholic processions presented many picturesque features. Many of the little girls who joined in the procession of St. Alban's Catholic School were beautifully attired in white dresses and white veils, and wore wreaths of white flowers on their heads. Others wore red sashes in token of their membership of the Guild of the Sacred Heart, and others again blue ribbons and medals as members of the Guild of the Children of Mary; while a number of the boys wore red badges as showing their connection with the Guild of the Sacred Heart. The day was observed as a general 'holiday throughout the town and the principal thoroughfares were gay with bunting hung out from tradesmen's windows and across the street, while along the route the upper windows both of private house and business premises were crowded with persons desirous of viewing the pro- cession from such advantageous altitudes. The streets had, to some extent, a fair-like aspect, for itinerant vendors of various comestibles and ;toys utilised the occasion, and having no competition to fear from the shops, easily conjured the children's surplus cash from their pockets. The Parish Church, during the service, was crowded, chiefly with chit- dren who entered heartily into the singing of the hymns selected for the occasion,led by the surpliced choir, Mr. W. S. Woods presiding at the organ. The Rev. F. W. Willis, the rector, read the first lesson and also the prayers, and a simple but effec- tive address was delivered to the children by the Rev. T. J. Madden, vicar of St. Luke's, Liverpool, whose address was practically an acrostic on the word scholar (Sunday school scholar). He the rev. gentleman took the first letter of the word as representing scholar (the Sunday scholar) and the remaining letters as standing for Christian, happy, obedient, loving, attentive, and retentive (in memory). Mr. Madden addressed the children quite colloquially, and catechised them upon his address, when they showed by their ready answers that they appreciated the meaning of his acrostic. The service was concluded with the benediction, and then the children dispersed, to betake them- selves to their various places of resort for the re- mainder of the day. SCHOOL REPORTS. Appended are details of the Schools and their pro- ceedings : BLUE COAT SCHOOL.—Number of scholars on books, 30 boys; 27 girls, average attendance, 30 boys; 27 girls ; number of teachers, 3 : number of books in library, 400; superintendents. Mr. E. Rose, governor; Mrs. Rose. matron. As usual the Blue Coat scholars with their own band, walked in the procession and attended service at the Parish Church.—They had dinner , at the school, and games,&c., in the school grounds. UNION Senoot.—Number of boys, 14; girls, 16; minister, Rev. H. V. Pigot ; master and matron, Mr. and Mrs. C. H. Ward. The children assembled in the park at 9.30, joined the procession, and attended the church. After dinner, they had games' &c., in the field. Tea was provided in the garden in front of the house, and there was a distribution of apples, nuts, oranges, and sweets, kindly given them by the Guardians. PADOATE INDUSTRIAL SCHOOL.—Number of scholars on books, 81 boys; 69 girls; average attendance, 81 boys; 69 girls; number of teachers, two male; one female; number of books in Library 73; minister, Rev. J. J. Longhorn; superintendent, Mr. H. M. Mines. The children came from Padgate by the 8-30 a.m. train to Warrington, joined the procession in the Park, and at- tenied the Parish Church. After service each child received a bun and some milk before marching home. The afternoon was spent in games and sports in Mr. Houghton's field at Woolston, and tea was there par- taken of. The school band was in attendance, under the conductorship of Mr. H. M. Mines. Nuts and oranges were distributed to the children, who returned home at nine o'clock. PARISH CHURCH BOYS SUNDAY SCHOOL—number of teachors. males 15, females 4 ; number of scholars in books, 240; average aetandance, morning 150, afternoon 180 ; young -men's Bible class, number on book 130, average attendance 60, number in procession 370. Ministers, the Rev, F. W. Willis (rector), D. S. Hodgson, F. C. Timing, and T. W. Cook. Superintendent. the Rev. T. W. Cook, and Messrs. James Scotson and 8. Davies. The principal feature in this school was the attendance in procession of the young men's Bible class. This school with the Mount girls and Mission schools assembled in St. Elphin's park in the afternoon when dancing, racing, and various games were kept up till eight o'clock. The various schools partaking of tea in their respective places of meeting. They had with them Lymm Nuited Band. BANK-ST. MISSION SCHOOL—Number of scholars on books, 90 boys •-, 110 girls; number of teachers, 3 ma!e ; 14 female; ministers, the Parish Church clergy ; superin- tendent, the Rev. D. S. Hodgson. After the procession the children attended service at church ; subsequently they had tea in the Mission Room; and later they were taken to St. Elvhin's field, where with the other Parish Church scholars, they indulged in the customary diver- sion. HOLY TRINITY CHURCH SCHOOL—Minister, the Rev. E. C. E.Carleton ; superintendent, Mr. H. G.Johnston ; number of scholars on books, about 300; number of teachers, 25 ; number of books in the library, 150. The children took part in the procession from the Park, and were-accompanied by. 'St. John's band (Walton). They were conveyed after service at the Parish Church, to Frodsliam. ST. PAUL'S CHURCH AND ALL SAINT'S MISSION SUNDAY SCHOOLS.—Number of scholars on books, 410 boys; 600 girls; number of teachers, 14 male; 30 female; Minister, the Rcv. H. V. Pigot ; Superintendents, J. Lawless, A. J. Jolley. and P. Sudlovv. The children joined in proces- sion, accompanied by the St. Paul's Sunday School Band. Subsequently they were taken to a field near St. James's Church, where they diverted themselves after the usual hearty juvenile fashion. ST. BARNABAS' Sciroor,.—Minister, the Rev. G. Allton; number of scholars on the books 350; number of teachers, 22. The scholars joined in the procession, accompanied by Fletcher's band, and after attending servi-te at the Parish Church adjoursed to a field adjoining the school, where they made themselves happy with sports and games of various descriptions until the shades of even- ing necessitated their return home, ST. JAMES'S SUNDAY SCHOOL.—Number of scholars on books, 183 boys ;167 girls; average attendance 125 boys; 115 girls; number of teachers 14 (female) ; Minister, Rev. F. Slater M.A. ; Superintendent, J. W. Tauranac. The schola,m, with the Lymm Volunteer Band, walked

COCKHEDGE MISSION -SCHOOL.—Minister. Rev. R. Davies; superintendents, Mr. J. Plinston, Mr. T. W. Malkin, number of scholars on books, 475 ; average attendance. 304; number of teachers, 10 male anci 11 female. The scholars after their procession, accom- panied by the Cockliedge Mission band, were taken to a field belonging to Mr. Bennett, at Padgate, and enter- tained with dinner and tea, and the usual intervening recreations.

BOLD-ST. WESLEYAN.—Number of scholars on books. 266 boys; 262 girls; average attendance, UT boys'; 218 girls ; number of teachers, 29 male; 27 female; nember of books in the library, 430; Ministers, the Revs. J. Gunnell, A. Freeman, and T. Ross; Superintendent, W. W. Silcock. The scholars assembled in the school- room at nine a.m., then, proceeded along Sankey-st.. and Parker-st.. to the Bank Quay, thence by the 10.15 train to Daresbury, then repaired to Mr. S. Done'a field at Keckwick, where they spent the day in games of various kinds, returning from Daresbury at about 8 p.m. SILVER-ST. WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL—Superinten- dent : Mr. W. Johnson ; number of scholars on books, 256 boys; 178 girls ; morning average attendance, 87 boys; 69 girls; afternoon, 154 boys ; 122 girls'; number of teachers, 19 male ; 15 female ; number of books in library, 400 ; Ministers: Revs. A. Freeman and T. Ross. The children left Silver-st. School, accompanied by the school band, about 9.15, walked along Winwick-street, Horsemarket-st., Bridge-st., Rylands-st., Suez-st.. (Bold- st. School and Cairo-st. School joining here), Bold-street, Sankey-st., and Parker-st.,to Ratak Quay Station. They then left by special train at 10.5 for Elelsby, where they disported themselves in a field at Rose Farm. Dinner and tea were provided for the children and friends at the farmhouse. FRIARS' GREEN SUNDAY SCHOOL—Number of scholars on books, 170; number of teachers, 13.; number of books in library, 240; superintendent, Mr. A. Jolley. The scholars assembled at Friars Green Chapel, Cairo-st., at nine o'clock. After marching round the town in con- junction with the Brick-st. school they were taken with them to a field at Padgate lent by Mr. Bennett of Bruche Hall Dinner and tea were provided for them, and the band accompanying them played selection at intervals and various sports were engaged in. At nine p.m. the children were regaled With nuts, after which they were conveyed home, the younger ones on lurries. BRICK-ST. SUNDAY SCHOOL—Number of scholars on books, 195 boys; 232 girls; average attendance, 130 boys; 155 girls ; number of teachers, 13 male; 14 female; number of books in library, 200: superintendents Messrs. J. Shaw. and J. G. Critchley. The Brick-st. and Friars'- Green Schools combined accompanied by a brass band, started from Friars'-Green Chapel at 9 o'clock, and after traversing most of the principal thorough fares,proceeded to the Brick-st. Sunday School. The scholars-were sub- sequently conveyed by lurries to a field at Orford, where they had dinner and tea, and amused themselves with cricket, football, skipping rope, swings, &c., selections from the band being played. PRIMITIVE METHODIST SUNDAY SCHOOL. LEG-ST.-- Number of scholars on books, 'l3B boys; 123 girls ; num- ber of teachers 16 male; 12 female'; number of books in library, 180 ; minister, the Rev. W. Graham ; superin- tendents,' Messrs. .1. B. !lore, J. Titchett. and W. G. Ward. The scholars, headed by the school brass band. and under the leadership of Messrs.J. Podmore and T. Miller, joined in the general precession, and proceeded through the principal streets,then to a field in Folly-lane, kindly lent by Mr. John Williams, Folly Farm, where they were supplied with dinner and tea, consisting of milk. tea, Melton Mowbray pies, scones, sugar bens, &c. They also diverted themselves with cricket. football, racing for toys, rounders &c. They remained in the field until about nine p.m., then returned to the school,where each scholar received (as a parting present) sweetmeats. &c. ACADEMY-STREET Messme.—Superintendents : Mr. W. Miller and Mr. Nathan Cook. Number of scholars on books. 74 boys; 95 girls'; number of teachers, 15 male ; 7 female. The children marched in procession through the principal streets of the town, headed be the Friars Green Brass Band, then went to a field in Marsh House-lane, for dinner and tea. A refreshment stand was erected in the field for the convenience of friends wishire, to spend the day with the children, Mr. Thorn- ton and Miss 0. Cook nreSiding. The day was spent in race-running for useful articles, and in cricket and foot- ball, the two last-named being the chief sports. METHODIST FREE CHURCH. BUCKLEY-ST.—NUMber of scholars on books 150 boys; 100 girls; average attend- ance 100 boys; 70 girls; number of teachers 7 male; 6 female. Superintendents. Mr. H. Woolley and Mr. J. J. Fairhurst. The scholars, teachers, and friends met at the school at 9 30,and, accompanied by Buckley-st. brass band, formed in procession and passed through the prin- cipal streets of the town and then to the market, where they sang several hymns, then returning to the. school. There they partook of a substantial dinner, consisting of meat pies, ham and beef sandwiches, &c. They after- wards proceeded to Messrs. Pearson and Knowles's cricket field, Lovely-lane, and enjoyed themselves . various games, such RS cricket, football, sack racing, &c. They' returned to the school for tea, consisting of ham and beef sandwiches, pies, buns, &c. Wonxneo-BEEN's Misseme.—Number of scholars on books, 308 boys; 302 girls average attendance. 242 boys ; 238 girls; number of teachers, 24 male; 11 fe- males; president. Mr. Joseph Monks; superintendents, Mr. T. Dale, and Mr. T. Ashley. The children had a pro- cession and were afterwards taken to the grounds of Mr. J. Crosfield, Walton Lea, where they had tea and games, enjoying themselves heartily till nightfall. CAIRO-ST. SUNDAY SCHOOL—Number of scholars on h00k5,149 boys ; 137 girls ; average attendance 110 boys; 95 girls; number of teachers, 13 male"; 14 female; num- ber of books in library, 1,370; minister. the Rev. F. K. Freeston ; superintendent, Mr. John Chalmers. The scholars went by special train in the morning from Bank Quay Station to Helsby, where they had a day's diversion in a field placed at their disposal by Mr. Wright, farmer. At intervals they had racing for prizes, and they dis- ported themselves in the hilarious juvenile fashion. They returned in the evening at 8 30. WARRINGTON RAGGEn SUNDAY SCHOOL.—Superinten- dents, James Skelland, John Owen'; secretary, Edmund Osborne, Fred Atkinson; treasurer, Thomas Welsby ; number a scholars on books, 140 boys; 160 girls; aver- acie attendance, 200; number of teachers, 10 male; 10 female.
