LADS' "LARKS," FORTY YEAR SIN'.
When aw wur a yungster, aw uset to play Some comical "Larks" welly every day, Such ez turnin' a dapple-breawn horse to grey, Wi' whitewash !
Aw've pured mony a Parson's dur wi' my clogs, An'—aw'm sorry to say it—aw've spangfued frogs; An' twitchelt sum h underts o' slancin' dogs,

Wi' tin kettles : A.w've clum iii' owd church steeple at dead O' neet, An' getten ith' belfry to strike a leet, Then gen hawve o'th' parish an awful freet, Wi' ringin' Aw've put aw thi place in a terrible funk, When they'll put up tiler shutters, an' "done a
_ bunk," Wi' nowt but just tieklin' a elephant's trunk, Wi' nettles !
Aw oncet playea a joke ez wtizrayther grim, On a greentio.rn a wanted to lam n to swim, Bi' teem' two bladders, for only a whim,
To his feet !
Wi' once't Mut 'a 'crow, wi' his wings spread eawt, Deawn an owd woman's chimbley, when hoo wur
abeawt, An' hoo rusht streyt th' lone,wi' a terrible sheawt The devil!

But times are aw changet, an' they'n gone to the bad, For. someheaw or other, the folk seem so glad fo keep a look-eawt till they'n collart a lad Forth' police! An'" Robert "keeps smilin' aw ovver his face, Thet he's getten, God bless him ! a gradely case For lodgin' an' grub in a Goverment place Caw'd th' Lock-up! Then a magistrate's fotched, an' he sez as its " cheek !" If yo speyk fer yeNer be it ever so meek, An' he tines yo "five shillin' an costs, or a week In Kirkda !" But oh ! for th' owd times, when booath welthy an' poor, Wad gie yo a welcome at every door; Tho' aw'm frickont they'n left us fer evermoor— Moor's th' pity. TIIM 0' PEGS.
Warriton, 25 June, 1891. VOLUNTEER ENCAMPMENT AT
BLACKPOOL.

On Saturday afternoon the Warrington Volunteer (Ist Volunteer Battalion, South Lancashire Regi- ment) took their departure amidst delightful weather and in high spirits, for Blackpool, to re- main under canvas in that picturesque and pleasant watering place until to-day. They assembled in front of the Drill Flail about four o'clock, and soon after started to catch a special train leaving War- rington at half-past four. The appearance ot the men was all that could be desired, and many were the complimentary remarks passed upon their mili- tary aspect and deportment, as they tiled through the streets, the observed of thousands of observers. The battalion comprises six companies hem War- rington and one from Newton, and its strength is about 530, and it is not unlikely that the favour- able weather which has prevailed during the early part of the week, has drawn almost the whole of that number to Blackpool, to enjoy the com- bined happiness of marine and martial' de- lights. The ground selected for the camp is a field situated at South Shore, which is within comfortable walking distance of Black- pool, and about a hundred yards from the sea. It lies between the Preston and IVyre railway and the highway from Blackpool to Lytham. The Volunteer's reached their destination about half- past six, and found that all preparations had been made for their reception by an industrious fatigue party sent some days in advance to convert the usually pastoral scene into one partaking of the characteristics of suggestively realistic though peaceful militarism. The officers in camp are— Colonel Greenall, commanding officer; Lieutenant-Col. Bolton, Captains Widdows, Gooch, Buckton, Baines, and Hogarth ; Lieutenants Smith, Edelsten, Appleton, Chorley, Fairclough, Barlow Captain and Adjutant Adam, Quarter-Master Hutchinson, and Surgeon Adams.—On Sunday morning divine service was celebrated in the midst of the tented field by the Rev. F. W. Willis, M.A., rector of Warrington, acting chaplain, of the battalion.; and through the charming weather which prevailed the congregation was augmented by a large accession of visitors from Blackpool. It happens that a considetable number of men belonging to the 2nd Derbyshire Regi- ment have their encampment at Blackpool, and as the Volunteers are to be seen with them thronging the pro- menade and the streets, the inhabitants arc experiencing something like the feeling of living in a military centre. The catering arrangments for the Volunteers, for which Mr. Higham, of Warrington, is responsible are such that despite the appetizing influence of the sea air, the demands of the inner man are amply met. For break- fast there is tea or coffee, at choice, with a substantial accompaniment of bread and butter and corned beef; for dinner, mutton or beef and potatoes. with beer and ginger beer are provided ; and for tea, the usual refersh- ing decoction with bread and butter, marmalade, and other preserves. The men commenced their camp drill- ing on Monday morning,when the battalion was paraded and had to perform evolutions throughout most Dart of the aay, with intervals for meals. The battalion may in- deed be congratulated alike on military, on aesthetic, and on hygienic grounds on their armed picnic. —we use this phrase in no spirit of detraction, but as broadly descriptive of a happy combination of business and pleasure—being held in such a delectable quarter. The field which their presence has converted into a mili- tary hamlet has been visited by large numbers of per- sons, among whom have been not a7few of the soldiers of the line, curious to see what sort of approximation to martial discipline the unpaid soldiery can show. Of this we are assured that the pleasurable encampment by the sea near Blackpool,will long remain in the minds of those who took part in it, conjured up as it will be by a host of novel associations. THE INSPECTION YESTERDAY.

Fortunately. in spite of ominous threatening meteorologically, the weather yesterday kept dry, though oppressively hot. The men assembled at 10.45, and a quarter of an hour later the inspection commenced. The Inspecting Officer was Colonel A. C. Twentyman, C.B. There were VI officers on parade, including Colonel Greenall, Quartermaster Hutchinson, Surgeon-major Lister, Surgeon 'Adams, Cap- tain and Adjutant Adam, Captain Buckton, Captain Ridgway, Capt. Baynes, Capt. Hogarth. Captain Gooch; Capt. Widdows ; Lieuts. Appleton, Smith, Edlestone, Lieutenant Fairclough, Lieutenant Chorley, and Lieu- tenant Barlow (second lieut.) The total was :-393 rank and file, of which 17 are officers, 23 sergeants ; on duty, sick, Sze., 6 sergeants, and 46 rank and file; absent with leave, 4 officers, 3 sergeants, 16 rank and file, total, •23. Absent without leave 34. The total enrolled strength is 502. The usual " routine" was gone through in the inspec- tion. After the inspection Colonel Twentyman ad- dressed the men, complimenting them highly on the way in which they had acquitted themselves, He remarked that he would certainly be able to speak favourably of what he had seen. Some guides, he said, did not keep their distances properly. Pioneer-Sergeant Warburton ha 4 had charge of the catering both in the canteen and Sergeants' mess ; and the men speak highly of the manner in which he has carried out his duties. The men return to Warrington to-day (Saturday.)

div.p: CROFT.

FUNERAL OF MRS. WILSON.—The remains of Mrs. Ellen Wilson, of Croft, who died on Friday, after a few days' illness from influenza, took place on Monday. The de- ceased was formerly a Sunday School teacher and mem- ber of the choir of the Unitarian Chapel, Croft. The officiating minister at the funeral was the Rev P. Holt,of Astley. UNITARIAN CHAPEL.—The annual sermons in aid of the Sunday School in connection with the Unitarian Chapel, Lady-lane, were preached on Sunday afternoon and evening, by the Rev. V. D. Davies, 8.A., of Toxteth An- cient Chapel, Liverpool. There was a large congrega- tion at each service. The ledges of the windows were tastefully decorated with ferns and flowers. A portion of the choir of Cairo-st. Chapel, Warrington, led the singing of the hymns and canticles (in which the con- gregation heartily joined). Anthems were also given, namely, "Praise the Lord, for He is gracious," and "The Lord is loving unto every man." Mr. Gray was at the organ. The collections amounted to £ll 16s. 6d., being a few pounds less than last year. Tea was pro- vided for friends from a distance in the schoolroom and under Mr. T. Welsby's bay shed (the schoolroom being too small to accommodate all). A large number of friends from Warrington attended the services. The , organist, choir, and their worthy conductor or Cairast. Chapel, deserve praise for their services,

YESTERDAYS CRICKET. Marylebone beat Oxford University by eight wickets ; Kent beat Middlesex by 34 runs. CAPTAIN VERNEY AGAIN. Last night's Gazette noti fies that Captain Verney's name has been removed from the list of deputy-lieutenants of Buckinghamshire. DESTRUCTIVE FIRE AT LEHI! :—A FIREMAN KILLED. A fire broke out at midnight at Messrs. Atkin and Wright's, wholesale provision merchants, Leith. The premises are four storeys high, and the flames were first seen in the upper flat. The damage amounts to £25,000. During the fire a gable roof fell on a fireman named Peter Duff, killing him on the spot. Another man,named George Henderson, who was buried in the debris, was rescued after an hour's work. MR. GLADSTONE'S BEALTIL—VISIT TO LO NESTOFT. A London correspondent writes —Mr. Gladstone's friends are seriously alarmed, all reports to the contrary notwithstanding. The right hon. gentleman made too free with himself after his attack of influenza, and the inevitable relapse has followed. I hear that Sir Andrew Clarke for the first time expresses alarm, and insists up- on cessation from all work. Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone arrived at Lowestoft, last evening, on a visit to Mr. Colman, M.P. Mr. Glad- stone's health has much improved. PRESENTATION TO THE PRINCESS LOUISE. THE LAUREATE'S WISH. Yesterday afternoon, at Buckingham-palace, repre- sentatives of the matrons, sisters, and nurses of the United Kingdom presented Princess Louise of Schleswig Holstein with a diamond crescent and a set of the Poet Laureate's poem as wedding gifts. Lord Tennyson has written those lines in the first volume of his works "Take lady, who your loyal nurses give Their full God bless, you with this book of song; And may the life which heart in heart you live With him you love be cloudless and be long."
THE DISASTROUS STORM IN lOWA. GREAT LOSS OF LIFE. A HUNDRED HOUSES WRECKED.

NEW YORE, THURSDAY EYENING.—Later reports of the storm in North-West lowa indicate that the results were even more disastrous than at first supposed. At Cherokee one hundred houses were wrecked and some thousand persons rendered homeless. The number of people reported drowned in the neighbourhood of Cor- rectinville is stated to be eight. Houses and barns are floating bodily down the swollen river past Cherokee and are supposed to have come from Sutherland. The damage done to railroads is most disastrous, and traffic is suspended, all the bridges over the Sioux River between Cherokee and Onawa having been destroyed.

YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMEN T. • HOUSE OF LORDS. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at aluarter past 4. Lord Tollemache took the oath and his seat in succes- sion. IRISH LAND BILL.—The adjourned debate on the Irish Land Bill was resumed ley Lord Camperdown. The Bill, he said, was very popular in Ireland, and showed that the Government did not desire simply to govern Ireland by coercion. He most cordially supported the measure. The EARL of KIMBERLY regretted the absence of Earl Spencer; he gave the Bill a general but modified support. Lord Herschell approvel of the main object of the Bill, and congratulated the Government on trying to deal with the congested districts. The Earl of Derby sup- ported the Bill and believed very little risk of loss to the British taxpayers was run. Lord Salisbury believed the 'Bill would prove effective. The Bill was read a second time. The House adjourned at 7.30 p.m. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The House met at three o'clock. GAMBLING IN THE ARMY.—Answering Mr. Cobb, the Secretary of State declined to grant a return of all non- commissioned officers who, during the last three years have been punished for allowing gambling or card play- ing, or participating in it. He stated that the two instances mentioned by Mr. Cobb had not been reported to headquarters, and he did not see that any good object would be secured by granting the return asked for. THE MANIPUR PRlNCES.—Replying to Mr. Schwann, the UNDER SECRETARY for India said that the Govern- ment of India possessed Paramount power with reference to the sentences on the Manipur princes, and they would no doubt exercise it. After perusal of the necessary papers, under these circumstances, it would be unusual for the Viceroy to hear counsel on their behalf as requested. PUBLIC HEALTH BILL.—The House then proceeded to the consideration of the London Public Health Bill. A number of amendments were discussed and rejected.

TEE Cutracn BELLS.—The new bells for Lvmm Church tower are expected from Loughborough in a day or two. INFLuzsza.—Though not so prevalent as it was a short time ago, this malady is still afflicting many of the villagers, and supplying Nurse. Grey with a consider- able number of patients. With a continuance of the pre- sent congenial weather, however, it is expected that the complaint will soon be eradicated from the district. ANNIVERSARY SERVICES.—On Sunday at the Congrega- ' tional Chapel the anniversary sermons were held. Ser- mons were preached morning and evening by the Rev. David Walters, of Chorlton-cum-Hardy, collections being taken after each service in aid of the chapel fund. There were good attendances throughout the day. THE FUSTIAN CurrEas' SOCIETY.—At a meeting of the Lymm Branch of the Fustian Federation, held on Mon- day, 77 new members were enrolled. This brings the strength of the Lymm society up to 300 members. The co-operation of the different districts has had a most ' beneficial effect already on the prices paid to the hands in several of the workshops in Lymm. The price of the cutting of a piece has gone up from is. to 3s. WORK ON Tim Suiv CANAL.—The dragging at the mouth of the Boliln, where it intersects the Ship Canal and joins the Mersey, has since Monday been worked night and day. Several powerful lights are in use. The dragging is considerably interfered with by the great number of the trees that have during centuries been swept down by floods into the bed of the river. The work is, however, progressing as rapidly as was anticipated. SHARPLY CAtronT.—Two men named Philip and George Hallworth, colliers, from Hazel Grove, were apprehended at the Jolly Thresher, Lymm, by Police Constable Ennion, on 'Tuesday, on the charge of being concerned in an indecent assault on two females at Norbury on the 21st. The prisoners had relations at Broom Edge, and it occurred to the Stockport police that in fleeing from the scene of the misdemeanour they might make to those friends. The surmise was correct. The police saw them within an hour of their arrival. They were handed over to Police Constable Washington, of Stock- port, on Wednesday, and removed to that borough for magisterial proceedings. LIBERAL REOISTRATION AGENT.—At a meeting of the Liberal Registration Committee at Lymm, on Monday night, Mr. David Daniels, Booth's-lane, Lymm, was ap- pointed the Liberal registration Agent for Lymm Polling District, which includes Lymm,Hiell Legh, Warburton, and Thelwall, and Mr. William Skilling was appointed the hon. agent. Communications relat;ng to the interest of the Liberal party in registration should be addressed to Mr. Daniels, at the above address. All voters who have changed their residence during the year, or who have come into the district from other polling districts of the Altrincham Division, should communicate with Mr. Daniels at once. GOOD TEMPLARY.—mThe Tower of Refuge Lodge of Good Templars held a meeting in the Coffee Fa vern, Lymm, on Tuesday evening, Bro. D. Ellison in the chair. As therewas a surprise visit the business was rapidly gone through. Bro. C. and Sister M. Newman were received as members from Cardiff. Bro. J. W. Roberts, of the young 40th Lodge, Military District of Orford Barracks, Warrington, read "The Village Grog Shop," and also spoke on the temperance question. Bro. A. Mortimer, of the Temperance Mission Lodge, Warrington, and Bro. Kean gave eloquent and amusing speeches, and Bro. Tomlin read •' Gone with a Handsome Man." NOTICE IS HEREBY GlVEN,that the next GENERAL QUARTER SESSIONS of the Peace for the County of Chester will be holden at the CASTLE OF CHESTER, in and for the said County, on MONDAY, the 29th day of June instant, at Hail-past Eleven o'clock ,in the Forenoon when the Grand Jury will be empannelled. Tbe hearing of all Appeals arising within the Hundreds of Broxton, Eddisbury, Nantwich and Wirrall, forming the Chester District, and the trials of all prisoners com- mitted from such Hundreds, will take place at such Ses- sions. The Grand and Petty Jury for the Chester Dis- trict must be in attendance at the Castle of Chester, at the opening of Court on MONDAY, the 29th day of June instant, at Half-past Eleven o'clock in the Forenoon.
